 Installation 

If necessary, install the fan shroud on the radiator with the four 
bolts, for manual transaxle vehicles. For vehicles with an automatic 
transaxle, install the fan shroud with three fan shroud bolts.

 NOTE: When installing the radiator, ensure the radiator support upper 
brackets are fully engaged on the radiator and that the mounting pins, located 
on the lower tank of the radiator, are in their proper slots in the core 
support crossmember and that the two radiator mounting insulators (8125) are

Install the radiator and fan shroud as an assembly in the engine 
compartment.

[FIGURE: Q3987A.gif]

Position the radiator support upper brackets and install the four 
radiator support upper bracket bolts. 

[FIGURE: Q3985A.gif]

Tighten the four radiator support upper bracket bolts to 8-10 Nm
 (71-89 lb-in).

Connect the overflow hose. 

Install the lower radiator hose and slide the hose clamp (8287) in place.

[FIGURE: Q3984A.gif]

Connect the upper radiator hose. and slide the hose clamp in place.

[FIGURE: Q3980A.gif]

On vehicles with automatic transaxles, connect the oil cooler hoses 
onto the radiator. Install the cooler hose bracket and the lower bolt.

Close the radiator draincock (8115). 

Connect the engine cooling fan motor electrical connector. 

Position the wiring harness in the routing clamps on the fan shroud. 

Fill the cooling system to the specified level with the recommended 
antifreeze/water mixture. Refer to the procedure in this section. 

Install the radiator cap on the radiator filler neck. 

[FIGURE: Q3979A.gif]

Warm up the engine (6007) and check for leaks.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Radiator Tubes

 CAUTION: If a radiator tube leak repair is to be repaired within approximately 
20mm (3/4 inch) from a tank, do not attempt to solder the area. Soldering heat 
may damage the plastic tank. 

Treat leaks close to the tanks with self-leveling, single-component 
silicone such as Dow Corning 1200 Clear Prime Coat and Silastic 734 RTV or 
equivalents.

If the leak is far enough from the tanks, solder it in the usual manner. 

If the exact location of the leak cannot be pinpointed, treat a larger 
area to assure the effectiveness of the repair.

 Radiator Tank 

 NOTE: The radiator tanks are plastic, and, unlike the core fins, cannot be 
soldered.

Apply a thin coat of Dow Corning 1200 Clear Prime Coat or equivalent to 
the area of the leak.

Allow the prime coat to dry for 10 minutes at room temperature.

Apply a coat of undiluted Dow Corning Silastic 734 RTV or equivalent 
over the prime coat.

Allow the Silastic 734 RTV to dry for one hour at room temperature.

Retest for leaks and repair as necessary.

Use a suitable tool to repress the flanges in the area of the leak. 

Retest the radiator (8005) for leaks. 

If the flange leak persists, repair with Dow Corning 1200 Clear Prime

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Radiator Coolant Level Check 

When the coolant is cold, the coolant level in the radiator coolant 
recovery reservoir (8A080) should be between the LOW and FULL marks. If the 
coolant level is low, add coolant to the FULL mark.

[FIGURE: Q3976B.gif]

 Coolant Condition Check 

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES WHILE THE ENGINE 
IS RUNNING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THIS INSTRUCTION COULD RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AS WELL AS DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE. TO PREVENT SCALDING 
COOLANT OR STEAM FROM BLOWING OUT OF THE RADIATOR, USE EXTREME CARE WHEN 
REMOVING THE RADIATOR CAP. WAIT UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, WRAP A THICK 
CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP, AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK 
WHILE THE COOLING SYSTEM PRESSURE IS RELEASED. AFTER ALL OF THE PRESSURE HAS 
BEEN RELEASED, USING THE THICK CLOTH, PRESS DOWN ON THE RADIATOR CAP, TURN IT, 
AND THEN REMOVE IT. 

With the radiator cap (8100) off, examine the coolant in the upper 
tank. Draw a sample with a Rotunda Battery/Antifreeze Tester 014-R1060 or 
equivalent. Check for rust, dirt, or oil. Also check the freezing point. It 
should be approximately -37°C (-35°F) if the 
mixture has not been diluted by adding plain water. Dilution of the mixture 
below the recommended 50/50 concentration reduces the effectiveness of the 
corrosion inhibitors in the antifreeze formula. If the mixture is diluted but 
not rusty, discolored, or weak full protection may be restored by partially 
draining the system and adding 100% antifreeze coolant Ford Premium Cooling 
System Fluid E2FZ-19549-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESE-M97B44-A.

[FIGURE: Q2636A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System Hoses and Clamps

The most frequent cooling system concerns deal with overheating and 
leakage. To inspect for leaks at the hoses and hose clamps (8287) use the 
following procedure:

Key ON and engine (6007) running.

Run the engine until normal operating temperature is reached.

Key OFF.

 WARNING: THE RADIATOR COOLING FAN MAY ACTIVATE AT ANY TIME, KEEP HANDS AND TOOLS 
AWAY FROM THE FAN BLADE. 

Inspect all hoses and hose clamp connections for leaks. All leaking 
hoses and hose clamps must be replaced. Refer to the procedure in this section.

If no leaks are visible, or if all visible leaks have been repaired, 
perform a cooling system pressure test to verify there are no more cooling 
system leaks. Refer to the Cooling System Pressure Test diagnostic procedure 
in this section.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Draining, Filling and Bleeding

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES WHILE THE ENGINE 
IS RUNNING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THIS INSTRUCTION COULD RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AS WELL AS DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE. TO PREVENT SCALDING 
COOLANT OR STEAM FROM BLOWING OUT OF THE RADIATOR, USE EXTREME CARE WHEN 
REMOVING THE RADIATOR CAP. WAIT UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, WRAP A THICK 
CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP, AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK 
WHILE THE COOLING SYSTEM PRESSURE IS RELEASED. AFTER ALL OF THE PRESSURE HAS 
BEEN RELEASED, USING THE THICK CLOTH, PRESS DOWN ON THE RADIATOR CAP, TURN IT, 
AND THEN REMOVE IT. 

If coolant is discolored or dirty, or if inspection reveals hoses, 
gaskets, or other components requiring service or replacement, the coolant 
must be drained and discarded, or saved for reuse depending on its condition. 
Remove the radiator cap (8100), observing precautions as previously described 
if the system is hot and pressurized. Position a drain pan under the radiator 
(8005) and open the radiator draincock (8115) and drain the system. The system 
may be partially drained this way as required by a service procedure and then 
refilled and bled as described below.

Clean the cooling system by flushing with clear water. If it is 
excessively rusty or dirty, reverse-pressure flush or use an approved flushing 
system. Refer to the Flushing Procedures in this section. 

Refill the system with equal parts of water and antifreeze coolant 
meeting Ford specifications. Use E2FZ-19549-AA or equivalent meeting 
specification ESE-M97B44-A. Fill to the FULL mark on the radiator coolant 
recovery reservoir (8A080) and install the radiator cap only to the first stop 
(non-pressurizing). Start the engine (6007) and run at fast idle only until the 
upper radiator hose (8260) feels warm, indicating the water thermostat (8575) 
has opened.

Stop the engine. Check the coolant level in the radiator and add 
coolant mixture if required to restore the coolant level. Install and tighten 
the radiator cap on the radiator, and fill the radiator coolant recovery 
reservoir to the FULL mark.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Cleaning

 Cooling System Flush Procedure 

When replacing coolant because of excessive rust or dirt, the system 
should be power flushed to break up and remove deposits of sludge, rust, and 
foreign matter. 

 Radiator Installed 

If closed-circuit pressure flushing equipment is not available, the 
cooling system may be reverse-pressure flushed with plain water as follows: 

Drain the cooling system. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Remove the water thermostat (8575). Reinstall the water hose connection 
(8592) without the water thermostat. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Disconnect the radiator overflow hose from the radiator coolant 
recovery reservoir (8A080) and plug the end of the hose. 

Disconnect the heater water hoses (18472) from the heater core (18476) 
and plug or cap both nipple and hose. 

Disconnect the lower radiator hose (8286) from the radiator (8005) and 
position the hose to drain clear of the vehicle.

 CAUTION: Flushing water flow must be limited so that pressure inside the 
radiator does not exceed 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Connect a high-pressure hose to the radiator lower hose outlet. 
Back-flush the engine (6007) until clear water runs out of the lower radiator 
hose. Turn water on and off several times, pulsing the flow to help break 
loose sludge deposits.

When the water flowing out of the lower radiator hose is clear, unplug 
the radiator overflow hose. When water flows clear from the overflow hose, 
replug it. 

Disconnect the equipment used for the cooling system flush procedure. 
Before reconnecting the cooling system hoses, the heater loop must be 
back-flushed separately to remove sediment in the heater core. Refer to the 
procedure in this section.

Install the water thermostat in the water hose connection. Refer to the 
procedure in this section.

[FIGURE: Q3978A.gif]

 Radiator Removed 

If closed-circuit pressure flushing equipment is not available, the 
cooling system may be reverse-pressure flushed with plain water as follows: 

Remove the radiator. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Position the lower radiator hose to drain into a suitable container.

 CAUTION: Flushing water flow must be limited so that pressure inside the 
radiator does not exceed 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Connect a high-pressure water hose to the upper radiator hose (8260). 
Back-flush the engine until clear water runs out of the lower radiator hose. 
Turn the water on and off several times, pulsing the flow to help break loose 
sludge deposits.

Disconnect the equipment used for the flush procedure. Before 
installing the radiator, the heater loop must be back-flushed separately to 
remove sediment in the heater core. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Install the radiator. Refer to the procedure in this section.

 Heater Core Back-Flushing 

 NOTE: Back-flushing the heater core has to be a separate operation to get the 
required reverse coolant flow.

Disconnect the heater hot water tube (18B402) from the water inlet 
connection (8K528) and install and clamp a garden hose female end fitting to 
the heater hot water tube.

Remove the RH heater water hose from the lower intake manifold (9424). 
Position the hose to drain directly into a pan. Connect the water supply hose 
to the female fitting that was installed in step 1, and flush the heater core 
circuit until the drain water runs clear. Pulse the flow by turning the water 
on and off several times. Allow full flow for approximately five minutes. 

Shut off the flushing water supply and remove the adapters installed 
for the flushing operation. Reconnect all cooling system connections, 
tightening all hose clamps to 2.5-3.5 Nm (22-31 lb-in). 

Refill the cooling system with approved antifreeze coolant mixture. 
Refer to the coolant replacement procedure in this section. 

With the cooling system warmed up and pressurized, inspect all system 
connections for leaks and tighten as necessary.

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel System

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE OR CARRY LIGHTED TOBACCO OR OPEN FLAME OF ANY TYPE WHEN 
WORKING ON OR NEAR ANY FUEL-RELATED COMPONENT. HIGHLY FLAMMABLE MIXTURES ARE 
ALWAYS PRESENT AND MAY BE IGNITED, RESULTING IN POSSIBLE PERSONAL INJURY. 

The sequential multiport fuel injection (SFI) system is a multi-point, 
pulse fuel injection system. This system supplies the engine (6007) with the 
air/fuel mixture necessary for combustion. An air induction system and fuel 
injection system work with an electronic engine control system which consists 
of various sensors, switches, and a powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650). 
All sensors and switches are connected to the PCM, which interprets the data 
it receives and computes when and for what period of time the 
electrically-operated fuel injectors (9F593) are energized. 

The PCM increases, decreases, or cuts off fuel delivery to the fuel 
injectors based on engine demands and driving conditions. 

The fuel charging system consists of: 

Fuel pump (9350) 

Fuel filter (9155) 

Fuel injection supply manifold (9D280) 

Fuel pressure regulator (9C968) 

Fuel injectors 

Fuel pump relay (9345)

Fuel tank (9002) 

Inertia fuel shutoff switch (IFS switch) (9341)

When the ignition is ON, the powertrain control module relay (PCM 
relay) (12A646) turns on, providing power to the PCM, fuel pump relay, and the 
fuel injectors. Power to the fuel pump is supplied through the fuel pump 
relay. The IFS switch is a safety device used to shut off the fuel pump in the 
event of a collision. The IFS switch is connected between the fuel pump and the 
fuel pump relay. If the IFS switch is "tripped", it must be reset by 
depressing the button on top of the IFS switch. During engine cranking, the 
fuel pump circuit is completed by the PCM closing the contacts in the fuel 
pump relay, energizing the fuel pump .

The basic fuel requirement of the engine is determined from the data 
supplied to the PCM by the mass air flow sensor (MAF sensor) (12B579). The MAF 
sensor measures the amount of air being drawn into the engine. Other sensors 
and switches are used to measure: 

Air temperature 

Atmospheric pressure 

Coolant temperature 

Engine crankshaft and camshaft speeds 

Exhaust oxygen content 

An electric fuel pump is mounted in the fuel tank and supplies 
filtered, pressurized fuel to each fuel injector through the fuel injection 
supply manifold. Fuel is filtered by an in-line fuel filter. The fuel pressure 
is regulated by a fuel pressure regulator which is located at the return line 
side of the fuel injection supply manifold.

================================================================================
PAGE 2276
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Injection Timing

Fuel is metered and injected into the intake ports according to the 
fuel injector (9F593) signals received from the powertrain control module 
(PCM) (12A650). When these injection signals are applied to the coil of the 
fuel injector, the needle valve is pulled off its seat. Fuel is then injected 
around the back face of the intake valve (6507). The amount of fuel supplied 
to the engine (6007) depends on the length of time that the fuel injectors 
stay open. 

Between idle and 6,500 rpm, fuel is injected to each cylinder 
independently, providing one injection per two crankshaft rotations (one 
injection per cycle) to all cylinders. When engine speed reaches 6,500 rpm, 
fuel injection is shut off in order to prevent the engine from over-speeding.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Throttle Body 

The throttle body (9E926) controls air flow to the engine (6007). The 
throttle position is controlled by an accelerator cable (9A758) and a throttle 
control lever (9A776). The throttle body is a single-piece die casting made of 
aluminum. The throttle body is fitted with an idle switch and throttle 
position sensor (TP sensor) (9B989). The idle switch sends a signal to the 
powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) informing the PCM of the vehicle idle 
conditions. The TP sensor sends a varying signal to the PCM. The PCM uses the 
signal to measure throttle valve angle and adjust the air/fuel mixture.

================================================================================

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Intake Manifold

The intake manifold (9424) is a two-piece (upper and lower) aluminum 
casting. Runner lengths are tuned to optimize engine torque and power output. 
Vacuum taps are provided to support various engine accessories. 

 Upper 

The upper intake manifold provides mounting flanges for the throttle 
body (9E926) and idle air control bypass air (IAC BPA) valve.

 Lower 

The lower intake manifold provides mounting flanges for the fuel 
injection supply manifolds (9D280), fuel injectors (9F593), and the EGR valve 
(EGR valve) (9D475). The engine coolant temperature sensor (ECT sensor) 
(12A648) is threaded into the right-hand side of the lower intake manifold.

PAGE 2280
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Injectors

The fuel injectors (9F593) are electro-mechanical devices which both 
meter and atomize fuel delivered to the engine (6007). The fuel injectors are 
mounted in the lower intake manifold (9424) and positioned so that their tips 
are directing fuel at the back face of the intake valve (6507). The body is a 
solenoid-actuated valve assembly. Fuel flow to the engine is regulated by how 
long the solenoid is energized. An electrical signal from the powertrain 
control module (PCM) (12A650) activates the solenoid, causing the needle valve 
to move inward off the seat, allowing the fuel to flow through the orifice. 
Atomization of the fuel is obtained by a director/metering plate where the 
fuel leaves the fuel injector.

Fuel Injection Supply Manifold

The fuel injection supply manifold (9D280) delivers high-pressure fuel 
from the fuel supply line to the fuel injectors (9F593). The fuel injection 
supply manifold consists of a tubular rail, a mounting flange for the fuel 
pressure regulator (9C968) and mounting attachments which hold the fuel 
injectors.

================================================================================
PAGE 2282

1997 Aspire

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Pressure Regulator

The fuel pressure regulator (9C968) is attached to the fuel injection 
supply manifold (9D280) downstream of the fuel injectors (9F593). The fuel 
pressure regulator is a diaphragm-operated relief valve in which one side of 
the diaphragm senses fuel pressure and the other side is subjected to intake 
manifold vacuum. The nominal fuel pressure is established by a spring preload 
applied to the diaphragm. Balancing one side of the diaphragm with manifold 
pressure maintains a constant fuel pressure across the fuel injectors. Fuel 
not used by the engine (6007) is bypassed through the fuel pressure regulator 
and returned to the fuel tank (9002).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Charging Wiring

The fuel charging wiring (9D930) connects the engine wiring harness to 
each fuel injector (9F593) and other electronic engine controls, such as the 
throttle position sensor (TP sensor) (9B989) and Idle Air Control Bypass Air 
(IAC BPA) valve. The fuel charging wiring sends fuel injector signals from the 
powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) to the fuel injectors. The signals 
from the PCM determine the fuel injection sequence, and how long each fuel 
injector will stay open, allowing fuel into the combustion chambers.

Section 03-04: Fuel Charging and Controls

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Inertia Fuel Shutoff (IFS) Switch

 CAUTION: Do not reset the inertia fuel shutoff switch (IFS switch) (9341) until 
the entire fuel system has been inspected for leaks. 

In the event of a collision, the electric contacts in the IFS switch 
open. With the IFS switch open, the fuel delivery circuit is opened, disabling 
the fuel system. The engine (6007) may continue to run for several seconds 
after the IFS switch has opened, due to fuel remaining in the fuel supply 
line. Once the fuel in the supply line has been used, the engine will stall.

To reset the IFS switch, depress the reset button on the switch located 
behind the LH luggage compartment side cover (45422).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Pump Relay

The fuel pump relay (9345) supplies power to the fuel pump (9350). 
During starting and engine running conditions, the powertrain control module 
(PCM) (12A650) closes the contacts inside the fuel pump relay, energizing the 
fuel pump.

[FIGURE: A20566B.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Compressor Clutch Control Relay

The A/C clutch control relay (19D572) is used to improve idle 
smoothness after engine start-up and to improve acceleration performance.

During engine start-up and while accelerating in automatic transaxle 
equipped vehicles, the powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) opens the 
ground side of the A/C clutch control relay, disengaging the A/C clutch (2884).

Refer to the chart below for the conditions, purposes and lengths of 
time A/C operation is cut.

 A/C COMPRESSOR CLUTCH CUT-OFF

Engine Condition

Purpose

Cut-Off Period

Engine Starting

Improve Starting

Approximately 4 seconds

Wide Open Throttle

Improve Acceleration

Approximately 5 seconds

Acceleration From Idle (Automatic Transaxle)

Improve Acceleration

Approximately 2 seconds

Coolant Temperature Above 116°C (241°F)

Reduce Load

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Charging System

 Pre-Service Procedures 

Prior to service or removal of any of the following components of the 
fuel charging system, the fuel pressure must be relieved.

The pressurized fuel charging system consists of:

Fuel pump (9350)

Fuel filter (9155)

Fuel injection supply manifold (9D280)

Fuel pressure regulator (9C968)

Fuel injectors (9F593)

Fuel tank (9002)

 Fuel Pressure Relief 

Remove the fuel tank filler cap (9030).

 CAUTION: The fuel system is normally pressurized to between 265-320 kPa (38-46 
psi). 

Locate the fuel pump relay electrical connector behind the LH side of 
the instrument panel.

Disconnect the fuel pump relay electrical connector.

Start the engine (6007)and allow it to run out of fuel and stall.

Turn the ignition switch (11572) to the OFF position. The fuel pressure 
is now relieved.

Disconnect the battery ground cable (14301).

Connect the fuel pump relay electrical connector.

 Post-Service Procedures 

After the service procedure is complete, the following steps must be 
taken:

Install the fuel tank filler cap on the fuel tank.

Connect the battery ground cable.

 CAUTION: The fuel system is normally pressurized to between 265-320 kPa (38-46psi). 

 NOTE: Check all of the connections at the fuel injection supply manifold, and 
fuel pressure regulator.

Cycle the ignition switch from ACC to ON several times without starting 
the engine and check for fuel leaks.

Start the engine and run it up to operating temperature. 

Perform the Self Test to check fuel charging system function. Refer to 
Section 4B in the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual for diagnosis and testing of the fuel 
charging system.

ADJUSTMENTS

Idle Speed

Before adjusting the idle speed, ensure the ignition timing is adjusted 
to specification. Refer to Section 03-07 for the procedure.

Turn off all lamps and other electrical loads. This adjustment must be 
done when the cooling fan motor is not operating.

Connect Rotunda 88 Digital Multimeter 105-R0053 or equivalent with 
inductive pickup attached to the number one spark plug wire.

Ground the PCM STI (TEN) pin at the data link connector (DLC).

[FIGURE: A20583B.gif]

Start the engine (6007). Run the engine until it reaches the operating 
temperature.

Make a note of the idle speed.

Adjust the idle speed adjustment screw for the correct idle speed.

[FIGURE: A20584A.gif]

The idle speed specifications should be as follows:

650-750 rpm (manual transaxle in NEUTRAL position)

700-800 rpm (automatic transaxle in PARK [P] position)

Turn the engine off and allow the engine to cool.

Remove the ground from the PCM STI (TEN) pin at the DLC.

After the engine has cooled, start and run the engine until it reaches 
operating temperature and ensure the idle speed is to specification.

Section 03-05: Drive Belts, Accessory

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drive Belts, Accessory

The generator (GEN) (10346) is driven by a vee ribbed drive belt that 
also drives the water pump (8501). If the vehicle is equipped with air 
conditioning and power steering, the A/C compressor (19703) and power steering 
pump (3A674) are driven by a separate vee ribbed drive belt.

Drive belts (8620) must be properly adjusted at all times. Loose drive 
belts will result in slippage which may cause a noise condition or improper 
accessory operation (e.g., the generator will not charge). Over-tightened 
drive belts will place an unnecessary load on the accessory bearings.

The generator drive belt is adjusted using the generator lower bolt and 
the generator adjustment bolt. The A/C compressor/power steering pump drive 
belt is adjusted through either the power steering pump or a separately mounted 
drive belt idler pulley (8679).

The A/C compressor drive belt is routed around three pulleys: the A/C 
clutch pulley (2E884); the crankshaft pulley (6312); and either the power 
steering pump pulley or the drive belt idler pulley.

The power steering pump drive belt is routed around three pulleys: the 
power steering pump pulley; the crankshaft pulley; and the A/C clutch pulley.

The generator drive belt is routed around three pulleys: the water pump 
pulley (8509); the crankshaft pulley; and the generator pulley (10344).

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification 

Verify customer concern by running the engine (6007).

Inspect the drive belts (8620) for cracks, fraying, and wear.

Check that the drive belts are correctly mounted and properly adjusted.

 Drive Belt Cracking/Chunking/Wear 

Under severe operating conditions (high temperatures, low humidity), 
drive belt rib cracking can occur at less than 48,000 km (30,000 miles). Drive 
belt rib cracking is not a reason for concern and has no detrimental effect on 
drive belt performance. The drive belt is still perfectly functional until rib 
"chunking" occurs. Drive belt "chunking" is where the rubber material actually 
falls out between the cracks. The drive belt should be replaced if chunking 
occurs.

Wear includes conditions such as fraying, glazing, etc. Fraying gives 
the belt a tattered look. Glazing will make the belt shiny. Determine what 
type of wear is evident and proceed to symptom chart.

 Vee Belt With Chunks of Rib Missing

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Component Tests 

 Drive Belt Tension 

Correct drive belt tension is essential for correct system and 
accessory operation. Check the tension of all drive belts (8620) according to 
scheduled maintenance. If excessive or insufficient drive belt tension is 
found during normal scheduled maintenance, inspect the drive belt(s) in 
question. If the drive belt(s) are found to be in good condition upon 
inspection, adjust the tension of each drive belt. Refer to Adjustment Procedures in this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Drive Belt Tension Adjustment

 CAUTION: Proper tensioning is important to drive belt life and proper operation 
of the driven components. A loose, slipping drive belt (8620) will rapidly 
glaze and may cause a noise or improper component operation. An overly tight 
drive belt exerts unnecessarily high loads on component bearings. 

If the vehicle is equipped with both air conditioning and power 
steering, refer to the power steering pump drive belt adjustment procedure in 
this section. 

 Drive Belt — A/C Compressor 

 NOTE: If the drive belt has been in service for some time, it should be 
inspected before adjustment. A drive belt that is severely glazed, frayed, 
cracked, or contaminated with oil must be replaced. Minor cracks in the back 
of the drive belt are acceptable as long as no large pieces are missing. 

 Tension Adjustment 

Loosen the drive belt idler pulley nut.

[FIGURE: Q2802B.gif]

 NOTE: Turn the fan belt idler pulley bolt (8688) clockwise to tighten the A/C 
compressor drive belt, and counterclockwise to loosen it. 

 NOTE: Ensure that the drive belt is seated properly on all of the pulleys 
before the tensioner is adjusted.

Adjust the A/C compressor drive belt tension with the fan belt idler 
pulley bolt. Use Rotunda Offset Belt Tension Gauge 014-R1066 or equivalent.

[FIGURE: Q2803B.gif]

NEW A/C COMPRESSOR DRIVE BELT (no run time): 50-60 kg (110-132 lb).

USED A/C COMPRESSOR DRIVE BELT (more than 10 minutes of run time): 
43-50 kg (95-110 lb). 

Tighten the drive belt idler pulley nut to 37-52 Nm 
(27-38 lb-ft).

 Deflection Adjustment 

Apply 98 N (22 lb) of pressure to the A/C compressor drive belt at a 
point midway between the drive belt idler pulley (8679) and the crankshaft 
pulley (6A312).

 NOTE: Always check the drive belt deflection when the engine (6007) is cold, 
or has been stopped for at least 30 minutes. A drive belt is considered new if 
it has been used on a running engine for less than 10 minutes.

The A/C compressor drive belt deflection should measure 8-9mm 
(0.31-0.35 inch) for a new A/C compressor drive belt or 9-10mm (0.35-0.39 
inch) for a used A/C compressor drive belt.

Loosen the drive belt idler pulley nut.

[FIGURE: Q2802B.gif]

Adjust the deflection of the A/C compressor drive belt with the fan 
belt idler pulley bolt.

Tighten the drive belt idler pulley nut to 37-52 Nm 
(27-38 lb-ft).

 Drive Belt — Power Steering Pump 

 NOTE: If the drive belt has been in service for some time, it should be 
inspected before adjustment. A drive belt that is severely glazed, frayed, 
cracked, or contaminated with oil must be replaced. Minor cracks in the back 
of the drive belt are acceptable as long as no large pieces are missing. 

 Tension Adjustment 

Remove the air cleaner intake tube (9C675) and the engine air cleaner 
(ACL) (9600). Refer to Section 03-12 for the removal procedure. 

Loosen the power steering pump bolt.

[FIGURE: Q3329B.gif]

Loosen the power steering pump adjustment locknut.

[FIGURE: Q3331B.gif]

Ensure that the drive belt is seated properly on all of the pulleys 
before the tensioner is adjusted.

[FIGURE: A20554A.gif]

Adjust the power steering pump drive belt tension with the power 
steering pump adjustment bolt. Use Rotunda Offset Belt Tension Gauge 014-R1066 
or equivalent.

[FIGURE: Q3330B.gif]

NEW POWER STEERING PUMP DRIVE BELT (no run time): 50-60 kg (110-132 lb).

USED POWER STEERING PUMP DRIVE BELT (more than 10 minutes of run time): 
43-50 kg (95-110 lb).

Tighten the power steering pump bolt to 37-52 Nm 
(27-38 lb-ft). 

Tighten the power steering pump adjustment locknut to 19-25 Nm
 (14-19 lb-ft). 

[FIGURE: Q3331B.gif]

Install the engine air cleaner and air cleaner intake tube. Refer to 
 Section 03-12 for the installation procedure.

 Deflection Adjustment 

Remove the air cleaner intake tube and the engine air cleaner. Refer to 
 Section 03-12 for the removal procedure.

Apply 98 N (22 lb) of pressure to the power steering pump drive belt at 
a point midway between the power steering pump pulley (3A733) and the 
crankshaft pulley.

 NOTE: Always check the drive belt deflection when the engine is cold, or has 
been stopped for at least 30 minutes. A drive belt is considered new if it has 
been used on a running engine for less than 10 minutes.

The power steering pump drive belt deflection should measure 8-9mm 
(0.31-0.35 inch) for a new power steering pump drive belt, or 9-10mm 
(0.35-0.39 inch) for a used power steering pump drive belt.

Loosen the power steering pump bolt.

[FIGURE: Q3329B.gif]

Loosen the power steering pump adjustment locknut.

[FIGURE: Q3331B.gif]

Adjust the power steering pump drive belt by turning the power steering 
pump adjustment bolt.

[FIGURE: Q3330B.gif]

Tighten the power steering pump bolt to 37-52 Nm 
(27-38 lb-ft).

Tighten the power steering pump adjustment locknut to 19-25 Nm
 (14-19 lb-ft). 

Install the air cleaner intake tube and the engine air cleaner. Refer 
to Section 03-12 for the installation procedure.

 Drive Belt — Generator 

 NOTE: If the drive belt has been in service for some time, it should be 
inspected before adjustment. A drive belt that is severely glazed, frayed, 
cracked, or contaminated with oil must be replaced. Minor cracks in the back 
of the drive belt are acceptable as long as no large pieces are missing. 

 Tension Adjustment 

Loosen the generator adjustment bolt.

[FIGURE: Q3327D.gif]

Raise and support the vehicle. 

Loosen the generator lower mounting bolt.

Lower the vehicle.

 CAUTION: Do not pry on the generator rear housing and bearing (10334). Position 
the pry bar against a stronger point such as the area around a case bolt. 

Ensure that the generator drive belt is seated properly on all of the 
pulleys before the tension is adjusted.

[FIGURE: A20554A.gif]

Adjust the tension of the generator drive belt. Use Rotunda Offset Belt 
Tension Gauge 014-R1066 or equivalent.

NEW GENERATOR DRIVE BELT (no run time): 39-47 kg (86-103 lb). 

USED GENERATOR DRIVE BELT (more than 10 minutes of run time): 31-39 kg 
(68-86 lb). 

Adjust the tension of the generator drive belt with a pry bar. Tighten 
the generator adjustment bolt to 19-25 Nm (14-19 lb-ft). 

[FIGURE: Q3328D.gif]

Raise and support the vehicle. 

Tighten the generator lower bolt to 37-52 Nm (27-38 
lb-ft). 

Lower the vehicle.

 Deflection Adjustment 

Apply 98 N (22 lb) of pressure to the drive belt at a point midway 
between the generator pulley (10344) and the crankshaft pulley.

 NOTE: Always check the drive belt deflection when the engine is cold, or has 
been stopped for at least 30 minutes. A drive belt is considered new if it has 
been used on a running engine for less than 10 minutes.

The drive belt deflection should measure 8-9mm (0.31-0.35 inch) for a 
new drive belt, or 9-10mm (0.35-0.39 inch) for a used drive belt. 

Loosen the generator adjustment bolt.

[FIGURE: Q3327D.gif]

Raise and support the vehicle.

Loosen the generator lower mounting bolt.

Lower the vehicle.

Adjust the deflection of the generator drive belt with a pry bar. 
Tighten the generator adjusting bolt to 19-25 Nm (14-19 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: Q3328D.gif]

Raise and support the vehicle.

Tighten the generator lower bolt to 37-52 Nm (27-38 
lb-ft).

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter System

 NOTE: Engine oil viscosity can affect engine cranking speed. 

The function of the starting system is to crank the engine (6007) at a 
speed fast enough to permit the engine to start. Heavy cables, connectors, 
switches, and a starter solenoid (11390) (attached to the starter motor 
housing) are used in the starting system because of the large amount of 
current the starter motor (11002) requires while it is cranking the engine. 
The amount of resistance in the starting circuit must be kept to an absolute 
minimum to provide maximum current for starter motor operation. A discharged 
battery (10655), loose or corroded connections, or partially broken cables 
will result in slower than normal cranking speeds and may even prevent the 
starter motor from cranking the engine.

If the starter motor or circuit is suspected of causing a no-start 
condition, use the diagnostic chart and the appropriate tests in this section 
to diagnose the condition.

================================================================================
PAGE 2310
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Motor

The starter motor (11002) is a positive engagement type that draws 150 
to 250 amperes of current under normal load and 60 amperes under no load. It 
produces a normal engine cranking speed of 180 to 250 rpm. The starter relay 
pull winding resistance is 3 to 5 ohms. Total maximum voltage drop is 0.5 volt.

[FIGURE: J4037D.gif]

 Starter Motor Cutaway 

[FIGURE: J4015F.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

11390

Starter Solenoid

2

11350

Starter Drive

3

11067

Drive Lever and Pin

4

11005

Starter Motor Armature

5

11057

Brush Set

The starter motor can be considered as having two electrical circuits: 
a low current circuit and a high current circuit. 

The low current circuit is the control circuit and includes the 
ignition switch (11572), starter solenoid (11390), park/neutral position 
switch (PNP switch) (7A247) (automatic transaxle), starter clutch pedal 
position (SCPP) switch (manual transaxle) and associated wiring. The low 
current circuit is controlled by the ignition switch. 

The high current circuit connects the battery positive terminal to the 
starter motor. Because of the high current flow required to operate the 
starter motor, the high current circuit requires heavy-gauge wiring. When the 
ignition switch is turned to the START position while the PNP switch 
(automatic transaxle) or the SCPP switch (manual transaxle) contacts are 
closed, battery current is applied to the S-terminal on the starter solenoid. 
The SCPP switch is mounted on the clutch pedal support bracket and is operated 
by depressing the clutch pedal (7519). The PNP switch is mounted on the 
automatic transaxle and indicates when the transaxle is in PARK (P) or NEUTRAL 
(N).

 Starter Motor System Components and Wiring 

[FIGURE: J3701E.gif]

S-Terminal (Part of 11390)

From the S-terminal of the starter solenoid, current flows through the 
pull-in coil to ground, energizing the pull-in coil. When energized, the 
pull-in coil produces an electromagnetic field which pulls the relay armature 
and contact disc into the closed position. This produces contact between the 
B- (battery) terminal and the M- (motor) terminal. Contact between the B- and 
M-terminals energizes the high current circuit and applies full battery 
voltage to the starter field coils (11082) and brush set (11057), causing the 
starter motor to crank. 

The relay coil is connected to the starter drive (11350) through the 
drive lever and pin (11067). As the electromagnetic field of the pull-in coil 
moves the relay armature forward, the starter drive moves toward the ring gear 
on the flywheel (6375). When the contact disc makes contact between the B- and 
M-terminals, the starter drive gear and flywheel ring gear are fully engaged, 
and the starter motor rotation causes the flywheel to rotate. A hold-in coil, 
energized through the S-terminal of the starter solenoid, supplies additional 
electromagnetic force to keep the contact disc engaged as the starter motor 
draws current and the system voltage drops.

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Sequence of Operation 

 NOTE: An overrunning clutch in the drive assembly protects the starter motor 
(11002) from excessive speeds during the brief period before the driver 
releases the ignition switch (11572) from the START position (as the engine 
(6007) starts). 

The ignition switch is turned to the START position. 

The starter solenoid (11390) is energized, creating a magnetic field in 
the solenoid coil. 

The iron plunger core is drawn into the solenoid coil. 

A drive lever and pin (11067) connected to the drive assembly engages 
the starter drive (11350) to the flywheel ring gear. 

When the iron plunger core is all the way into the coil, its contact 
disc closes the circuit between the battery (10655) and the starter motor 
terminals. 

The current flows to the starter motor, and the starter drive cranks the 
flywheel (6375) and the crankshaft (6303). 

As current flows to the starter motor, the pull-in coil is bypassed. 

The hold-in coil keeps the starter drive engaged with the flywheel. 

The starter drive remains engaged until the ignition switch is released 
from the START position.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Component Tests

 Starter 

 Load Test 

 WARNING: WHEN SERVICING THE STARTER MOTOR OR PERFORMING OTHER UNDERHOOD WORK IN 
THE VICINITY OF THE STARTER MOTOR, BE AWARE THAT THE HEAVY GAUGE BATTERY INPUT 
LEAD AT THE STARTER SOLENOID IS "ELECTRICALLY HOT" AT ALL TIMES.

A PROTECTIVE CAP OR BOOT IS PROVIDED OVER THIS TERMINAL ON ALL CARLINES 
AND MUST BE REPLACED AFTER SERVICING. BE SURE TO DISCONNECT THE NEGATIVE 
BATTERY CABLE BEFORE SERVICING THE STARTER MOTOR. 

Before this test, test the battery (10655) to determine its state of 
charge. Perform a load test using Rotunda Alternator, Regulator, Battery and 
Starter Tester (ARBST) 010-00725 or equivalent to determine if the battery is 
serviceable. Refer to Section 14-00 for the procedure. 

 NOTE: When disconnecting the plastic hard shell connector at the solenoid 
S-terminal, grasp the plastic connector, depress the plastic tab and pull off 
the lead assembly. Do not pull on the lead wire or damage may result. 

If the starter motor (11002) won't crank with a fully-charged battery, 
connect the positive (+) lead of Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 
105-R0051 or equivalent, to the S-terminal on the starter solenoid (11390). 
Connect the negative (-) lead to the outside surface of the brush end plate 
and bushing (11049). 

[FIGURE: J3703E.gif]

 NOTE: If the starter solenoid is extremely hot, it may not function even 
though voltage at the S-terminal is eight volts or more. Allow the starter 
solenoid to cool and test again. 

Turn the ignition switch (11572) to the START position while watching 
the voltage reading. 

If the voltage at the S-terminal is eight volts or more, there is a 
starter motor or high current circuit malfunction. Perform the starter motor 
circuit checks explained later in this section. 

If there is no voltage, there is a malfunction in the low current 
circuit to the S-terminal.

To find the problem in the low current circuit, refer to Section 07-14A 
(automatic transaxle) or Section 07-14B (manual transaxle).

 Voltage Drop Tests — Motor Feed Circuit 

Prevent the engine (6007) from starting by disconnecting the 
distributor connectors.

Connect a remote starter switch between the starter solenoid S-terminal 
and the battery positive (+) terminal. 

Connect a voltmeter positive lead to the battery positive (+
) post. Connect the voltmeter negative lead to the starter 
solenoid M-terminal. 

Engage the remote starter switch. Read and record the voltage on the 
lowest voltmeter scale. The voltmeter reading should be 0.5 volt or less. 

[FIGURE: J3706F.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

If the voltage at the M-terminal is higher than 0.5 volt, move the 
voltmeter negative (-) lead to the starter solenoid B-terminal and repeat the 
test. 

If the voltage reading at the B-terminal is higher than 0.5 volt, the 
problem may be in the connections at the starter solenoid, or in the solenoid 
contacts. 

Remove the wires from the solenoid's B- , S- , and M-terminals. Clean 
the cables and connections and reinstall the cables to the proper terminals. 
Repeat steps 1 through 6 above. If the voltage reading is still higher than 
0.5 volt at the M-terminal, and 0.5 volt or lower at the B-terminal, the 
problem is in the starter solenoid contacts. Remove the starter solenoid for 
repair. 

If the voltage reading taken at the starter solenoid B-terminal is 
still higher than 0.5 volt after cleaning the cables and connections at the 
starter solenoid, the problem is either in the positive (+) 
battery cable connection, or in the battery to starter relay cable (14300) 
itself. Perform the individual cable test found in this section.

 Voltage Drop Tests — Ground Circuit 

 NOTE: Make all voltmeter connections at the component terminal rather than 
the cable or wiring terminal.

A slow cranking condition can be caused by resistance in the ground or 
return portion of the cranking circuit. Check the voltage drop in the ground 
circuit as follows: 

Prevent the engine from starting by disconnecting both connectors from 
the distributor (12127). 

Connect a remote starter switch between the starter solenoid S-terminal 
and the battery positive (+) terminal. 

Connect the positive (+) lead of Rotunda 73 Digital 
Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent to the starter motor housing. The 
connection must be clean and free of rust or grease. Connect the negative (-) 
voltmeter lead to the battery negative (-) terminal. 

Engage the remote starter switch and crank the engine. Read and record 
the voltmeter reading. The reading should be 0.2 volt or less. 

[FIGURE: J5296C.gif]

If the voltage drop is more than 0.2 volt, clean the negative ground 
cable connections at the battery and body connections, and retest. If the 
voltage drop is still excessive, repair or replace the battery ground cable 
(14301) and/or the engine ground cable as necessary.

Always repeat the starter motor circuit checks after repairs to ensure 
the problem has been corrected. If the battery and cables test good, and the 
starter motor still cranks slowly or not at all, remove the starter motor for 
repair. Refer to the removal procedure in this section.

 Individual Cable 

Connect the positive (+) lead of Rotunda 73 Digital 
Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent, to the battery positive (+) 
post. Connect the negative (-) lead to the B-terminal of the starter solenoid.

To locate the excessive voltage drop in the cable, move the voltmeter 
negative (-) lead toward the battery and check each mechanical connection 
point. When the high reading disappears, the last mechanical connection point 
that was checked is the problem.

 Starter Drive Test 

Remove the starter motor. Refer to the removal procedure in this section.

Place the starter motor in a vise to secure it.

Connect the negative lead of a fully charged battery to the case of the 
starter motor.

 CAUTION: Do NOT leave the positive lead of the battery connected to the starter 
motor for more than 10 seconds. 

Touch the positive lead from the battery to the S-terminal and verify 
that the starter drive (11350) ejects.

If the starter drive does not eject, repair or replace the starter motor.

Remove the positive lead from the starter motor. The ejected starter 
drive should return to its original position.

If the starter drive does not return to its original position, repair 
or replace the starter motor.

Check the starter drive. It should turn freely in one direction and 
positively engage to the armature when turned in the opposite direction. If 
not as specified, repair or replace the starter motor.

 No Load Test 

Connect a remote starter switch between the starter solenoid S- and 
B-terminals. 

Connect the positive lead of Rotunda Alternator, Regulator, Battery and 
Starter Tester (ARBST) 010-00725 or equivalent, to the positive (+
) post of a fully charged battery. 

Connect the negative lead of the VAT-40 tester to the battery negative 
(-) post. 

Connect a heavy wire between the battery positive (+) 
post and the starter solenoid B-terminal. 

Install the inductive pickup of the Rotunda Alternator, Regulator, 
Battery and Starter Tester (ARBST) 010-00725 or equivalent onto the wire 
between the battery positive (+) post and the starter solenoid 
B-terminal. 

Connect a heavy ground wire between the battery negative (-) post and a 
good clean ground on the starter motor housing. 

Press the remote starter switch and observe the starter motor, 
voltmeter gauge, and ammeter gauge.

 Armature 

 Open Circuit Test 

An open circuit in the starter motor armature (11005) may sometimes be 
detected by examining the commutator for evidence of burning. A burn spot on 
the commutator is caused by an arc formed every time the commutator segment, 
connected to the open circuit winding, passes under a brush. 

 Grounded Circuit Test 

Using Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent, determine 
if the armature is grounded by checking for continuity between the commutator 
and core. 

If there is continuity between the commutator and armature core, 
replace the starter motor armature.

[FIGURE: J3723F.gif]

Use Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent to determine 
if the starter motor armature is insulated by checking for continuity between 
the commutator and the shaft. If there is continuity, replace the starter 
motor armature.

[FIGURE: J5297B.gif]

 Starter Solenoid 

 Solenoid S-Terminal Circuit Resistance 

Use Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051, or equivalent to check for 
continuity between the M-terminal and the S-terminal. Replace the starter 
solenoid if there is no continuity.

[FIGURE: J5298B.gif]

 Solenoid M-Terminal 

Check for continuity between the M-terminal and the starter solenoid 
body using Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent. Replace the 
starter solenoid if there is no continuity.

[FIGURE: J3733F.gif]

Check for continuity between the M- and B- terminals using a Rotunda 73 
Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent. Replace the starter solenoid if 
there is continuity.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Assembly 

 NOTE: When the brush set (11057) extends past the brush spring (11059), 
release the brush spring. The tension of the brush spring will hold the brush 
set in a retracted position. 

Use a suitable tool to pull back on the brush spring while pushing the 
brush set upward through the brush holder frame.

[FIGURE: J4052D.gif]

Install the starter motor armature (11005) into the starter field coil 
(11082).

[FIGURE: J4056B.gif]

Release the brush spring tension on the brush set and push it into 
position against the starter motor armature. Ensure the tension brush springs 
are properly positioned in the brush holder (11061) and against the brush set. 

Install the armature washers onto the starter motor armature shaft.

[FIGURE: J4050C.gif]

Install the two brush end plate screws and the brush end plate and 
bushing (11049). 

Install the starter drive (11350) and the retaining collar. 

Install the starter drive stop ring (11222). 

Compress the starter drive stop ring and slide the starter drive stop 
ring and the retaining collar up. Ensure the retaining collar is firmly seated 
on the starter drive stop ring.

[FIGURE: J4073E.gif]

Position the drive lever and pin (11067) on the starter drive.

[FIGURE: J4067D.gif]

Position the drive end housing on the starter motor armature shaft. 

Coat the drive lever and pin plate, drive lever and pin seal, and drive 
end housing with a thin film of contact cement.

[FIGURE: J4068D.gif]

Install the drive lever and pin plate and drive lever and pin seal in 
the drive end housing. Seat the drive end housing against the starter field 
coil.

[FIGURE: J4046C.gif]

Install the thru bolts (11091). Tighten the thru bolts to 6-8 Nm
 (55-75 lb-in). 

Install the plunger and spring. 

 NOTE: If shims were removed during disassembly, make sure they are installed 
with the starter solenoid (11390). 

Position the starter solenoid and install the starter solenoid screws.

Connect the field strap connector to the M-terminal. 

Install the nut onto the M-terminal. Tighten the M-terminal nut to 8-12 Nm
 (71-106 lb-in). 

Install the starter motor (11002). Refer to the installation procedure 
in this section.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Armature Coil, Starter Motor 

Inspect the starter motor armature coil windings for broken or burned 
insulation and unwelded or open connections.

Check starter motor armature (11005) for open circuits, shorts, and 
grounds. Check for pole rub or rub on magnetic shunts.

Place the starter motor armature on V-blocks. 

Rotate the starter motor armature and use Dial Indicator With Bracketry 
TOOL-4201-C or equivalent to measure the runout of the commutator. 

[FIGURE: J3724C.gif]

If the runout is 0.05mm (0.002 inch) or greater, repair the commutator 
in a lathe. Replace the starter motor armature if the runout is excessive.

Verify that there is no play in the bearing surfaces at the V-blocks. 

Use calipers to measure the outer diameter of the commutator. 

If the commutator outer diameter is 31mm (1.22 inches) or less, replace 
the starter motor armature.

[FIGURE: J3725B.gif]

Check the surface of the commutator. 

 CAUTION: Do not use emery cloth on the commutator. 

If the commutator surface is dirty, clean the surface with a clean cloth.

If the commutator surface is burned, replace the starter motor armature.

If the commutator surface is excessively scored, replace the starter 
motor armature.

Check the depth of insulating material between the commutator segments. 

If the depth of the groove between commutator segments is 0.2mm (0.008 
inch) or less, use a sharpened section of a hacksaw blade to undercut the 
insulating material to a depth of 0.5-0.8mm (0.020-0.030 inch).

[FIGURE: J3726B.gif]

Check the condition of the starter motor armature laminations. 

If the starter motor armature laminations show indications of having 
contacted the field coil pole pieces, either the armature bushings are worn, 
the field coil pole pieces are loose, or the starter motor armature shaft is 
bent, replace the starter motor armature. 

Verify that the field coil pole pieces are tightly secured in the 
starter field coil (11082).

If the field coil pole pieces are loose, replace the starter field coil. 

Check the starter motor armature shaft side play. 

If the starter motor armature shaft side play exceeds 0.2mm (0.008 
inch), the end cover and drive end housing bushings are worn and/or the 
starter motor armature shaft ends are worn. Replace the bushings. 

Check the condition of the starter motor armature shaft ends. 

If the starter motor armature shaft ends are worn or damaged, replace 
the starter motor armature.

[FIGURE: J3728E.gif]

ADJUSTMENTS

Starter Drive Pinion Depth Adjustment

 NOTE: This procedure is performed with the starter motor (11002) removed from 
the vehicle. To remove the starter motor, refer to the removal procedure in 
this section.

Remove the M-terminal nut from the M-terminal. 

Disconnect the field strap connector from the M-terminal. 

Connect a wire from the positive terminal of a 12-volt battery (10655) 
to the S-terminal. 

 CAUTION: Do not keep the starter solenoid (11390) engaged for longer than 10 
seconds. Wait at least three minutes between tests to allow the starter 
solenoid to cool. 

Connect wires from the negative terminal of a 12-volt battery to the 
M-terminal and the starter solenoid body.

[FIGURE: J3735E.gif]

Verify that the starter solenoid activates and kicks out the starter 
drive (11350).

If the starter drive does not kick out when the battery is connected to 
the starter motor as described in Steps 1 to 4, perform further diagnosis. 
Refer to Diagnosis and Testing in this section. 

While the starter drive is extended, measure the gap between the 
starter drive and the retaining collar. 

[FIGURE: J4880A.gif]

If the starter drive gap is not 0.5-2.0mm (0.02-0.08 inch), add or 
subtract shims between the starter solenoid and drive end housing as necessary 
to achieve the proper gap. 

Disconnect the battery from the starter motor. 

Connect the field strap connector to the M-terminal of the starter 
solenoid. 

Install the M-terminal nut onto the M-terminal. Tighten the M-terminal 
nut to 8-12 Nm (71-106 lb-in).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Ignition System Features 

The distributor ignition system features a camshaft driven distributor 
which uses no centrifugal or vacuum advance. The diecast housing incorporates 
a Hall effect stator assembly. 

Initial timing adjustments are not required unless the distributor 
(12127) has been moved from its factory setting or removed from the engine 
(6007). Ignition timing procedures are included in this section. 

 Distributor Ignition System 

[FIGURE: B5522D.gif]

Ignition timing is controlled entirely by the PCM. Crankshaft position 
and engine rpm are read by the CKP sensor. This information is sent to the 
PCM. The PCM then signals the ICM to fire the ignition coil. The ICM controls 
the current through the ignition coil primary winding. The ICM turns the 
current on between firing points to build up a magnetic field around the coil 
windings. Then it turns the current off on a signal from the PCM. Once the 
current is turned off, the field collapses and a high voltage pulse of about 
28,000 volts is induced in the coil secondary winding. This pulse is 
transmitted to the central terminal in the distributor cap (12106), through the 
distributor rotor (12200) to the distributor cap terminal and through the 
distributor to spark plug wire (12286) to the appropriate spark plug (12405). 
At the spark plug electrodes in the combustion chamber, the high voltage arcs 
to ground and ignites the compressed air/fuel charge.

[FIGURE: B5517B.gif]

High-altitude spark advance correction is entirely electronic and does 
not affect the relative positions of the armature or distributor stator. All 
vehicles are equipped with a barometric pressure (BARO) sensor housed in the 
PCM. When barometric pressure drops below 670mm (26.4 in-Hg), the PCM alters 
the spark output (SPOUT) signal to initiate high altitude spark advance 
operation.

================================================================================
PAGE 2335
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Ignition Components, Electronic

The electronic components in the ignition system are as follows:

Camshaft position (CMP) sensor.

Crankshaft position (CKP) sensor.

Ignition coil.

Ignition control module (ICM).

Distributor (12127).

The CMP sensor, ignition coil and ICM are not serviceable. If any of 
these components need to be serviced, the distributor will have to be 
replaced. Refer to the procedure in this section for the replacement procedure.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Crankshaft Position Sensor

The crankshaft position (CKP) sensor reads the crankshaft position and 
the engine rpm and transmits the information to the powertrain control module 
(PCM) (12A650). The CKP sensor is mounted on the oil pump housing and monitors 
crankshaft rpm speed.

Camshaft Position Sensor

The camshaft position (CMP) sensor is part of the distributor (12127). 
The CMP sensor sends a signal to the powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) 
when the number one cylinder is at top dead center (TDC).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Ignition Coil

The ignition coil transforms the battery voltage in its primary circuit 
into approximately 28,000 volts on its secondary circuit each time it receives 
a signal from the ignition control module (ICM).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Ignition Control Module

The ignition control module (ICM) receives a spark output (SPOUT) 
signal from the powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650), and opens and closes 
the ignition coil primary circuit to fire the spark plugs (12405).

PAGE 2340
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-07: Ignition, Distributor

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Distributor

The distributor (12127) is mounted on the rear (flywheel end) of the 
cylinder head (6049), and is direct-driven by the camshaft (6250) at one-half 
the crankshaft speed. Two offset drive tangs pinned to the distributor shaft 
engage with the camshaft in only one position. Rotation is counterclockwise as 
seen from the left of the vehicle.

[FIGURE: B5516A.gif]

The distributor houses the camshaft position (CMP) sensor, ignition 
coil, ignition control module (ICM) and the distributor rotor (12200). Within 
the distributor, the ignition coil transfers the secondary voltage to the 
distributor rotor. The distributor rotor transfers the voltage to each 
distributor to spark plug wire (12286).

The distributor uses a Hall effect vane switch assembly, causing the 
ignition coil to be switched off and on by the powertrain control module (PCM) 
(12A650) and Ignition Control Module (ICM). The vane switch is an encapsulated 
package consisting of a Hall effect device on one side and a permanent magnet 
on the other side. 

[FIGURE: B5518A.gif]

A rotary vane cup, made of ferrous metal, is used to trigger the signal 
off and on. 

[FIGURE: B5519A.gif]

When the window of the vane cup is between the magnet and the Hall 
effect device, a magnetic flux field is completed from the magnet through the 
Hall effect device and back to the magnet. 

[FIGURE: B5520A.gif]

As the vane passes through this opening, the flux lines are shunted 
through the vane and back to the magnet. 

During this time, a voltage is produced as the vane passes through the 
opening. When the vane clears the opening, the window edge causes the signal 
to drop to almost zero volts. The signal is then used by the PCM for 
crankshaft position sensing and the computation of the desired spark advance 
based on engine demand and calibration. The conditioned spark advance and 
voltage distribution is accomplished through the distributor rotor, 
distributor cap (12106) and distributor to spark plug wires. 

[FIGURE: B5521B.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Distributor to Spark Plug Wires

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable (14301). 

Mark the distributor cap towers with the cylinder numbers to ensure 
installation in the correct position. Disconnect the distributor to spark plug 
wires (12286) from the distributor cap (12106) by twisting and pulling the 
distributor to spark plug wire boots (not the distributor to spark plug wires) 
until the distributor to spark plug wires are free. 

Note the differing lengths and the numbering of distributor to spark 
plug wires, with Number 1 being the longest wire. This should help prevent 
confusion when determining the correct wire-to-plug connection. 

Disengage the distributor to spark plug wires from the ignition wire 
separator (12297) and disconnect the distributor to spark plug wires from the 
spark plugs (12405) using Spark Plug Boot Puller D79P-6666-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specifications. 

[FIGURE: B4663E.gif]

 Installation 

Whenever a distributor to spark plug wire is removed for any reason 
from the spark plug or distributor cap, or a new distributor to spark plug 
wire is installed, Silicone Brake Caliper Grease and Dielectric Compound 
D7AZ-19A331-A (Motorcraft WA-10) or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESE-M1C171-A must be applied to the distributor to spark plug wire boot before 
the distributor to spark plug wire is connected. Using a small, clean tool, 
coat the entire interior surface of the distributor to spark plug wire boot 
with Silicone Dielectric Compound D7AZ-19A331-A (Motorcraft WA-10) or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M1C171-A. 

Connect the longest distributor to spark plug wire to the Number 1 
spark plug, then to the Number 1 tower on the distributor cap. 

Connect progressively shorter wires to the Number 2, 3, and 4 spark 
plugs and distributor cap towers. 

Secure the distributor to spark plug wires in the ignition wire 
separator. 

Connect the battery ground cable. 

Check for proper operation.

ADJUSTMENTS

Ignition Timing

Check and adjust the ignition timing using the following procedure: 

Start the engine and allow it to warm up to normal operating temperature.

Shut off all of the accessories.

Connect Rotunda Timing Analyzer 164-R0257 or equivalent.

Using a jumper, ground the self-test input (STI) terminal at the data 
link connector (DLC).

[FIGURE: B5550A.gif]

Check the base ignition timing. The ignition timing mark should 
line up with the pointer on the timing belt cover.

[FIGURE: B5551B.gif]

If the timing marks do not line up, continue with the following steps. 

Loosen the distributor bolts. 

Rotate the distributor (12127) until the timing marks are properly 
aligned.

[FIGURE: B5531A.gif]

Tighten the distributor bolts to 19-25 Nm (14-19 
lb-ft). 

Check the timing marks to ensure they did not move when the distributor 
bolts were tightened. 

Remove the jumper from the STI terminal at the DLC. 

Remove the Rotunda Timing Analyzer 164-R0257 or equivalent.

Section 03-08: Engine Emission Control

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) System

 CAUTION: Do not remove the PCV system from the engine (6007). Operating the 
engine without the PCV system will reduce both fuel economy and engine 
ventilation. This will weaken the engine's performance and shorten the 
engine's life. 

The positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) system vents harmful blow-by 
fumes from the engine crankcase into the upper intake manifold (9424) for 
burning with the fuel and air mixture. Thepositive crankcase ventilation valve 
(PCV valve) (6A666) limits the fresh air intake to suit the engine's demand. 
It also prevents combustion from backfiring into the engine crankcase. The 
benefits of the PCV system include:

Venting moisture and corrosive vapors from the engine crankcase.

Preventing engine crankcase explosions.

Automatically regulating the ventilation system air flow to the engine 
air intake as required by engine operating conditions.

The PCV valve is operated by the engine vacuum. As the engine runs, 
blow-by gas is drawn into the intake manifold to be burned. When the engine is 
running at idle, the PCV valve is fully open. A large amount of blow-by gas is 
drawn into the intake manifold to be burned. As the engine speed rises, the 
PCV valve gradually closes, allowing less blow-by gas to be drawn into the 
intake manifold.

================================================================================
PAGE 2365
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-08: Engine Emission Control

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System 

The exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) system recirculates exhaust gas 
into the intake manifold (9424). This lowers combustion temperatures and 
reduces the formation of oxides of nitrogen (NOX). 

The amount of exhaust gas reintroduced and the timing of the cycle 
varies by calibration. Timing and volume are controlled by the powertrain 
control module (PCM) (12A650). The EGR valve (EGR valve) (9D475) is vacuum 
actuated. The vacuum hose routing diagram is shown on the Vehicle Emission 
Control Information (VECI) decal. EGR operation stops when the engine 
temperature is cold, to improve driveability. The PCM controls the EGR 
solenoid vacuum valve (9D474). When energized the intake manifold vacuum 
outlet fitting and cap (9A474) allows exhaust gas to be circulated in the 
engine to be burned.

================================================================================
PAGE 2366
================================================================================

Exhaust Emission Control System

 Vehicle Emission Control Information Decal 

Vacuum hoses on the engine (6007) use a color stripe to aid in hose 
routing checks. The stripe will usually be the same color as on the Vehicle 
Emission Control Information (VECI) decal, but the correct vacuum hose routing 
must be verified by using the correct component connections shown on the VECI 
decal.

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Evaporative Emission Control System 

As a part of the fuel system, vehicles are equipped with a fuel 
evaporative emission control system designed to meet federal and state 
requirements in effect at the time of production.

================================================================================
PAGE 2392
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fill Control Vent System 

Fill control is accomplished through a vent line attached to the fuel 
tank filler pipe (9034) extending inside the fuel tank (9002). The evaporative 
emission valve (9B593), mounted in the top panel of the fuel tank, and the 
attached vapor line leading to the evaporative emissions canister (EVAP 
canister) (9D653), also contribute to fill control. These components control 
the pressure in the fuel tank when the fuel level rises and covers the fill 
vent opening in the fuel tank. The vent system provides an air space above the 
fuel level in a full fuel tank. The air space is approximately 10 percent of 
the fuel tank volume and allows for thermal expansion of the fuel while 
providing clearance between the fuel level and the evaporative emission valve. 
The clearance allows sufficient vapor venting through the evaporative emission 
valve under all static and most dynamic vehicle conditions.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

System Components

 Fuel Tank Evaporative Emission System 

This system consists of: 

Sealed fuel tank (9002) and fuel tank filler pipe (9034).

Fuel tank filler cap (9030) with pressure/vacuum relief.

Evaporative emission valve (9B593) with pressure relief and open flow 
to vacuum.

Two-way check.

Evaporative emission separator (2-door models only).

Evaporative emission tube and evaporative emission hoses (9G297).

Evaporative emissions canister (EVAP canister) (9D653).

Evaporative emission canister purge valve (EVAP canister purge valve) 
(9C915).

 Engine Evaporative Emission System 

This system consists of: 

Evaporative emission canister purge valve.

EVAP canister.

The use of these components depends on the calibration of the complete 
vehicle. 

System control and operation are accomplished through five separate 
basic functions in the system: 

Fill control venting.

Fuel tank vapor venting and storage system. 

Fuel vapor return system. 

Fuel vapor purge system. 

Pressure and vacuum relief system (fuel tank filler cap and evaporative 
emission valve).

================================================================================
PAGE 2394
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Evaporative Emission (EVAP) Canister 

Fuel vapor generated from the fuel tank (9002) is normally stored in a 
carbon-filled evaporative emission (EVAP) canister until the vehicle is 
operated. Then it is drawn into the intake manifold (9424).

[FIGURE: A21004C.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 2395
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Evaporative Emission Hose

The evaporative emission hose (9G297) transmits vapor from the 
evaporative emission canister purge valve (EVAP canister purge valve) (9C915), 
the return hose, and the regulator valve assembly to the EVAP canister.

================================================================================
PAGE 2396
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Evaporative Emission (EVAP) Canister Purge Valve

The evaporative emission canister purge valve (EVAP canister purge 
valve) (9C915) is in-line with the EVAP canister and controls the flow of fuel 
vapors leaving the EVAP canister. The EVAP canister purge valve is normally 
closed. When the engine (6007) is shut off, vapors from the fuel tank (9002) 
flow into the EVAP canister. After the engine is started, the valve opens, 
purging the vapors into the intake manifold (9424). 

The powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) actuates the EVAP canister 
purge solenoid based on readings it receives from various sensors.

[FIGURE: GA0975A.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 2397
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Pressure and Vacuum Relief System 

 Evaporative Emission Separator 

The evaporative emission separator is on 2-door models only. It is 
attached to the evaporative emission valve (9B593). The evaporative emission 
separator prevents liquid fuel from flooding the evaporative emissions 
canister (EVAP canister) (9D653) when the fuel in the fuel tank (9002) splashes.

 Fuel Tank Filler Cap 

The fuel tank filler cap (9030) is a sealed cap with a built-in 
pressure-vacuum relief valve. Fuel system vacuum relief is provided after 
negative 1.7 kPa (0.25 psi) and pressure relief is provided above 14 kPa (2 
psi). Under normal operating conditions, the fuel tank filler cap operates as 
a check valve, allowing air to enter the fuel tank as fuel is used, while 
preventing vapors from escaping the fuel tank through the fuel tank filler cap.

================================================================================
PAGE 2398
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Evaporative Emission Valve 

The evaporative emission valve (9B593) uses a small orifice and shutoff 
valve to allow only fuel vapor, not liquid, to pass into the fuel evaporation 
pipe (9038) and forward to the evaporative emissions canister (EVAP canister) 
(9D653). This evaporative emission valve mounts directly to the fuel tank 
(9002) with a rubber grommet.

 2-Door 

[FIGURE: A21005B.gif]

 4-Door 

[FIGURE: A20631A.gif]

Fuel vapors in the fuel tank are vented through the orifice in the top 
of the fuel tank. The vapors are transmitted through a single vapor tube to 
the EVAP canister at the front of the vehicle. A spring-loaded poppet valve 
provides pressure relief ahead of the orifice to the EVAP canister. The poppet 
valve gradually opens to vent vapors to the atmosphere through a second vapor 
tube.

================================================================================
PAGE 2399
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-13: Evaporative Emissions

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Two-Way Check Valve

The two-way check valve allows air to pass in or out of the fuel tank 
(9002) to equalize the pressure within the fuel tank. This protects the fuel 
tank from heat build-up rupture and cool-down collapse.

[FIGURE: A21012B.gif]

The two-way check valve is located behind the left quarter trim panel 
(31012) on 2-door models and under the rear seat cushion and cover (60030) on 
4-door models.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Control Systems, Electronic 

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE, CARRY LIGHTED TOBACCO, OR OPEN FLAME OF ANY TYPE WHEN 
WORKING ON OR NEAR ANY FUEL RELATED COMPONENT. HIGHLY FLAMMABLE MIXTURES ARE 
ALWAYS PRESENT AND MAY BE IGNITED, RESULTING IN POSSIBLE PERSONAL INJURY. 

The sequential multiport fuel injection (SFI) system is classified as a 
multi-point, pulse time, mass airflow, fuel injection system. 

To maintain the required exhaust emission levels, the fuel metering 
system must be kept in good operating condition and adjusted to the 
specifications listed in/on the following sources: 

Section 3B of the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual.

The applicable section of this group. 

The Engine/Emissions Facts Book. 

The vehicle emission control information (VECI) decal. 

Additional engine performance checks are required to keep the exhaust 
emissions at the specified minimum pollutant level. Refer to Section 00-03 for 
these performance checks and their recommended intervals.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Powertrain Control Module (PCM) 

The powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) detects engine operating 
and driving conditions along with exhaust gas oxygen content. Various 
switches, sensors, and components provide the PCM with information which 
allows it to control the amount of fuel injected into the engine (6007). The 
PCM also has some control of the evaporative emission, ignition, and 
deceleration systems. Refer to the appropriate section for information on 
these systems. The following illustration identifies the electronic fuel 
system inputs and outputs to and from the PCM.

 Relation of Inputs and Outputs 

[FIGURE: A20549G.gif]
