DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Throttle Position (TP) Sensor

The throttle position sensor (TP sensor) (9B989) is a variable 
resistor-type sensor. It is mounted on the left-hand side of the throttle body 
(9E926). The TP sensor detects the angle the throttle valve has been opened 
and sends a signal to the powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) to regulate 
the air/fuel mixture.

Section 03-14: Engine Controls, Electronic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Mass Air Flow (MAF) Sensor

The mass air flow sensor (MAF sensor) (12B579) detects the intake air 
quantity and converts the measurement to a voltage reading by means of a 
heated resistor. The voltage signal is sent to the powertrain control module 
(PCM) (12A650) , which in turn determines injection quantities, engine speed, 
etc.

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Intake Air Temperature (IAT) Sensor 

The intake air temperature sensor (IAT sensor) (12A697) is a 
thermistor. It is mounted on the side of the upper engine air cleaner (ACL) 
(9600) and senses the intake air temperature. It sends information to the 
powertrain control module (PCM) (12A650) , which uses the information to 
calculate the fuel injection amount.

PAGE 2413
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 03-14: Engine Controls, Electronic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Idle Air Control Bypass Air (IAC BPA) Valve

The idle air control bypass air (IAC BPA) valve consists of the bypass 
air valve and the idle air control valve.

The bypass air valve functions during cold engine operation to increase 
engine idle speed. The bypass air valve consists of a thermowax bead and a 
valve.

Engine coolant is directed around the thermowax, which opens and closes 
the valve. During cold engine operation (below 60°C [
140°F]), the thermowax is contracted 
enough to allow the air valve to open. As the engine coolant directed around 
the thermowax heats, the thermowax begins to expand. When the engine coolant 
reaches temperatures above 60°C (140°F), the 
thermowax expands and closes the valve.

In order to ensure idle smoothness for all operating conditions, the 
IAC BPA valve controls the amount of air bypassing the throttle valve. In 
order to maintain factory-set idle speed when the engine (6007) is cold, air 
also flows through the IAC BPA valve during all modes of engine operation.

Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) Sensor

provides engine coolant temperature information to the powertrain control 
module (PCM) (12A650).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Speed Sensor (VSS)

The vehicle speed sensor (VSS) is integral to the speedometer (17255). 
When the vehicle is driven, the speedometer gear assembly turns the 
speedometer cable (17260). The speedometer cable turns the speedometer and 
VSS. As the VSS rotates, it sends a vehicle speed signal to the powertrain 
control module (PCM) (12A650) to control fuel injection.

ADJUSTMENTS

Throttle Position (TP) Sensor

 Disconnect the throttle position (TP) sensor electrical connector.

[FIGURE: A20531D.gif]

Connect Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051, or equivalent, between 
terminals A and B.

[FIGURE: A20548C.gif]

Turn the throttle lever to the wide open throttle (WOT) position and 
check the resistance reading on the multimeter. The reading should be 
approximately 1 Kohm.

Turn the throttle lever to the fully closed position and check the 
reading on the multimeter. The reading should be approximately 5 Kohms.

If the resistances are not within the specifications, adjust the TP 
sensor as follows:

Loosen, but do not remove, the TP sensor screws.

[FIGURE: A20532C.gif]

With the throttle lever in the closed position, adjust the TP sensor 
until the multimeter reads below 1 ohm.

Turn the throttle lever to the WOT position and check the resistance. 
The resistance should be approximately 5 Kohms. If the TP sensor cannot be 
adjusted to specification, the throttle body (9E926) must be replaced. Refer 
to Section 03-04 for the removal and installation procedure.

After the TP sensor resistance readings are to specification, tighten 
the TP sensor screws to 1.6-2.3 Nm (14.2-20.3 lb-in).

Connect the TP sensor electrical connector.

Section 04-00: Suspension — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Component Replacement

 Suspension, Front 

The front suspension system is a MacPherson strut layout with single 
pivot forged front suspension lower arms (3078). The following components may 
be replaced individually or as an assembly:

The front shock absorber and front coil spring assembly may be 
disassembled in order to replace any of the individual components. They do not 
need to be replaced in pairs.

The front suspension lower arm includes an integral ball joint replaced 
as an assembly. The ball joint dust seal and the front suspension lower arm 
inner pivot bushing may be replaced individually.

All front stabilizer bar components may be replaced individually.

The left front wheel knuckle (3K185) or right front wheel knuckle 
(3K186) may be replaced individually.

The wheel hub (1104) may be replaced individually.

The front wheel bearing (1216) inner and outer races and rollers are 
replaced as a set.

 Suspension, Rear 

The following rear suspension components may be replaced either 
individually or as an assembly:

The rear shock absorber and rear spring assembly may be disassembled in 
order to replace any of the individual components. They do not need to be 
replaced in pairs.

The rear brake drum (1126) and rear wheel hub are replaced as an 
assembly.

The rear wheel bearings (1225) inner and outer races and rollers are 
replaced as a set.

The left rear wheel spindle (4A013) or right rear wheel spindle are 
replaced individually.

The axle torsion beam and axle torsion beam arms are replaced as an 
assembly.

The torsion bar bracket (5596) may be replaced individually.

The axle torsion beam bushings may be replaced individually.

PAGE 2443
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-00: Suspension — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification

 Tire Wear 

The tires should be equally and correctly inflated, and uniformly worn, 
left and right. Abnormal tread wear patterns provide clues to suspension and 
other conditions. For example, non-uniform tread wear across the face of the 
tire which is greater toward the inboard or outboard edge, indicates incorrect 
camber. While two camber settings are available, the range of adjustment is 
limited. If camber problems are severe enough to produce one-side tire wear, 
look for worn or damaged suspension parts or distortion of body mounting 
points. 

Sawtooth tread wear, with tread ribs higher on the inboard or outboard 
edges, indicates excessive toe-in or toe-out, respectively. Cupping wear or 
flat spots indicate an imbalance or runout of wheels (1007) and/or tires. If 
evident, refer to Section 04-04 for corrective procedures. Severely worn tires 
should be replaced.

 Vibration and Roughness 

Vibration, roughness, tramp, shimmy, and thump may be caused by 
excessive tire or wheel runout, worn or cupped tires, or wheel and tire 
imbalance. These conditions may also be caused by rough road surfaces. Drive 
the vehicle on different road surfaces to determine whether the surfaces are 
actually the cause of the condition.

Do not immediately suspect the tires or wheels when attempting to 
diagnose a vibration problem. Other sources of vibration include: 

Loose or worn wheel bearings

Loose or worn suspension or steering components 

Worn upper front suspension bearing and seal (3B455)

Worn or damaged front wheel driveshaft joints (3B414)

Front disc brake rotor (1125) or brake drum (1126) runout 

Loose engine or transaxle supports 

Engine-driven accessories

 Road Test 

Always begin a suspension diagnostic procedure with a road test. The 
road test and customer interview (if available) will provide much information 
needed to find the source of the vibration. 

During the road test, drive the vehicle on a smooth road. If vibration 
is apparent, note and record the following: 

The speed(s) at which the vibration occurs.

The type of vibration (mechanical and/or audible) occurring in each 
speed range.

How changes in vehicle speed, engine speed, and engine torque affect 
the vibration.

The type of vibration sensitivity (torque sensitive, engine speed 
sensitive, or vehicle speed sensitive).

Check the cold tire air pressure. Air pressure should be as follows: 

Front Tires — 220 kPa (32 psi)

Rear Tires — 220 kPa (32 psi)

 WARNING: TO AVOID PERSONAL INJURY DUE TO LOSS OF VEHICLE CONTROL, THE INSPECTION 
SHOULD BE PERFORMED BY TWO PEOPLE TO MAINTAIN SAFE DRIVING CONDITIONS. ONE 
PERSON SHOULD DRIVE WHILE THE OTHER CHECKS THE TIME. ADEQUATE GRIP SHOULD 
ALWAYS BE MAINTAINED ON THE STEERING WHEEL. 

The following conditions must be met when evaluating the vehicle. 

Be sure that no crosswinds or gusting breezes are present. 

Drive the vehicle in both (opposing) directions at least twice. 

Average the results. 

Drive the vehicle at 88 km/h (55 mph) on a level and straight road. 
Drive in the center lane of a three lane freeway.

If the vehicle changes one complete 12 foot wide lane within seven 
seconds, it has a drift.

[FIGURE: F8575B.gif]

Rotate the tires as shown in the following illustration. Perform Step 
A, and then if necessary, Step B. 

[FIGURE: F8573B.gif]

 Torque Sensitive 

When the vibration is torque sensitive, the condition can be improved 
or worsened by accelerating, coasting, or maintaining a constant vehicle speed.

 Vehicle Speed Sensitive 

When the vibration is linked to vehicle speed, the vibration always 
occurs at the same vehicle speed or in the same range of vehicle speed and is 
not affected by engine torque, or transaxle gear selected.

 Engine Speed Sensitive 

When the vibration is linked to engine speed, the vibration occurs at 
varying vehicle speeds when a different transaxle gear is selected. It can 
sometimes be isolated by increasing or decreasing engine rpm with the 
transaxle in NEUTRAL (N), or by stall testing with the transaxle in gear. If 
the vibration is linked to engine speed, the problem is probably not a wheel 
or tire condition. 

If the road test indicates that the vibration is related to the tires or 
wheels, refer to the Symptom Chart in Section 04-04 . If the vehicle drifts to 
one side during the road test, refer to the Symptom Chart in this section.

If the road test reveals tire whine, but no shaking or vibration, the 
noise is caused by contact between the tires and the road surface. Tire whine 
can be distinguished from axle whine because axle noise diminishes or changes 
according to load or speed. Tire noise remains the same over a range of 
speeds. A thumping noise usually means that the tire has flat or soft spots 
that make noise as they slap the road surface or that the road surface has 
evenly spaced (expansion joints) bumps.

 Front End 

Do not check and adjust front-wheel alignment without first making the 
following inspections for front end damage or wear:

Check for specified air pressures in all four tires. 

Raise the vehicle off of the floor. Check the front suspension for 
looseness, wear, and damage. Tighten any loose nuts and bolts to 
specification. Replace any worn parts. Refer to Section 04-01 for the 
procedures. 

Check the steering gear mountings and all steering linkage connections 
for looseness. Tighten all mountings to specification. If any of the linkage 
is worn or bent, replace the parts. Refer to Section 11-01 (Manual Steering) 
or Section 11-02 (Power Steering) for the procedures. 

Check the action of the struts and the condition of their attachments. 
Refer to Shock Absorber Checks in this section. A sticking or binding shock 
absorber may not allow the vehicle to settle in a normal level position, 
possibly affecting the front wheel alignment. 

 Ball Joints, Lower — Inspection 

Check for ball joint wear by raising the vehicle until the wheel and 
tire is clear of the floor. Support the front suspension lower arm (3078) so 
that there is no load on the front shock absorber (18124). Try to rock the 
wheel top-to-bottom; if any wobble is felt, look for movement between the 
front suspension lower arm and front wheel knuckle (3K185). If the ball joint 
appears tight, check and adjust the front wheel bearings (1216). Refer to 
 Section 04-01 for the procedure. Then repeat the wobble check. Otherwise, any 
movement present indicates ball joint wear. If wear is present, the tie rod 
end (3A130) and the front suspension lower arms and front stabilizer bars 
(5482) should be checked. Since the ball joint is integrated into the front 
suspension lower arm, the front suspension lower arm must be replaced. Refer 
to Section 04-01 for the procedure.

[FIGURE: F5572B.gif]

Front wheel bearings that need replacing may be indicated by a noise 
that occurs only when turning. To diagnose the front wheel bearings: 

Road test the car on a smooth road. Make sharp turns to the right and 
left. 

If the vehicle makes noises on right turns, the left front wheel 
bearings may need to be replaced. 

If the vehicle makes noises on left turns, the right front wheel 
bearings may need to be replaced. 

If front wheel bearing noise is heard on either right or left turns, 
the wheel hub and front wheel bearing assembly on the suspected side should be 
disassembled and inspected.

Raise the front of the vehicle and check for loose front wheel bearings 
by rocking the tires at top and bottom.

 NOTE: Be careful not to confuse lower ball joint looseness with bearing 
looseness. If abnormal looseness or noise is found, replace the bearings. 
Refer to Section 04-01 or Section 04-02 for the removal and installation procedure.

Spin the tire quickly by hand and make sure the tire turns smoothly 
without noise from the bearings.

[FIGURE: F8572A.gif]

Remove the wheel and disc brake caliper (2B120). Hang the disc brake 
caliper from the front coil spring (5310) using a cord or piece of wire.

Position Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or equivalent 
against the wheel hub (1104), then push and pull the wheel hub. Measure the 
end play of the wheel hub and bearing assembly. There should be no end play. 
If there is end play, replace the front wheel bearings. Refer to Section 04-01 
or Section 04-02 for the removal and installation procedure.

To check the tie rod end, perform the following procedure:

With one front wheel raised, try to rock it back and forth with the 
opposite wheel grounded or blocked. If any play is felt, check the tie rod end 
for play or looseness. If any is present, replace the tie rod end. Repeat for 
the other tie rod end.

[FIGURE: F8571A.gif]

To check the front suspension lower arm and front stabilizer bar, 
perform the following procedure:

Check the front suspension lower arms, the front stabilizer bar, and 
the axle torsion beam arms for signs of damage and possible deformation due to 
curb impacts, improper hoisting, etc. If any such damage is evident, carefully 
measure and compare the component with its opposite-side counterpart to detect 
any differences. Check all front and rear suspension rubber bushings for wear 
or deterioration while supporting the vehicle and the bushed component so that 
the bushing carries no load. If any unrestrained motion (free play) is 
apparent in a shake test, the bushing should be replaced.

 Shock Absorber Checks 

Visually inspect each component of the strut assembly for leakage or 
other signs of damage. To check the strut assembly perform the following:

Bounce test the vehicle at each front corner and at the rear bumper to 
check shock absorber function. Damping action should be positive and uniform 
all around. Inspect the shock absorber for evidence of oil leakage. A thin 
film is normal. Check the rear strut upper and lower bushings by shake-testing 
with the vehicle raised just enough to unload the struts (wheels still on the 
ground). Any looseness is indicative of worn or deteriorated bushings, which 
must be replaced.

Cycle the shock absorber piston rod up and down to check for proper 
fluid resistance.

[FIGURE: F8566A.gif]

 Suspension, Rear 

Replace any damaged or worn components. Refer to Section 04-02 for the 
procedure. 

At regular intervals, the following rear suspension checks should be 
made: 

Check for evidence of fluid leaks on rear shock absorbers (18125). 
(Make sure fluid is not from sources other than rear shock absorber).

Check rear shock absorber operation. 

Check condition of axle torsion beam bushings. 

The rear wheel bearings should be checked using the following procedure:

Raise the rear of the vehicle and check for loose rear wheel bearings 
(1225) by rocking the tires at top and bottom.

Spin the tire quickly by hand and verify that the tire turns smoothly 
without noise from the rear wheel bearings.

[FIGURE: F8572A.gif]

If any looseness or noise is found, replace the rear wheel bearings. 
Refer to Section 04-02 for the removal and installation procedure.

ADJUSTMENTS

Alignment, Front

Wheel alignment should be checked only after the following conditions 
have been met: 

All excessive mud, dirt, and road deposit accumulation have been 
removed from chassis and underbody.

Inspection has ruled out the possibility of worn or damaged suspension 
components which need to be replaced. 

Heavy cargo items have been removed and vehicle attitude is correct. 

Spare tire, wheel (1007), jack (17080), and jack handle are in position.

Front seats are in rearmost position.

Tire condition and inflation (cold) have been verified to be uniform 
and correct. 

Wheel bearing preload has been checked, and adjusted if necessary.

Fuel tank (9002), oil pan (6675), and radiator (8005) are filled to 
specification. If necessary, add 3 kg (6 lb) of weight to the trunk for each 
gallon of gasoline missing from the fuel tank.

 Equipment Installation 

Equipment used for front-wheel alignment inspection must be accurate. 
All wheel alignment readings must be performed on an alignment rack level to 
within 1.5mm (1/16 inch) side-to-side and front-to-rear. The instrumentation 
used must have a means of compensating for wheel runout.

The alignment rack must be level and the front tires positioned on 
swivel plates. If using magnetic-type hub gauges, the lug bolt (1107) must be 
removed and replaced with hub gauge adapters. Clip-on type gauges may be 
seated directly on the face of the wheel bearing bore once the hub grease cap 
(1131) is removed.

Install the wheel alignment equipment on the vehicle and follow the 
installation and inspection instructions provided by the manufacturer.

[FIGURE: F5574B.gif]

 Caster and Camber 

Caster is controlled by fixed vehicle dimensions and is not adjustable, 
but it is checked as a possible cause of a variety of suspension system 
problems. If not within specification (refer to Specifications in this 
section), look for damaged suspension components, deteriorated bushings, or 
distorted body mounting points.

The front struts can be mounted in the strut towers two ways, resulting 
in a camber variation of approximately 1/2 degree. White alignment marks on 
the front shock absorber mounting brackets (18183) indicate which setting is 
in effect. These marks should be on the outboard side of the struts if the 
setting has not been changed from the original installation. Changing the 
setting will increase camber by approximately 1/2 degree. Conversely, if the 
marks are inboard, camber can only be reduced. 

If camber is not within specification limits, increase or reduce the 
camber setting:

Raise the vehicle until the tire is clear, and remove the wheel and 
tire assembly.

Remove the front shock absorber mounting bracket nuts at the top of the 
strut tower. 

[FIGURE: F8168B.gif]

Lower the front coil spring (5310) and front shock absorber (18124) to 
clear the studs and rotate the front shock absorber mounting bracket 180 
degrees. 

[FIGURE: F8169B.gif]

Install the front coil spring and front shock absorber in the shock 
tower and tighten the front shock absorber mounting bracket nuts to 46-63 Nm
 (34-46 lb-ft).

 Toe 

Raise the front tires and rotate them through one revolution while 
marking a chalk line at the center of the tire tread. Verify that the line is 
centered all the way around the tire, to rule out the possibility of wheel or 
tire runout. 

Lower the vehicle and bounce the front end to normalize wheel position. 

Measure the distance between right and left tread center lines at front 
wheel knuckle height at the front and rear of the tires. Subtract the front 
measurement from the rear to determine the toe-in. If the front measurement is 
greater than the rear, a toe-out condition exists which must be corrected. 

If toe is not within specification limits, prepare for adjustment as 
follows:

Place alignment marks on the front wheel spindle tie rods (3280), tie 
rod end (3A130), and front wheel spindle tie rod or tie rod end jam nuts. 

Release the bellows clamps. 

Be sure the bellows are free on the front wheel spindle tie rods to 
prevent twisting them.

Loosen the front wheel spindle tie rod or tie rod end jam nuts.

Adjust toe by turning both front wheel spindle tie rods into or out of 
the tie rod end to decrease or increase toe-in, respectively. Adjust by equal 
amounts right and left to avoid changing the steering wheel centering. 

If the steering angle and wheel centering adjustments described 
elsewhere in this section resulted in unequal steering angles, the toe 
adjustments should be made to reduce, rather than increase, the difference.

 Reference Definitions 

[FIGURE: F8171B.gif]

 Wheel/Tire Runout 

Excessive radial and lateral runout of a wheel and tire assembly can 
cause roughness, vibration, wheel tramp and steering wheel nibble (tremor).

Check runout only after the vehicle has been driven to avoid false 
readings caused by temporary flat spots in the tires. Visually inspect the 
tire carcass for abnormal bulges or distortions.

Runout should be measured with Rotunda Radial Runout Gauge 007-0056A or 
equivalent. All measurements should be made on the vehicle with the tires 
inflated to recommended tire pressures.

Measure the wheel radial and lateral runout at the positions shown in 
the following illustration. The wheel runout must not exceed 1.0mm (0.039 
inch) in either position.

Measure the radial runout of the tires at the center and outside ribs 
of the tread face using Rotunda Radial Runout Gauge 007-0056A or equivalent. 
Measure the lateral runout of the tire just above the buffing rib on the tire 
sidewall. Mark the high points of lateral and radial runout for future 
reference. On tires, radial runout should not exceed 1.5mm (0.06 inch), and 
lateral runout should not be more than 2.5mm (0.10 inch). 

[FIGURE: F5303B.gif]

 Tire Lead 

"Lead" is the deviation of the vehicle from a straight path on a level 
road with no pressure on the steering wheel. Lead can be caused by: 

Incorrect wheel alignment 

Uneven brake adjustment 

Uneven or incorrect tire inflation pressure 

Faulty tire construction 

The way in which a tire is constructed can produce a lead. Off-center 
belts on a radial tire can cause the tire to develop a side force while 
rolling straight down the road. If one side of the tire is slightly larger in 
diameter than the other, the tire will have a tendency to roll to one side. 
This will develop a side force which can produce lead.

 Tire Wear Condition Chart 

[FIGURE: F8028F.gif]

 Bearing, Front Wheel 

Refer to Section 04-01 for the front wheel bearing adjustment procedure.

 Bearing, Rear Wheel

adjustment procedures.

ADJUSTMENTS

Alignment Procedure

The MacPherson strut suspension system is integrated into the vehicle 
structure at all four wheels. This minimizes the number of points that can be, 
or need to be, adjusted. Front toe is adjustable, and two available settings 
make limited camber adjustment possible. Caster is established by front 
suspension mounting points and can be adjusted only by replacing worn or 
damaged components. 

Before measuring and setting the front-wheel alignment, rest the front 
tires on turn plates. 

Before setting any alignment angle, bounce the vehicle three times at 
each end. This establishes the actual standing curb height (trim height).

Always perform a wheel alignment on a level alignment rack. Do not 
attempt to check or adjust the front wheel alignment without first making a 
preliminary inspection of the front end parts. 

Check all the factors of the front-wheel alignment except turning angle 
before making any adjustments. Check the turning angle only after the camber 
and toe have been adjusted to specification. Check the front-wheel alignment 
under the following curb load conditions: 

Standing curb height established. 

Heavy weights in trunk removed (i.e., golf clubs, tool box, etc.). 

All tires inflated to specified pressure (cold). 

Fuel tank (9002), oil pans (6675) and radiator (8005) filled to 
specification. If necessary, add 3 kg (6 lb) of weight to the trunk for each 
gallon of gasoline missing from the fuel tank. 

Front seats in full rear position. 

Rear toe checked.

Always road test a vehicle after an alignment. If the vehicle still 
pulls, never condemn the alignment until first switching the front tires. This 
will usually cure any pull problem. If the vehicle still pulls in the same 
direction, double check the alignment and rear tracking. If the vehicle pulls 
in the opposite direction, rotate the tires and road test the vehicle again. 
Refer to Section 04-04 for proper rotation procedure.

================================================================================
PAGE 2449
================================================================================

Section 04-00: Suspension — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Toe and Steering Wheel Spoke Position

When making a toe adjustment, turn the front wheel spindle tie rods 
(3280) by equal amounts in order to avoid changing the steering wheel 
centering. If the steering wheel (3600) is off-center after making a toe 
adjustment, center the steering wheel. Refer to the procedure in this section.

PAGE 2450
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-00: Suspension — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Steering Wheel Centering 

Shift the steering gear rack to the equal angle setting. 

With the wheels (1007) straight ahead, remove and shift the steering 
wheel (3600) on the column serrations as close as possible to the centered 
position. 

Install the steering wheel.

 NOTE: If the toe is to be checked, do not tighten the tie rod end jam nuts at 
this time. 

Tighten the tie rod end jam nuts to 34-50 Nm (25-36 
lb-ft). 

Position the bellows in the undercuts on the front wheel spindle tie 
rods (3280), and secure with the front wheel spindle tie rod bellow clips.

 Steering Angle Check 

 NOTE: Perform the steering angle check before toe measurement (if any 
steering angle corrections have been made). 

Check the wheel steering angles at full right and left positions. If 
the angles are not equal from wheel to wheel, the front wheel spindle tie rods 
must be adjusted to the right or left until the steering angles are equal.

Front wheel spindle tie rod adjustment affects the centering of the 
steering wheel in the straight ahead position. Adjustments can be fine-tuned 
by shifting the front wheel spindle tie rods a small amount away from the 
equal angle setting. If the steering wheel cannot be centered with the 
steering angles within specification, check for improper assembly or 
installation of the following steering components:

Steering gear housing (3548)

Steering column

Steering column intermediate shaft coupling (3A525)

Steering wheel

If necessary, refer to Section 11-00 for steering system servicing.

Adjust the steering angles as follows:

With paint or marking pen, mark both tie rod ends (3A130), front wheel 
spindle tie rods, and tie rod end jam nuts in their original positions. These 
reference marks will help in equalizing right and left adjustments.

[FIGURE: F5286B.gif]

Remove the bellows clamps and free the bellows to prevent them from 
being twisted when the front wheel spindle tie rods are turned. 

Loosen and back off the tie rod end jam nuts. 

To avoid toe change, turn one front wheel spindle tie rod into, and the 
other out of, the tie rod ends, by equal amounts. This shortens one front 
wheel spindle tie rod and lengthens the other, shifting the steering gear rack 
right or left until the steering gear rack teeth are centered on the steering 
gear input worm gear and bearing, and steering gear rack travel from the 
centered position is equal in both directions. This equalizes the wheel 
steering angles, but also rotates the steering gear input worm gear and 
bearing and steering wheel. 

[FIGURE: F5580D.gif]

Position the wheels straight ahead and check the steering wheel 
centering. If close to correct, turn both front wheel spindle tie rods left or 
right without turning the wheels to center the steering wheel. A shift to the 
left will turn the steering wheel clockwise, and a shift to the right will 
turn it counterclockwise, as seen from the driver seat.

Verify that the wheel steering angles are still within specification. 
If not within specification, the steering wheel can be removed and shifted on 
the steering column to center it. Refer to the procedure in this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Suspension, Rear

Rear wheel alignment is controlled by axle torsion beam arms carrying 
the rear wheel spindles (4A013), connected and aligned by a semi-rigid axle 
torsion beam . Torsional flexing of the axle torsion beam permits, and 
stabilizes, semi-independent rear wheel action. 

Limited side-to-side adjustment of the axle torsion beam is provided to 
center the suspension for true tracking. This adjustment is part of the rear 
suspension installation and seldom requires service attention. 

Deviations from the specification for rear wheel camber and toe can 
only result from distortion of the axle torsion beam structure by improper 
hoisting, road impact, or collision damage.

================================================================================
PAGE 2453
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-00: Suspension — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Alignment, Rear

The only rear suspension adjustment that can be made in service is the 
lateral positioning of the axle torsion beam for tracking. Refer to Section 04-02 for the procedure. 

 Toe, Rear 

Rear wheel toe is determined by the axle torsion beam arms and is not 
adjustable. Toe out of specification indicates axle torsion beam distortion, 
resulting from curb impacts, collision damage, or improper hoisting. 
Correction of rear toe out of specification (other than a lateral adjustment) 
requires replacement of the axle torsion beam. Refer to Section 04-02 for the 
removal and installation procedure.

 Camber, Rear 

Rear wheel camber is determined by the axle torsion beam arms and is 
not adjustable. Camber out of specification indicates axle torsion beam 
distortion, resulting from curb impacts, collision damage, or improper 
hoisting. Correction of rear camber out of specification (other than a lateral 
adjustment) requires replacement of the axle torsion beam. Refer to Section 04-02 for the removal and installation procedure.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suspension

The front suspension system is a MacPherson strut layout with single 
pivot forged front suspension lower arms.

The front wheel driveshaft and joints (3B436) connect the transaxle to 
the wheel hubs (1104). The front wheel knuckle (3K185) is the steering, 
suspension, and support member for the wheels (1007). As a steering member, the 
front wheel knuckle is connected to the tie rod end (3A130). As a suspension 
member, the front wheel knuckle is connected to the front suspension lower arm 
(3078) and the front spring and shock. As a support member, the front wheel 
knuckle contains the inner and outer front wheel bearings (1216). The brake 
components associated with the wheel hub include the front disc brake caliper 
(2B120), which is mounted on the front wheel knuckle, and the front disc brake 
rotor (1125), which is mounted on the wheel hub flange. 

The upper end of each front spring and shock is seated in shock towers 
in the engine compartment which govern camber and caster settings. Caster is 
not adjustable, but the front spring and shock mounting studs are located 
off-center to give a choice of two camber settings.

================================================================================
PAGE 2457
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-01: Suspension and Wheel Hubs, Front

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Components

The front suspension consists of the following: 

Transverse front stabilizer bar (5482): Limit sway and double as a 
trailing arm on each side to maintain front suspension lower arm alignment. 
The front stabilizer bar also transmits forces to control vehicle roll during 
cornering.

Front suspension lower arms (3078): Include integral front suspension 
lower arm ball joints which are pivot points for suspension travel and wheel 
turning. The front wheels (1007) are mounted on front wheel knuckles (3K185), 
which are clamped to the front suspension lower arm ball joints and bolted to 
the front spring and shock lower ends. The front suspension lower arm also 
controls lateral (side-to-side) movement of each front wheel.

Front shock absorber mounting brackets (18183): Isolate the front shock 
absorber (18124) and front coil spring (5310) from the body. 

Front coil springs: Allow proper setting of suspension ride heights and 
control suspension travel during driving/handling maneuvers. 

Front wheel knuckles: Transmit steering input by pivoting about the 
front suspension lower arm ball joints and struts, house driveline components 
which propel the vehicle and support the disc brake calipers (2B120) . 

Stabilizer bar brackets (5486): Attach the front stabilizer bar to the 
vehicle.

Front shock absorbers: Provide dynamic damping of suspension and limit 
upward and downward movement of the front wheels. Provide lateral, 
longitudinal, and vertical support for the front wheels.

Rubber bushings at the front suspension lower arm and front stabilizer 
bar mounting points: Cushion road shocks and control suspension alignment.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Component Replacement

The front suspension system is a MacPherson strut layout with single 
pivot forged front suspension lower arms (3078). The following components may 
be replaced individually or as an assembly:

The front shock absorber (18124) and front coil spring (5310) assembly 
may be disassembled in order to replace any of the individual components. They 
do not need to be replaced in pairs.

The front suspension lower arm includes an integral front suspension 
lower arm ball joint that is replaced with the front suspension lower arm. The 
front suspension lower arm inner pivot bushing may be replaced individually.

All front stabilizer bar components may be replaced individually.

The left front wheel knuckle (3K185) or right front wheel knuckle 
(3K186) may be replaced individually.

The wheel hub (1104) may be replaced individually.

The inner and outer front wheel bearings (1216) and the inner and outer 
races are replaced as a set.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fasteners, Suspension 

Suspension fasteners are important attaching parts in that they could 
affect performance of vital components and systems, and/or could result in 
major service expense. They must be replaced with fasteners of the same part 
number or with an equivalent part if replacement becomes necessary. Do not use 
a replacement part of lesser quality or substitute design. Torque values must 
be as specified during assembly to ensure proper retention of parts. New 
fasteners must be used whenever old fasteners are loosened or removed and when 
new components are installed.

================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-01: Suspension and Wheel Hubs, Front

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Shock Absorber 

The function of the front shock absorber (18124) in the MacPherson 
suspension system is to guide, dampen, and limit wheel motion. Acting as a 
structural member of the suspension system, the front shock absorber dampens 
the up and down loads that are placed on a vehicle body when changing road 
conditions are met. 

In addition to allowing for the up and down movement of the wheel, the 
front shock absorber is part of the axis that is needed for wheel turning. The 
front shock absorber (upper) mounting bracket and outer canister is allowed to 
rotate relative to the front shock absorber piston rod. The rotating movement 
of the front shock absorber must be free from binding, sticking and friction 
conditions to ease steering effort. To reduce friction, a garter spring seal 
surrounding the piston rod shaft and a low-friction bearing surface between 
the front shock absorber piston and pressure tube have been provided. 

Since the front shock absorber carries a side load at all times on a 
vehicle, its dampening forces are much higher while on a vehicle than the 
dampening forces when the front shock absorber is out of the vehicle. Side 
loading increases dampening resistance of a front shock absorber by providing 
higher friction internally, and for this reason, front shock absorbers are 
designed with low dampening forces while standing in the free state (not on 
the vehicle). 

When a gas-pressurized front shock absorber is held in a vertical 
position, it is normal for it to be fully extended. 

The following definitions will indicate when a front shock absorber 
should or should not be replaced because of oil weepage or leakage: 

 Weepage is a condition in which a thin film of 
oil may be deposited on the front shock absorber outer tube (body), and is 
normally noticed due to the collection of dust in this area. This condition is 
normal during the front shock absorber seal break-in period of 4827-8045 km 
(3000-5000 miles) and may or may not occur in some front shock absorbers. 
Although the film of oil may be noticed on most of the front shock absorber 
body, the amount of weeped oil required to cause this film is less than one 
percent of the total front shock absorber oil and, therefore, does not affect 
the performance of the front shock absorber. Normally, weepage stops after the 
initial dampening (wetting) of the front shock absorber body and seal break-in 
period. No sign of new oil is visible. 

 Leakage is a condition in which the entire front 
shock absorber body is covered with oil that has dripped down onto the front 
suspension lower arm (3078) and onto the pavement during overnight parking. In 
this case, the front shock absorber always shows a wet surface and does not 
dry as in weepage. 

A front shock absorber should only be replaced if it shows signs of 
leakage as described, but not if it falls under the description of weepage. 

 NOTE: If a front shock absorber needs replacement, it is not necessary to replace both RH and LH front shock absorbers. Only the 
front shock absorber in question should be replaced.

If the front shock absorber piston rod does not extend on a front shock 
absorber when removed from the vehicle, the front shock absorber should be 
replaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Bearing and Wheel Hub

The wheel hub (1104) is supported in the front wheel knuckle (3K185) on 
opposed outer and inner front wheel bearings (1216). A press fit secures the 
bearing inner races to the wheel hub and the bearing outer races in the front 
wheel knuckle. Front wheel bearing preload is set using a selective front 
wheel outer bearing retainer washer (1195). The front wheel outer bearing 
retainer washer is located between the outer front wheel bearing and the inner 
front wheel bearing.

The front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B436), which is splined to the 
wheel hub, is secured to the wheel hub with a staked front axle wheel hub 
retainer (3B477) and a large front axle wheel hub retainer washer (3Z499). 
Whenever the front axle wheel hub retainer is loosened, it must be replaced 
with a new front axle wheel hub retainer.

[FIGURE: F5943C.gif]

assembly must rotate freely by hand. 

Install a new front axle wheel hub retainer. Tighten the front axle 
wheel hub retainer to 157-235 Nm (116-174 lb-ft).

 CAUTION: Do not use a pointed tool. If the front axle wheel hub retainer cracks 
even slightly during staking, replace it with a new front axle wheel hub 
retainer. 

Stake the front axle wheel hub retainer into the shaft groove.

[FIGURE: E8893B.gif]

Connect the tie rod end to the front wheel knuckle and install the tie 
rod end nut. Tighten the tie rod end nut to 29-44 Nm (22-33 
lb-ft).

 NOTE: If the openings in the tie rod end nut and the hole in the tie rod end

point of alignment. Never loosen the tie rod end nut. 

Install a new cotter pin through the tie rod end nut and the tie rod 
end ball stud.

Install the wheel and tire assembly. Tighten the lug bolts (1107) to 
88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft). 

Lower the vehicle.

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Spring and Shock Assembly

 Removal 

Raise the front of the vehicle until the front coil springs (5310) and 
front shock absorbers (18124) are fully extended, and support the vehicle on 
jack stands. 

Remove the wheel and tire assembly. 

Remove the brake hose clip (2814) from the front shock absorber lower 
bracket and disengage the front brake hose (2078). 

[FIGURE: F5943C.gif]

Remove the two front spring and shock bracket bolts and nuts. 

[FIGURE: F5925C.gif]

Remove the two front shock absorber mounting bracket nuts. 

Remove the front spring and shock bracket from the front wheel knuckle 
(3K185) and lower the front shock absorber clear of the wheel well.

 Installation 

Position the front shock absorber, with front spring insulator (5414) 
in place, in the front shock absorber tower with the white alignment spot 
facing outboard. 

Install the front shock absorber mounting bracket nuts. Tighten the 
front shock absorber mounting bracket nuts to 46-63 Nm (34-46 
lb-ft). 

Install the front wheel knuckle in the front spring and shock bracket 
and install the two front spring and shock bracket bolts and nuts. Tighten the 
front spring and shock bracket nuts to 93-117 Nm (69-86 
lb-ft). 

[FIGURE: G6070C.gif]

Position the front brake hose in the cutout on the front shock absorber 
lower bracket and secure it with the brake hose clip. 

Install the wheel and tire assembly. Tighten the lug bolts (1107) to 
88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft). 

Remove the jack stands and lower the front of the vehicle.

C-Frame and Clamp Assembly

T74P-3044-A1

Lower Control Arm Bushing Tool

T81P-5493-B

 Removal 

Raise and support the vehicle.

Remove the wheel and tire assembly.

Remove the front suspension lower arm-to-chassis bolt and washer. 

Remove the front suspension lower arm ball joint bolt, washer, and nut 
from the front wheel knuckle (3K185). 

[FIGURE: G6072C.gif]

Remove the cotter pin and the front stabilizer bar nut from the rear of 
the front suspension lower arm (3078), and remove the front stabilizer bar 
washer and front stabilizer bar bushing. 

Lower the front suspension lower arm, prying the front suspension lower 
arm ball joint stud out of the front wheel knuckle, if necessary. Disengage the 
front suspension lower arm from the front stabilizer bar end and remove the 
front suspension lower arm.

Before installing the front suspension lower arm, inspect the front 
suspension lower arm and the front suspension lower arm mounting bolt bushing 
(3069). Refer to the procedure in this section.

 Installation 

Inspect the front suspension lower arm mounting bolt bushing for damage 
or excessive wear. If necessary, install a new front suspension lower arm 
mounting bolt bushing. Refer to the procedure in this section.

With the front stabilizer bar washer and the front stabilizer bar 
bushing positioned on the front stabilizer bar end, position the front 
suspension lower arm over the front stabilizer bar (5482). 

Raise the front suspension lower arm inner end into the pivot bracket 
on the chassis, and finger-tighten the front suspension lower arm-to-chassis 
bolt to hold it in place. 

Position the front suspension lower arm ball joint stud in the front 
wheel knuckle bore and install the front suspension lower arm ball joint bolt 
and the front suspension lower arm ball joint nut.

[FIGURE: F5556C.gif]

Install the front stabilizer bar bushing, washer and the front 
stabilizer bar nut. Tighten the front stabilizer bar nut to 64-77 Nm
 (47-57 lb-ft). Install a new cotter pin. 

Tighten the front suspension lower arm-to-chassis bolt to 54-68 Nm
 (40-50 lb-ft). 

Use a second wrench to hold the front suspension lower arm ball joint 
bolt and tighten the front suspension lower arm ball joint nut to 43-54 Nm
 (32-40 lb-ft).

Install the wheel and tire assembly. Tighten the lug bolts (1107) to 
88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft).

Lower the vehicle.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Stabilizer Bar

 Removal 

Raise and support the vehicle.

Remove the four stabilizer bar bracket nuts and the two stabilizer bar 
brackets (5486).

[FIGURE: F5553C.gif]

Remove the lower suspension arm stabilizer bar insulators (5493) from 
the front stabilizer bar (5482).

Remove the cotter pins and front stabilizer bar nuts at the front 
suspension lower arms (3078), and remove the rear washers and front stabilizer 
bar bushings. Discard the cotter pins.

[FIGURE: F5519C.gif]

Pull the stabilizer bar forward to remove it from the front suspension 
lower arms. 

Inspect the front stabilizer bar bushings and washers. If they are 
warped or damaged, replace the front stabilizer bar bushings and washers.

 Installation 

Install half of the stabilizer bar bushings and washers on the ends of 
the front stabilizer bar.

Insert the front stabilizer ends into the front suspension lower arms 
and position the rear half of the front stabilizer bar bushings and washers on 
the front stabilizer bar ends, installing the front stabilizer bar nuts 
finger-tight. 

[FIGURE: F5536B.gif]

Install the lower suspension arm stabilizer bar insulators on the front 
stabilizer cross bar with the split side forward, and position them next to 
the white locating marks on the front stabilizer bar.

Install the two stabilizer bar brackets. Tighten the four stabilizer 
bar bracket nuts to 54-68 Nm (40-50 lb-ft).

Tighten the front stabilizer bar nuts to 64-77 Nm 
(47-57 lb-ft). Install new cotter pins.

Lower the vehicle.

 Bushing 

 Removal 

Remove the front stabilizer bar. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Remove the two front stabilizer bar bushings and washers from the front 
stabilizer bar end.

[FIGURE: F5536B.gif]

 Installation 

To install, reverse the removal procedure.

 Mounting Bracket Insulator 

 Removal 

Raise and support the vehicle.

Remove the four stabilizer bar bracket nuts and the stabilizer bar 
brackets. 

[FIGURE: F5553C.gif]

Remove the lower suspension arm stabilizer bar insulator.

 Installation 

To install, reverse the removal procedure.

Tighten the stabilizer bar bracket nuts to 54-68 Nm 
(40-50 lb-ft).

 Bracket 

 Removal 

Remove the two stabilizer bar bracket nuts and the stabilizer bar 
bracket.

[FIGURE: F5553C.gif]

 Installation 

To install, reverse the removal procedure.

Tighten the stabilizer bar bracket nuts to 54-68 Nm 
(40-50 lb-ft).

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Spring and Shock Assembly

 Front Spring and Shock — Exploded View 

[FIGURE: F5555E.gif]

 Disassembly 

Pry out the front shock absorber strut cover cup (18A179) and remove 
the front suspension nut and front suspension lockwasher. 

Secure the front shock absorber mounting bracket (18183) in a vise. 
Turn the shock absorber piston rod nut one revolution to loosen.

Use Rotunda Spring Compressor 164-R3571 or equivalent, and compress the 
front coil spring (5310) to unload the front shock absorber (18124).

[FIGURE: F6603D.gif]

Remove the front shock absorber mounting bracket and front spring 
insulator (5415). 

Remove the front suspension washer (5Z318), front suspension seal 
(5A318), and front suspension bearing and seal (3B455) from the front shock 
absorber piston rod. 

Remove the spring seat, front spring insulator (5414), and front coil 
spring. 

Slide the front shock absorber jounce bumper (18A085) off the front 
shock absorber.

 CAUTION: If replacing a front coil spring, release the spring compressor 
progressively to prevent spring arching. Open the compressor jaws wide enough 
to grip the new front coil spring in the same position, and tighten the 
compressor screws progressively, compressing the front coil spring until the 
front shock absorber can be assembled without interference. 

Before assembly, inspect the front shock absorbers. Refer to the 
procedure in this section.

 Assembly 

Slide the front shock absorber jounce bumper (18A085) onto the front 
shock absorber piston rod and over the front shock absorber body. 

Install the compressed front coil spring (5310), front spring insulator 
(5414), and spring seat, positioning the front coil spring end against the 
step in the spring seat. 

Install the front suspension bearing and seal (3B455), front suspension 
seal (5A318), and front suspension washer (5Z318) on the front shock absorber 
piston rod. 

Install the front shock absorber mounting bracket (18183) with the 
white alignment spot on the same side of the front shock absorber (18124) as 
the front wheel knuckle mounting bracket. 

Install the front spring insulator. 

Secure the front shock absorber piston rod in the front shock absorber 
mounting bracket with the front suspension lockwasher and front suspension 
nut. Tighten the front suspension nut to 54-67 Nm (40-50 
lb-ft). 

Release and remove the spring compressor.

from the front wheel knuckle (3K185) is not part of normal bearing service.

Use Knuckle Puller T87C-1104-A and Hub/Bearing Remover Adapter

 NOTE: The front wheel outer bearing retainer washer (1195) is preselected to

Remove the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer from the wheel hub.

[FIGURE: F5067D.gif]

Remove the outer front wheel bearing (1216) from the wheel hub using 
Bearing Pulling Attachment D84L-1123-A or equivalent, Shaft Protector 
D80L-625-2 or equivalent, and a press.

[FIGURE: F5525D.gif]

Remove the inner wheel bearing oil seal (1177) from the wheel hub.

[FIGURE: F5948B.gif]

 Assembly 

 NOTE: If the inner or outer front wheel bearing or front wheel knuckle have 
been replaced, bearing preload must be checked before assembly. Refer to the 
procedure in this section. 

If the front disc brake rotor shield was removed for replacement, 
install a new one using Dust Shield Replacer T94C-1175-B and Driver Handle 
T80T-4000-W.

[FIGURE: F5522D.gif]

Use Bearing Cup Replacer D79P-1202-A, or equivalent, and Driver Handle 
T80T-4000-W, and install the bearing races in the front wheel knuckle.

[FIGURE: F5529C.gif]

Pack the inner and outer front wheel bearings with Premium Long Life 
Grease XG-1-C, or -K, or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Pack the wheel hub area, as shown in the installed view below.

[FIGURE: F5074C.gif]

Place the inner front wheel bearing into the front wheel knuckle bore, 
so that it rests in a level position.

[FIGURE: F5952C.gif]

 NOTE: Form the lubricant into a strip, concentrated along the edges of the 
inner wheel bearing oil seal lips.

Lubricate the lip of the new inner wheel bearing oil seal with Premium 
Long Life Grease XG-1-C, or -K, or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M1C75-B.

[FIGURE: F5078B.gif]

Use Seal Replacer T87C-1175-A and Driver Handle T80T-4000-W and install 
the new inner wheel bearing oil seal in the bore.

[FIGURE: F5528E.gif]

Place the original front wheel outer bearing retainer washer, or the 
front wheel outer bearing retainer washer selected from the front wheel 
bearing adjustment procedure, in the front wheel knuckle bore. 

Position the outer front wheel bearing in the front wheel knuckle bore.

 NOTE: Form the lubricant into a strip, concentrated along the edges of the 
inner wheel bearing oil seal lip. 

Lubricate the lip of a new inner wheel bearing oil seal with Premium 
Long Life Grease XG-1-C, or -K, or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M1C75-B.

Use Seal Replacer T87C-1175-A and Driver Handle T80T-4000-W and install 
the new inner wheel bearing oil seal in the front wheel knuckle bore.

Use spacer from Spacer Selection Tool T87C-1104-B and position the 
wheel hub/front disc brake rotor assembly in the front wheel knuckle bore and 
press it into position.

[FIGURE: F5527B.gif]

Install the front wheel hub, wheel knuckle and wheel bearing assembly. 
Refer to the procedure in this section.

Front Wheel Knuckle

Tighten the nut, in increments, to 49, 98, 147, and 196 Nm
 (36, 72, 108, and 145 lb-ft). After tightening the nut to 
each specified increment, seat the bearings by rotating the front wheel 
knuckle. 

Remove the front wheel knuckle and Spacer Selection Tool T87C-1104-B 
from the vise. 

Mount the front wheel knuckle in a vise, clamping the front wheel 
knuckle where the spring and shock mount to the front wheel knuckle.

 NOTE: The torque wrench reading must be taken just as the tool starts to 
rotate. 

Measure the amount of torque required to rotate the Spacer Selector 
Tool T87C-1104-B, using an inch-pound torque wrench.

If the torque wrench indicates 0.25-1.8 Nm (2.2-10.4 
lb-in), the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer (1195) is the correct 
thickness. 

If the torque wrench indicates less than 0.25 Nm (2.2 
lb-in), a thinner front wheel outer bearing retainer washer must be installed. 

If the torque wrench indicates more than 1.8 N.m (10.4 lb-in), a thicker 
front wheel outer bearing retainer washer must be installed.

Select a front wheel outer bearing retainer washer using the 
measurement obtained above and the following chart.

Each front wheel outer bearing retainer washer is assigned a numerical 
code that identifies its thickness. The code is stamped into the outer 
diameter of the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer. The numbers range 
from 1-21, with one being the thinnest front wheel outer bearing retainer 
washer. 

If the number stamped on the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer 
is not legible, measure the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer with a 
micrometer and compare it to the chart to determine which number it is. 

Changing the front wheel outer bearing retainer washer thickness by one 
number, either higher or lower, will change bearing preload by 0.2-0.4 Nm
 (1.7-3.5 lb-in).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suspension 

The rear suspension system is a MacPherson strut system, with a rear 
shock absorber (18125) and rear spring (5560) at each wheel, seated in a tower 
in the cargo compartment. 

The rear suspension system works as follows: 

Suspension action is semi-independent, with the wheels carried on the 
axle torsion beam arms rigidly connected to each other by the axle torsion 
beam. 

The axle torsion beam provides positive control of axle torsion beam 
arm alignment, yet flexes in torsion to permit limited independent wheel 
action and doubles as a stabilizer to limit sway. 

For isolation of road vibration, heavy rubber bushings are installed at 
the torsion bar brackets (5596), and rear spring anti-squeak inserts (5586) 
cushion the spring seats in the strut towers. 

Other than rear wheel bearing service, the system is maintenance-free.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Components

 Inspection 

Check for evidence of fluid leaks on therear shock absorbers (18125). A 
light film of fluid is permissible. Verify fluid is not from sources other 
than the rear shock absorber.

Check the rear shock absorber operation (whether operation is stiff, 
tough, or spongy).

Check the condition of axle torsion beam bushings.

If the above checks reveal evidence of excessive wear, deterioration, 
or improper operation, replace damaged components.

 Rear Spring 

The rear spring (5560) provides suspension travel and controls ride 
height. If loading is normal and vehicle attitude is not, check for spring 
damage, spring sag, or non-standard replacement springs.

Check the condition of the jounce bumper, rear shock absorber dust boot 
(18159), rear spring anti-squeak insert (5586), and shock absorber rod 
bushings. If damaged or deteriorated, replace with new parts.

 Wheel Bearings 

The rear wheel and tire assembly is mounted to the brake drum (1126). The
brake drum is supported on opposed tapered roller bearings. The rear wheel 
bearings ride on the left rear wheel spindle (4A013) or right rear wheel 
spindle which is attached to the axle torsion beam arm. The bearings are 
pressed into a hub that is an integral part of the brake drum. The bearing 
lubricant is protected from contamination by an inner wheel bearing oil seal 
(1177) on the inboard side and a hub grease cap (1131) on the outboard side.

 Shock Absorber 

The rear shock absorber reacts to braking forces and provides necessary 
suspension damping. It also provides rebound control through an internal 
rebound stop.

Bounce test the vehicle to check shock absorber function. Damping 
action should be positive and uniform all around.

Inspect the rear shock absorbers for evidence of oil leakage. A thin 
film is normal. Check the rear shock absorber upper and lower bushings by 
shake-testing with the vehicle raised just enough to unload the rear shock 
absorbers (wheels still on the ground). Any looseness is indicative of worn or 
deteriorated bushings, which must be replaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Component Replacement

The following rear suspension components may be replaced either 
individually or as an assembly:

The rear spring and shock absorber assembly may be disassembled in 
order to replace any of the individual components, or it may be replaced as an 
assembly. They do not need to be replaced in pairs.

The rear wheel bearing hub is replaced with the brake drum (1126) as an 
assembly.

Rear wheel bearings are replaced as a set.

The left rear wheel spindle (4A013) and stem or right rear wheel 
spindle and stem are replaced as an assembly.

If equipped with anti-lock brakes, the rear brake anti-lock sensor 
indicator (2C189) is replaced individually.

The axle torsion beam arms and axle torsion beam are replaced as an 
assembly.

The torsion bar brackets (5596) may be replaced individually.

The axle torsion beam bushings may be replaced individually.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Assembly

The rear wheel (1007) and brake drum (1126) are supported on opposed 
tapered roller bearings. The inner rear wheel bearings ride on the left rear 
wheel spindle (4A013) or right rear wheel spindle which are attached to the 
axle torsion beam. The outer rear wheel bearings are housed in a hub that is 
an integral part of the brake drum. Contamination of the bearing lubricant is 
prevented by an inner wheel bearing oil seal (1177) on the inboard side and a 
hub grease cap (1131) on the outboard side. The brake drum is attached to the 
rear wheel spindle with a wheel bearing nut, wheel bearing nut cover, and 
cotter pin. This cotter pin must be discarded after removal. The wheel bearing 
nut and washer are used to hold the bearings and hub in position on the rear 
wheel spindle and to set the rear wheel bearing preload.

Raise and support the vehicle.

Remove the wheel and tire assemblies. 

Remove the leftrear wheel spindle (4A013) and right rear wheel spindle. 
Refer to the procedure in this section. 

Disconnect the rear wheel brake hose (2A442).

Disconnect the front parking brake cable and conduit clevises at the 
brake backing plates (2211). 

Remove the front parking brake cable and conduit (2853) from the axle 
torsion beam. 

Remove the brake shoe hold-down spring (2068) and release the rear 
brake shoe and lining (2001).

Release the brake adjusting hole covers (2092) and pull the rear brake 
anti-lock sensors (2C190) through the brake backing plates.

[FIGURE: F8577B.gif]

Remove the brake backing plate and brake assemblies.

Remove the axle torsion beam nuts. 

[FIGURE: F8557D.gif]

Remove the axle torsion beam bolts (5Z596) from the torsion bar 
brackets (5596) and remove the axle torsion beam.

 NOTE: If the torsion bar brackets are not to be replaced, it may be desirable 
to leave them in place on the body. The torsion bar bracket mounting holes are 
slotted to permit side-to-side adjustment of the axle torsion beam for true 
tracking of the rear suspension. If removed, they require alignment when the 
axle torsion beam is installed. However, if the axle torsion beam is repaired 
or replaced, the alignment must be checked at assembly. 

If necessary, remove the four upper axle torsion beam bolts (5Y596) and 
two lower axle torsion beam bolts. Remove the two torsion bar brackets.

 Installation 

If removed, install the twotorsion bar brackets on the body with 
flatwashers, lockwashers, two upper axle torsion beam bolts, and one lower 
axle torsion beam bolt on each side. Do not tighten the bolts at this time. 

If installing a new axle torsion beam, install the axle torsion beam 
bushings. Refer to the procedure in this section. 

Install the bushing flange washers and position the axle torsion beam 
arms in the torsion bar brackets. 

Align the bolt holes and install the axle torsion beam bolts and 
lockwashers. Loosely install the axle torsion beam nuts.

Position the brake backing plates.

Route the rear brake anti-lock sensor through the brake backing plates 
and secure the rear brake shoe and lining.

Install the left rear wheel spindle and right rear wheel spindle. Refer 
to the procedure in this section.

Install the front parking brake cable and conduit equalizer on the axle 
torsion beam and connect the front parking brake cable and conduit clevises to 
the levers with clevis pins and cotter pins. 

Connect the right and left rear wheel brake hose at the rear brake hose 
support bracket (2073) and clip in place. 

Install the wheel and tire assemblies, tighten the lug bolts (1107) to 
88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft) and lower the vehicle to load the 
suspension to normal ride height. 

Tighten the axle torsion beam nuts to 93-117 Nm (69-86 
lb-ft). 

Check rear suspension alignment by locating and marking the center of 
the underbody, at a point of equal distance from the inner and upper right and 
left axle torsion beam bolts. From this point, measure the distance to the 
centers of the shock absorber bolts, right and left. If these measurements are 
not within 5mm (0.2 inch), shift the torsion bar brackets side-to-side to 
center the suspension.

[FIGURE: F5560E.gif]

When centered, tighten the four upper axle torsion beam bolts to 54-68 Nm
 (40-50 lb-ft), and the two lower axle torsion beam bolts 
to 93-117 Nm (69-86 lb-ft). 

Bleed the rear brakes. Refer to Section 06-06 for the procedure.

suspension is fully loaded in its normal riding position. 

Install the axle torsion beam nuts. Tighten the axle torsion beam nuts 
to 93-117 Nm (69-86 lb-ft). 

Bleed the rear brakes. Refer to Section 06-06 for the procedure.

ADJUSTMENTS

Bearing Preload 

Make sure the parking brake is fully released. 

Remove the wheel and tire assembly. 

Remove the hub grease cap (1131).

[FIGURE: H5714C.gif]

Rotate the brake drum (1126) to make sure there is no brake drag. If 
the brakes drag, refer to Section 06-00 for diagnosis.

[FIGURE: F5597C.gif]

Remove the cotter pin, wheel bearing nut cover, and wheel bearing nut. 
Discard the cotter pin.

Install the wheel bearing nut. 

Seat the rear wheel bearings by tightening the wheel bearing nut to 
25-29 Nm (18-22 lb-ft). While tightening the wheel bearing 
nut, rotate the brake drum.

Loosen the wheel bearing nut slightly until it can be turned by hand. 

Before bearing preload can be set, the amount of seal drag must be 
measured and added to the required preload. 

To measure seal drag, install one lug bolt (1107) onto the lug bolt 
positioned at 12 o'clock, and measure the amount of force required to rotate 
the brake drum. 

Pull the torque wrench and note the reading when rotation starts.

Loosely tighten the wheel bearing nut. 

Place In-Lb Torque Wrench D81L-600-A or equivalent onto the lug bolt 
positioned at 12 o'clock and measure the amount of pull required to rotate the 
brake drum. 

Continue tightening the wheel bearing nut until the bearing preload 
specification of 2.6-8.5 N (0.6-1.91 lb) plus the seal drag measurement is 
obtained with the torque wrench.

Install the wheel bearing nut cover and a new cotter pin.

Install the hub grease cap.

Install the wheel and tire assembly. 

Tighten the lug bolts to 88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tire, Temporary Spare

The temporary spare tire is a T105/70D14 mounted on a steel wheel and 
stowed in the spare wheel stowage well. A scissors-type jack (17080) is 
secured to the left of the rear body panel just below the liftgate door.

[FIGURE: Y4950A.gif]

 Directions for Use 

 WARNING: THE TEMPORARY SPARE TIRE IS PROVIDED ONLY FOR TEMPORARY EMERGENCY USE. 
DO NOT USE AS A REGULAR TIRE. SERVICE AND REPLACE THE REGULAR TIRE AS SOON AS 
POSSIBLE. ANY CONTINUOUS ROAD USE OF THIS TEMPORARY, EMERGENCY TIRE MAY RESULT 
IN TIRE FAILURE, LOSS OF VEHICLE CONTROL, AND POSSIBLE INJURY TO VEHICLE 
OCCUPANTS. 

Consider the following:

Check pressure in spare tire at least monthly. If spare tire is in use, 
check pressure when vehicle has been stopped at least three hours or driven 
less than 1.6 km (1 mile). Do not reduce pressure when tire is hot. Use tire 
gauge to check pressure and maintain at 415 kPa (60 psi).

Never overload tires on vehicle. Each individual tire load should never 
exceed tire load capacity molded on sidewall of the tire or the vehicle 
maximum load rating. Refer to the Owner Guide for additional information on 
driving with a heavy load, trailer towing, and limiting your vehicle load.

Do not use tire for extended mileage or for speeds above 80 km/h (50 
mph).

Remove the temporary spare tire as soon as the conventional tire can be 
serviced or replaced.

Avoid abusive use such as driving over potholes and curbs. Tires should 
be replaced when 1.5 mm (1/16 inch) of tread depth remains as indicated by 
tread wear indicators molded into tread grooves.

Do not use tire chains with temporary spare.

Do not use temporary spare for maintenance tire rotation.

Do not attempt to service or remove the temporary spare from its wheel.

Do not attempt to use the wheel for any other type of tire.

================================================================================
PAGE 2502
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 04-04: Wheels and Tires

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tires

 WARNING: DO NOT MIX DIFFERENT TYPES OF TIRES ON THE SAME VEHICLE SUCH AS RADIAL, 
BIAS, OR BIAS-BELTED TIRES EXCEPT IN EMERGENCIES (TEMPORARY SPARE USAGE), 
BECAUSE VEHICLE HANDLING MAY BE SERIOUSLY AFFECTED AND MAY RESULT IN LOSS OF 
CONTROL. 

When replacing tires, it is recommended to use tires of the same size, 
speed rating, load range, and construction type (radial) as originally 
installed on the vehicle. Use of any other tire size or type may seriously 
affect ride, handling, speedometer/odometer calibration, vehicle ground 
clearance, and tire clearance to the body and chassis. 

Consider the following when replacing tires:

To achieve best all around vehicle performance, tires of different 
construction should not be mixed on the same vehicle.

New tires should be installed in pairs on the same axle.

When replacing only one tire, it should be paired with the tire having 
the most tread, to equalize braking traction.

Snow tires should be of a size and type equivalent to other tires on 
the vehicle as recommended on the Tire Size and Inflation Pressure Chart. The 
tire size and inflation pressure chart is on the RH center body pillar of 
2-door vehicles and on either of the two RH doors of 4-door vehicles.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheels

Wheels (1007) must be replaced when they are bent, dented, heavily 
rusted, have air leaks or elongated bolt holes, and have excessive lateral or 
radial runout. Wheels with a lateral or radial runout greater than the 
recommended specification may cause an objectionable, high-speed vehicle 
vibration. 

Replacement wheels must be equal to the original equipment wheels in 
load capacity, diameter, width, offset and mounting configuration. An improper 
wheel may affect wheel and bearing life, ground and tire clearance, or 
speedometer/odometer calibrations.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Assembly 

 Front 

Each front wheel (1007) is bolted to the front wheel hub (1104) and 
front disc brake rotor (1125). The front wheel hub is supported on the left 
front wheel knuckle (3K185) or right front wheel knuckle (3K186) on opposed 
tapered roller bearings. The bearing inner races are press fit to the wheel 
hub and the outer races are press fit in the front wheel knuckle. Bearing 
preload is set using a selective spacer that is installed in the front wheel 
knuckle between the outer bearing and the front axle wheel hub retainer.

 Rear 

The rear wheel is to the brake drum (1126) . The brake drum is 
supported on opposed tapered roller bearings. The bearing inner races ride on 
a left rear wheel spindle (4A013) or right rear wheel spindle which is 
attached to the axle torsion beam. The bearing outer races are pressed into a 
rear wheel hub that is an integral part of the brake drum. The bearing 
lubricant is protected from contamination by an inner wheel bearing oil seal 
(1177) on the inboard side and a hub grease cap (1131) on the outboard side.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification — Wheels and Tires

Inspect the threads and shoulder of the lug bolts (1107) for excessive 
wear or damage, replace as necessary. Tighten lug bolts to 88-118 Nm
 (65-87 lb-ft). Loose lug bolts can cause shimmy and 
vibration, and may also stretch and damage the bolt holes in the wheel (1007).

Ensure wheels and wheel hubs (1104) are clean. Lumps of mud and grease, 
or stones lodged onto the wheel may cause the wheel to be out of balance.

Check for dented, or bent wheels or any other damage. Wobble or shimmy 
caused by a damaged wheel will eventually damage the bearings. 

 Wheel and Tire Checking Procedure 

In order to accurately diagnose concerns about the wheels and tires, 
there are many procedures which may be necessary. These include:

Vibration Concerns Check

Wheel and Tire Runout

Tire Runout

Wheel Runout

Match Mounting Tires

Tire Lead Diagnosis

Always begin with a road test to verify concern. Then, refer to the Vibration Troubleshooting Symptom Chart 
 in this section to identify the area 
of concern. If the concern cannot be isolated, refer to the following 
procedures as applicable:

Vibration concerns check: Vibration, roughness, tramp, shimmy, and 
thump may be caused by excessive tire or wheel runout, worn or cupped tires, 
or wheel and tire imbalance. These conditions may also be caused by rough road 
surfaces. Drive the vehicle on different road surfaces to determine whether 
the surface is the cause of the condition.

Inspect the tires and refer to the Vibration Troubleshooting Symptom 
Chart in this section.

This section of the manual covers only those vibration problems 
actually associated with tires and wheels.

Refer to Section 00-04 for diagnostic procedures and repairs for 
non-tire-related vibrations.

Wheel and tire runout: Excessive radial and lateral runout of a wheel 
and tire assembly can cause roughness, vibration, wheel tramp and steering 
wheel nibble (tremor). 

To avoid false readings caused by temporary flat spots in the tires, 
check runout only after the vehicle has been driven. Visually inspect the tire 
carcass for abnormal bulges or distortions. 

Runout should be measured with a Rotunda Radial Run-Out Gauge 007-0056A 
or equivalent. All measurements should be made on the vehicle with the tires 
inflated to recommended load inflation pressures and with the wheel bearings 
adjusted to specification. Refer to Section 04-00 if necessary.

[FIGURE: F5303B.gif]

Tire runout: Using Rotunda Radial Run-Out Gauge 007-0056A or 
equivalent, measure radial runout of the tire at the center and outside ribs 
of the tread face. Measure lateral runout of the tire just above the buffing 
rib on the tire sidewall. Mark the high-points of lateral and radial runout 
for future reference. On tires, radial runout should not exceed 1.5mm(0.06 
inch), and lateral runout should not be more than 2.5mm (0.10 inch).

Wheel runout: Measure radial and lateral wheel runout at the positions 
shown in the illustration. Runout should not exceed 1.0mm (0.04 inch) in 
either position.

Match mounting tires: Match mounting is a technique used to reduce 
radial runout tire and wheel assemblies. Excessive runout is a source of ride 
complaints and match mounting can be used to minimize the runout. There are 
two ways to use match mounting: positioning of the tire on the wheel and 
positioning the wheel on the wheel hub. 

Measure total indicated runout on the center of the tire tread rib, and 
record it. Mark the tire and rim at the point of greatest runout, and record 
the reading. Mark the tire at the location of the air valve for reference. 

Break down the tire and remount it 180 degrees on the rim so the air 
valve reference mark is opposite the air valve on the wheel. 

Reinflate the tire and measure total indicated runout, and again mark 
the high spot. 

If runout is reduced to acceptable guidelines the tire is ready to be 
put back into service. If runout is still excessive, one of the following 
steps must be performed: 

If the high spot is within 100mm (4 inches) of the first high spot on 
the wheel, the wheel may be out of tolerance. Check the wheel for runout. 

If the high spot is within 100mm (4 inches) of the first high spot on 
the tire, and is still outside of the guidelines, replace the tire. 

Tire lead diagnosis: "Lead" is the deviation of the vehicle from a 
straight path on a level road without pressure on the steering wheel (3600). 
Lead is usually caused by: 

Incorrect wheel alignment. 

Uneven brake adjustment. 

Uneven or incorrect tire inflation pressures. 

Faulty tire construction.

Faulty tire construction, such as off-center radial belts, can produce 
lead. Off-center belts cause a tire to roll to one side, developing a side 
force which causes the tire to lead.

 Tire Lead Diagnosis Chart 

[FIGURE: CF3971D.gif]
