DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Road Test 

Always begin a tire diagnostic procedure with a road test. The road 
test and customer interview (if available) will provide much information 
needed to find the source of the concern. 

During the road test, drive the vehicle on a smooth road. If the 
concern is apparent, note and record the following: 

The speed(s) at which the concern occurs. 

The type of concern (mechanical and/or audible) occurring in each speed 
range. 

How changes in vehicle speed, engine speed, and engine torque affect 
the concern. 

The type of concern sensitivity (torque sensitive, engine speed 
sensitive, or vehicle speed sensitive).

Read the following explanations to help isolate the source of the 
concern.

 Torque Sensitive 

When the concern is torque sensitive, the condition can be improved or 
worsened by heavy acceleration, followed by coasting.

 Vehicle Speed Sensitive 

When the concern is linked to vehicle speed, the concern always occurs 
at the same vehicle speed and is not affected by engine torque, engine speed, 
or the transaxle gear selected.

 Engine Speed Sensitive 

When the concern is linked to engine speed, the concern occurs at 
varying vehicle speeds when a different transaxle gear is selected. It can 
sometimes be isolated by increasing or decreasing engine rpm with the 
transaxle in NEUTRAL (N), or by stall testing with the transaxle in gear. If 
the vibration is linked to engine speed, the problem is probably not a wheel 
(1007) or tire condition. 

If the road test indicates that the concern is related to the tires or 
wheels, refer to the Symptom Chart in this section. If the vehicle leads to 
one side during the road test, refer to the Tire Lead Diagnosis 
Chart in this 
section.

If the road test reveals tire whine, but no shaking or vibration, the 
noise is caused by contact between the tires and the road surface. Tire whine 
can be distinguished from axle whine because axle noise diminishes or changes 
according to load or speed. Tire noise remains the same over a range of speeds 
and changes slightly with changes to the road surface. A thumping noise 
usually means that the tire has flat or soft spots that make noise as they 
slap the road surface or the road surface that revealed the concern has evenly 
spaced (expansion) joints. Make sure that the road surface is smooth. 

 Vibration Troubleshooting Symptom Chart

[FIGURE: F8027B.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Tire Service 

 WARNING: TIRE SEALANTS THAT ARE INJECTED THROUGH THE VALVE STEM MUST NOT BE 
USED TO SERVICE PUNCTURED TIRES BECAUSE THEY CAN PRODUCE WHEEL RUST AND TIRE 
IMBALANCE. 

Punctured tires should be removed from the wheel (1007) and permanently 
serviced from the inside using a combination service plug and vulcanized 
patch. When servicing a puncture, always follow the manufacturer's 
instructions for using the service kit. 

Service punctures in the tread area only. Never attempt to service 
punctures in the tire shoulders or sidewalls. In addition, do not service any 
tire that has sustained the following damage: 

Bulges or blisters 

Ply separation 

Broken or cracked beads 

Fabric cracks or cuts 

Tires worn to the fabric or if wear indicators are visible 

Punctures larger than 6mm (1/4 inch) diameter

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Wheel Replacement

 WARNING: REPLACE THE WHEELS IF THEY ARE BENT, CRACKED, LEAKING AIR OR HEAVILY 
RUSTED OR IF THE WHEEL HUB BOLTS OFTEN BECOME LOOSE. DO NOT USE BENT WHEELS 
THAT HAVE BEEN STRAIGHTENED AND DO NOT USE INNER TUBES IN LEAKING WHEELS. DO 
NOT REPLACE WHEELS WITH USED WHEELS. WHEELS THAT HAVE BEEN STRAIGHTENED OR ARE 
LEAKING AIR OR ARE USED, MAY HAVE STRUCTURAL DAMAGE AND COULD FAIL WITHOUT 
WARNING. CHECK FOR DAMAGE THAT COULD AFFECT THE RUNOUT OF THE WHEELS. WOBBLE 
OR SHIMMY WILL EVENTUALLY DAMAGE THE WHEEL BEARINGS. 

 WARNING: AFTERMARKET WHEEL ASSEMBLIES MAY NOT BE COMPATIBLE WITH THE VEHICLE. 
USE OF INCOMPATIBLE WHEEL ASSEMBLIES MAY RESULT IN EQUIPMENT FAILURE AND 
POSSIBLE INJURY. USE ONLY APPROVED WHEEL ASSEMBLIES. 

 Removal 

Set the parking brake and block the diagonally opposite wheel (1007). 
On vehicles equipped with an automatic transaxle, place the selector lever in 
PARK (P) position. On vehicles equipped with a manual transaxle place the 
shift lever in REVERSE (R).

With the weight of the vehicle still on the tires, break the lug bolts 
(1107) loose. DO NOT REMOVE THE LUG BOLTS AT THIS TIME.

Raise the vehicle until the wheel and tire clears the floor.

Remove the lug bolts. Remove the wheel and tire assembly.

 Installation 

 WARNING: WHENEVER A WHEEL IS INSTALLED, ALWAYS REMOVE ANY CORROSION, DIRT OR 
FOREIGN MATERIAL THAT MAY BE PRESENT ON THE MOUNTING SURFACE OF THE WHEEL OR 
THE SURFACES OF THE HUB, BRAKE DRUM OR FRONT DISC BRAKE ROTOR THAT CONTACTS 
THE WHEEL. INSTALLING WHEELS WITHOUT PROPER METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT AT THE 
WHEEL MOUNTING SURFACES CAN CAUSE THE LUG NUTS TO LOOSEN AND COULD ALLOW THE 
WHEEL TO COME OFF WHILE THE VEHICLE IS IN MOTION, CAUSING LOSS OF CONTROL. 

Position the wheel and tire assembly and loosely install the lug bolts.

With the lug bolts loosely installed, turn the wheel until one lug bolt 
is at the top of the bolt circle. Tighten the lug bolt until snug. In a 
crisscross type pattern, tighten the remaining lug bolts until snug to 
minimize runout. Lower the vehicle.

Evenly tighten the lug bolts in the torque sequence shown in the 
illustration, to 88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Lug Bolt Torque Requirement

 WARNING: IMPROPERLY TIGHTENED WHEEL HUB BOLTS COULD ALLOW THE WHEEL TO COME OFF 
WHILE THE VEHICLE IS IN MOTION, CAUSING LOSS OF CONTROL. 

Tighten the lug bolts (1107) in a crisscross pattern. The wheel hub 
bolt torque specification is 88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft).

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Wheels

 Steel 

Wheel services that use welding, heating, or peening are not approved. 
An inner tube is not acceptable service for leaky wheels (1007) or tires.

Keep the wheels and wheel hubs (1104) clean. Stones or lumps of mud 
wedged between the wheel and mounting surface will unbalance a wheel and tire 
assembly.

Check for damage that would affect the runout of the wheels. Wobble or 
shimmy caused by a damaged wheel will eventually damage the wheel bearings and 
cause uneven tire wear. Inspect the wheel rims for dents that could permit air 
to leak from the tires.

 Aluminum 

 CAUTION: Do not use steel wool, abrasive type cleaner, or strong detergents 
containing high alkaline or caustic agents. Damage may occur to the protective 
coating and cause discoloration. 

To clean the wheels, use a mild soap and water solution and rinse 
thoroughly with clean water.

 Mounting Area 

Smooth all projections in the mounting area to assure even pressures 
when tightening lug bolts (1107).

 Flange Area 

Corrosion buildup can result in wheels sticking to the axle or rotor 
flange after extensive service. To prevent this from recurring once the wheel 
and tire assembly is removed, use the following procedure:

Clean drum/rotor flange and wheel bore of corrosion with wire brush, 
steel wool, or other suitable material.

Coat wheel bore with Disc Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ- 19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C172-A. Do not apply grease to the 
lug bolts or the wheel hub bolt seats.

Install wheel and tire assembly on vehicle.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tires

The tires should be checked frequently to be sure that the air 
pressures agree with those specified for the tires and vehicle model. Inspect 
the tire tread, and remove all stones, nails, glass, or other objects that may 
be wedged in the tread. Check for holes or cuts that may permit air leakage 
from the tire, and make the necessary repairs.

Inspect the tire side walls for cuts, bruises, and other damage. If 
internal damage is suspected, demount the tire from the wheel for further 
inspection, repair, or replacement.

Check the air valve for air leaks, and replace the air valve if 
necessary. Replace any missing air valve caps.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Leaks 

Slow air leaks may occur in cast aluminum wheels (1007) because of 
porous wheel castings. Perform the following procedure to repair the air leak.

Remove the wheel and inspect for structural damage. If the wheel is 
damaged, replace it.

If the wheel is not damaged, check for air leaks (with the tire mounted 
on the wheel) using a water bath or an equivalent method. Mark the air leak 
location.

Demount the tire.

Replace the valve stem if necessary.

Thoroughly clean the leaking area (on the tire side of the wheel) using 
either: 

Carburetor Tune-Up Cleaner D9AZ-19579-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M14P9-A. 

80 grit sandpaper. Be sure to scrub the wheel surface to improve 
sealant adhesion. 

Prepare an adequate area around the leak to ensure complete leak 
coverage.

Use a clean rag to remove all cleaner or sanding dust.

 CAUTION: Do not use an oxyacetylene torch to perform the next step. 

 CAUTION: Apply only enough heat to melt the sealant. 

Using either a propane torch or Rotunda Heat Gun 107-R0301 or 
equivalent, heat the prepared wheel area until the Aluminum Wheel Repair 
Compound E7AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M4G280-A 
begins to melt.

Apply a liberal amount of sealant over the prepared area using a wiping 
motion to ensure complete leak coverage.

Allow the wheel to cool until it can be handled safely.

Mount the tire and inflate it to the recommended pressure.

Check that the leak is repaired using the procedure in Step 2. If the 
leak is still present, replace the wheel.

Balance the wheel then install it on the vehicle.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Maintenance and Protection in Corrosive Environments

Wheels (1007) have a protective coating to resist corrosion. Care 
should be taken to avoid damaging the wheel or corrosion may occur. Washing 
them (do not use highly alkaline cleaning agents) when washing the rest of the 
vehicle will be enough to keep wheels looking good for many years. Certain 
environments created by some operations can lead to corrosion. Some of these 
are: livestock hauling, salt, chloride compounds used for snow removal, dust 
control and highly alkaline materials. When these conditions are encountered, 
the following practice is recommended:

Clean the wheels frequently with steam or high-pressure water from a 
hose. Use of a mild detergent will speed up the cleaning process.

When tires are removed, the entire wheel should be cleaned and 
inspected. For maximum protection, there are various types of coatings which 
give good results. The following procedures are suggested:

 Surface Preparation 

Remove all the soil and oil from the wheel surface with either 
high-pressure steam or solvent. Suitable solvents would be mineral spirits and 
regular paint thinner, obtained in paint stores.

Remove any adherent soil or oxidation products by using a wire brush.

Clean the surface again with solvent, using mineral spirits to remove 
loose products.

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING USED WHEELS, DO NOT USE EXCESSIVE AMOUNTS OF PAINT. THIS 
COULD CAUSE WHEEL HUB BOLT LOOSENING WHICH COULD LEAD TO PREMATURE WHEEL 
FAILURE OR LOOSE WHEELS, WHICH COULD LEAD TO A SERIOUS, IF NOT FATAL, INJURY. 

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING WHEELS, ALWAYS ALLOW THE PARTS TO DRY COMPLETELY PRIOR TO 
MOUNTING. IF THE PAINT IS NOT DRY WHEN THE WHEEL IS MOUNTED, TORQUE VALUES 
WILL NOT BE MAINTAINED BECAUSE OF THE PAINT BEING "FORCED OUT". 

Apply a clear protective or pigmented product as described below.

 Clear Protective Coating 

Spray about 1-1/2 to 2 mils wet film thickness, air curing clear epoxy 
polyamide meeting Military Specification MIL-C-22750 (WEP) or equivalent. To 
properly spray this particular coating, mix components A and B of the two-part 
organic coating and thin where necessary with 10 percent toluol. Spray apply 
with a spray gun at a pressure of 207-276 kPa (30-40 psi) (suction feed).

 Pigmented Protective Coating 

Primer: spray the inhibited primer, meeting Military Specification 
MIL-C-23377 (SEP) or equivalent. Spray this primer at a 1 to 2 mil wet film 
thickness. Allow to air dry from 2 to 4 hours before top-coating.

Top Coat: spray a 1-1/2 to 2 mil wet film of a leafing aluminum 
pigmented epoxy. Allow enough time to air dry before handling; overnight will 
usually be sufficient.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Wheel Maintenance

 During Tire Inspection 

Check all metal surfaces thoroughly while making tire inspections. 
Watch for:

Excessive rust or corrosion buildup

Cracks in metal

Worn or elongated wheel hub bolt holes

Bent flanges, resulting from road obstructions

Loose, missing or damaged lug bolts (1107)

 WARNING: EXCESSIVELY CORRODED OR CRACKED RIMS CAN BE DANGEROUS. DEFLATE TIRES 
PRIOR TO THE REMOVAL FROM THE WHEELS. 

Replace damaged wheels (1007).

Inflate tires only to recommended air pressures.

Check the wheel hub bolt torque and retighten the lug bolts to 88-118 Nm
 (65-87 lb-ft).

 During Tire Changes 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE VERY DANGEROUS. THESE 
COMPONENTS COULD FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE 
VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Check all metal surfaces. Watch particularly for the following items:

Cracks in the rim bead seat or drop well radii area. These are caused 
by deep rim tool marks, overloading and overinflating tires or by using larger 
than recommended tire sizes.

Cracks in the front disc brake rotor (1125), between the wheel hub bolt 
holes. These are caused by loose lug bolts, improper installation procedures 
or by the use of incorrect sizes or types of attaching parts.

 CAUTION: Make sure that replacements are made with the proper sizes and types of 
wheels. 

Replace the parts as necessary.

Thoroughly remove rust, dirt and other foreign materials from all 
surfaces. Hand or electric wire brushes, sand blasting or chemical baths may 
be used. Bead seat areas of rim should be free of rust and rubber deposits. 

Paint rim by brush or spray with a fast-drying metal primer. Surfaces 
should be clean and dry prior to painting. Make sure that bare metal areas on 
the outside or tire side of rim are covered. 

Lubricate the tire side of the rim base just prior to mounting tire. 
Avoid the use of any lubricant which contains water or solvent that is 
injurious to rubber such as WD40. A combination lubricant and rust-preventive 
compound is preferable such as a ready-to-use liquid soap meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1B6-A. 

Inflate tire to recommended air pressure.

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Maintenance

To maximize tire performance, inspect them for signs of improper 
inflation and uneven wear, which may indicate a need for balancing, rotation 
or front suspension alignment. Tires should also be checked frequently for 
cuts, stone bruises, abrasions, blisters, and for objects that may have become 
imbedded in the tread. More frequent inspections are recommended when rapid or 
extreme temperature changes occur, or where road surfaces are rough or 
occasionally littered with debris.

As a further visible check of tire condition, tread wear indicators are 
moulded into the bottom of the tread grooves. The tire should be replaced when 
these indicator bands become visible.

To clean tires, use a mild soap and water solution only, and rinse 
thoroughly with clear water. Do not use any caustic solutions or abrasive 
materials. Do not use steel wool, wire brushes, gasoline, paint thinner or 
similar materials having a mineral oil base. These materials are harmful to 
the tires and will eventually discolor the whitewalls and raised letters.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Inflation

 CAUTION: Radial-ply tires have highly flexible sidewalls which produce a 
noticeable sidewall bulge, making the tires appear underinflated. This is a 
normal condition for radial-ply tires. Do not attempt to eliminate this bulge 
by overinflating the tires. 

The tire inflation pressure is carefully calculated to give the vehicle 
satisfactory ride and steering characteristics without compromising long tire 
tread life.

Always check tire inflation pressure using an accurate pressure gauge. 
Never inflate the tires to levels above or below the recommended pressure. 
Tire inflation pressures are carefully calculated to give the vehicle 
satisfactory ride and steering characteristics, without compromising tire 
tread life.

[FIGURE: F5391B.gif]

The tire inflation pressure chart at the end of this section gives the 
recommended cold tire inflation pressure. The cold tire inflation pressure can 
be measured after the vehicle has been parked for three hours or has been 
driven less than 3.2 km (2 miles) at speeds less than 64 km/h (40 mph).

Do not reduce the tire inflation pressure when the tires are hot, or 
after the vehicle has been driven over 3.2 km (2 miles) at speeds in excess of 
64 km/h (40 mph). Under such conditions, pressures can increase as much as 41 
kPa (6 psi) over cold inflation pressures. 

After checking or adjusting the tire inflation pressures, make certain 
to install the tire air valve caps. The caps help prevent air leaks and keep 
dust and dirt out of the air valves. 

Check the air valves. If any air valve is worn, cracked, loose, or 
leaking air, replace it.

[FIGURE: F5299A.gif]

 WARNING: OVER- OR UNDER-INFLATED TIRES CAN REDUCE TIRE LIFE, ADVERSELY AFFECT 
VEHICLE HANDLING, AND POSSIBLY LEAD TO A SUDDEN FAILURE THAT COULD RESULT IN 
THE LOSS OF VEHICLE CONTROL WITHOUT WARNING. 

A higher tire inflation pressure than the recommended pressure can 
cause a hard ride, tire bruising, carcass damage, and rapid wear at the center 
of the tire. Low tire pressure can produce tire squeal, hard steering, rim 
dents, high temperatures, and rapid wear on the outer edges of the tires. 
Unequal inflation pressures in tires using the same axle can cause uneven 
braking and reduce handling.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Rotation 

 CAUTION: Never use the temporary spare for tire rotation or as a regular tire. 

To equalize tire wear, tires may be rotated, but not until the cause of 
unusual or uneven tire wear is determined and corrected. 

Front and rear tires perform different jobs and can wear differently 
depending on the type of vehicle and driving habits. To equalize wear and 
optimize tire life, rotate tires at approximately 8,000 km (5,000 miles). 

If abnormal wear is detected, find and correct the cause and rotate the 
tires following the diagram to allow more even wear.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tread Wear Indicators 

The original equipment tires have built-in tread wear indicators to 
show when the tires need replacement. These indicators will appear as 12mm 
(1/2 inch) wide bands when the tire tread depth becomes 1.5mm (1/16 inch). 
When the indicators appear in two or more adjacent grooves, at three locations 
around the tire, or when cord or fabric is exposed, tire replacement due to 
tread wear is recommended.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Halfshafts, Front Wheel

The front wheel driveshaft and joints are the mechanical links that 
transfer engine torque from the transaxle to the front wheels. At the 
transaxle end, the front wheel driveshaft joint (3B414) is splined to the 
differential side gear (4236). Disengagement of the front wheel driveshaft 
joint from the differential side gear is prevented by an expanding spring steel 
driveshaft bearing retainer circlip (3Z498). During installation, the 
driveshaft bearing retainer circlip compresses around the front wheel 
driveshaft joint as it enters the differential side gear. Once through the 
differential side gear, the driveshaft bearing retainer circlip expands into a 
counterbore machined into the back side of the differential side gear. 

The wheel end of the front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B436) is 
splined to the wheel hub (1104) which is supported on opposed tapered front 
wheel bearings. Disengagement of the front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B437) 
from the wheel hub is prevented by the front axle wheel hub retainer washer 
(3Z499) and the front axle wheel hub retainer (3B477).

Backlash between the wheel hubs and front wheel driveshaft and joints 
is eliminated by the splines. The front wheel hub splines are machined 
straight while the front wheel driveshaft and joint splines are machined with 
a slight helical cut. The difference in splines provides a tight, 
backlash-free coupling without the removal and installation problems 
associated with an interference fit.

Front wheel driveshaft joints exist at both ends of the front wheel 
driveshafts. 

Two different types of front wheel driveshaft joints are used. The 
inboard front wheel driveshaft joints are repairable tripod-type front wheel 
driveshaft joints. The outboard front wheel driveshaft joints are 
non-repairable Birfield-type front wheel driveshaft joints. 

Tripod-type front wheel driveshaft joints are used to prevent the 
transfer of engine vibration through the front wheel driveshafts to the 
vehicle body. Additional reduction of vibration is provided by a dynamic 
damper installed approximately in the middle of the RH front wheel driveshaft 
and joint.

Front wheel driveshaft joints are necessary because the front wheel 
driveshaft is required to transmit torque while compensating for front 
suspension movement. As the suspension moves, the front wheel driveshaft 
joints allow the front wheel driveshafts to change length and operate smoothly 
through varying angles. 

For the necessary flexibility, Birfield-type front wheel driveshaft 
joints use ball bearings positioned by a cage. The tripod-type front wheel 
driveshaft joint uses three balls mounted on needle bearings and a spider. In 
both types of front wheel driveshaft joints, the outer race is machined into 
the front wheel driveshaft joint housing. 

The inboard, tripod-type front wheel driveshaft joints can be 
disassembled and serviced. Other than the front wheel driveshaft joint boot 
(3A331), the outboard Birfield-type front wheel driveshaft joint is serviced 
only as an assembly with the RH front wheel driveshaft and joint or the LH 
front wheel driveshaft and joint.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Halfshaft Handling 

 CAUTION: Never hold a front wheel driveshaft and joint by the inboard tripod-type 
front wheel driveshaft joint (3B414) only. 

Care should be exercised during front wheel driveshaft and joint 
removal and installation, and during the disassembly and assembly procedures. 

Do not remove the inboard tripod-type front wheel driveshaft joint by 
pulling on the front wheel driveshaft. 

The complete front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B436) should be handled 
by the front wheel driveshaft to avoid pulling apart or damage to the inboard 
tripod-type front wheel driveshaft joint. 

Do not over-angle front wheel driveshaft and joint beyond their 
capacity. 

Ensure that machined surfaces and splines are not damaged. 

Do not allow front wheel driveshaft joint boots (3A331) to come into 
contact with sharp edges or hot engine (6007) and exhaust components. 

Do not drop assembled front wheel driveshaft and joints as the impact 
will cut the front wheel driveshaft joint boots from the inside without 
external evidence of damage. 

The front wheel driveshaft and joint is not to be used as a lever arm 
to position other front end components. Always support the free end of the 
front wheel driveshaft and joint.

Ensure internal front wheel driveshaft joint cleanliness and proper 
grease refill when the front wheel driveshaft joint boot is replaced. 

An assembled inboard front wheel driveshaft joint may be damaged if it 
is "over-plunged" outward from the outer race. 

Never use a metallic hammer to remove or install front wheel driveshaft 
joints.

Wheel and Tire Balancing, Front 

 WARNING: ON-VEHICLE FRONT WHEEL AND TIRE BALANCING WITH FRONT SUSPENSION IN THE 
FULLY EXTENDED (REBOUND) POSITION MAY OVERHEAT AND DAMAGE THE FRONT WHEEL 
DRIVESHAFT JOINTS. PROPER BALANCING REQUIRES THAT THE FRONT WHEEL(S) AND 
TIRE(S) BE LIFTED OFF THE GROUND BY PLACING A JACK UNDER THE FRONT SUSPENSION 
LOWER ARM.

ANOTHER METHOD IS TO REMOVE THE FRONT WHEEL(S) AND TIRE(S) FROM THE 
VEHICLE FOR BALANCING.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Undercoating and Rustproofing 

Extreme care must be taken during undercoating and rustproofing 
procedures to protect the front wheel driveshaft joint boots (3A331) from 
coating materials. Foreign materials on the rubber boot convolutions will 
cause advanced wear.

Inspect the front wheel driveshaft joint boots (3A331) for cuts,

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Halfshaft Assembly

 NOTE: The following procedure applies to either the LH or RH front wheel 
driveshaft and joints.

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Differential Plugs

T87C-7025-C

 Removal 

Raise and support the vehicle. 

Drain the transmission fluid from the transaxle. Refer to Section 07-01 
for automatic transaxles or Section 07-03 for manual transaxles.

Remove the lug bolts (1107) and the front wheel and tire assembly. 

Use a small cape chisel to carefully raise the staked portion of the 
front axle wheel hub retainer (3B477).

[FIGURE: E8883B.gif]

While another technician applies the brakes, loosen, but do not remove, 
the front axle wheel hub retainer.

[FIGURE: F5936C.gif]

Remove the front suspension lower arm ball joint bolt and nut. 

[FIGURE: E7604C.gif]

 CAUTION: Take care not to damage the ball joint dust boot. 

Carefully pry down on the front suspension lower arm (3078) to separate 
the front suspension lower arm ball joint from the front wheel knuckle (3K185).

[FIGURE: E8891B.gif]

 CAUTION: Separate the front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B437) from the 
transaxle gradually. If it is suddenly yanked out of the transaxle, the 
differential oil seal may be damaged. 

Use a pry bar to separate the front wheel driveshaft and joint from the 
transaxle.

[FIGURE: E8892B.gif]

Remove the front axle wheel hub retainer and front axle wheel hub 
retainer washer (3Z499). Discard the front axle wheel hub retainer.

 CAUTION: Take care not to damage the inner wheel bearing oil seal (1177) while 
removing the front wheel driveshaft and joint from the front wheel hub (1104). 

 NOTE: If necessary, use a brass drift and hammer to tap the front wheel 
driveshaft and joint from the front wheel hub. 

Separate the front wheel driveshaft and joint from the frontwheel hub.

[FIGURE: E7607C.gif]

Pry the driveshaft bearing retainer circlip (3Z498) off of the front 
wheel driveshaft joint (3B414). Discard the driveshaft bearing retainer 
circlip. 

Install Differential Plugs T87C-7025-C. 

 Installation 

Before installing the front wheel driveshaft and joint, inspect the 
differential oil seals and inner wheel bearing oil seals and replace, if 
necessary. Refer to Section 04-01 , Section 07-01 or Section 07-03 for the procedures.

 NOTE: The original driveshaft bearing retainer circlip must not be reused. 

Install a new driveshaft bearing retainer circlip on the front wheel 
driveshaft joint. 

Lubricate the end of the front wheel driveshaft joint with grease.

[FIGURE: E7610C.gif]

Remove the Differential Plugs T87C-7025-C.

 CAUTION: Insert the front wheel driveshaft joint carefully so as not to damage 
the differential oil seal. 

Install the end of the front wheel driveshaft joint into the 
differential side gear (4236).

Lubricate the end of the front wheel driveshaft and joint with grease.

 CAUTION: Insert the front wheel driveshaft and joint carefully so as not to 
damage the inner wheel bearing oil seal. 

Insert the end of the front wheel driveshaft and joint into the front 
wheel hub.

Install the front axle wheel hub retainer washer and a new front axle 
wheel hub retainer onto the front wheel driveshaft and joint and finger-tighten.

 CAUTION: Avoid damaging the ball joint dust boot. 

Install the front suspension lower arm by placing the front suspension 
lower arm ball joint into the front wheel knuckle.

Install the front suspension lower arm ball joint bolt and nut on the 
front suspension lower arm. Tighten the front suspension lower arm ball joint 
nut to 43-54 Nm (32-40 lb-ft). 

While another technician applies the brakes, tighten the front axle 
wheel hub retainer to 157-235 Nm (116-174 lb-ft).

 CAUTION: If the front axle wheel hub retainer splits or cracks after staking, it 
must be replaced with a new front axle wheel hub retainer. 

 NOTE: Make sure the front axle wheel hub retainer flange is bent at least 4mm 
(0.16 inch) into the slot in the front wheel driveshaft and joint to ensure 
locking effectiveness. After staking the front axle wheel hub retainer, pull 
strongly on the wheel hub to verify that the front wheel driveshaft and joint 
is installed properly. Turn the front wheel hub by hand to check for smooth 
operation. Make repairs as necessary.

Use a cape chisel with the cutting edge rounded to stake the front axle 
wheel hub retainer.

[FIGURE: E8893B.gif]

Install the front wheel and tire assemblies and the lug bolts. Tighten 
the lug bolts to 88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft). 

Fill the transaxle to the proper level with the specified grade of 
transmission fluid. Refer to Section 07-01 or Section 07-03 .

Lower the vehicle.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Halfshaft Assembly, Inboard

 Disassembly 

Clamp the front wheel driveshaft and joint (3B437) in a vise equipped 
with protective jaw caps to prevent damage to any machined parts. 

 NOTE: Peel the front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp (3B478) away from the 
front wheel driveshaft joint boot (3A331) as shown.

Remove the large front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp and discard. 
Side cutters can be used to cut the front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp. 
After removing the front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp, roll the front 
wheel driveshaft joint boot back over the front wheel driveshaft and joint.

[FIGURE: E6873C.gif]

If this procedure is being performed to replace only a damaged front 
wheel driveshaft joint boot, the grease should be checked for contamination. 
The grease can be checked for contamination by rubbing it between two fingers. 
Any gritty feeling indicates a contaminated front wheel driveshaft joint. 

A contaminated front wheel driveshaft joint (3B414) must be completely 
disassembled, cleaned, and inspected. If the grease is not contaminated and 
the front wheel driveshaft joint has been operating satisfactorily, replace 
only the front wheel driveshaft joint boot and add the required lubricant. 

[FIGURE: E8899B.gif]

Remove the wire ring bearing retainer.

[FIGURE: E6866C.gif]

Paint alignment marks on the outer race and tripod bearing for assembly 
reference.

[FIGURE: E6874C.gif]

Remove the outer race.

[FIGURE: E8962B.gif]

Remove the snap ring.

[FIGURE: E8963B.gif]

Use a brass drift and hammer to gently tap the tripod bearing from the 
front wheel driveshaft.

[FIGURE: E8964B.gif]

If the front wheel driveshaft joint boot is to be reused, wrap the 
front wheel driveshaft splines with tape before removing the boot from the 
front wheel driveshaft. 

If necessary, remove the small front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp 
and the front wheel driveshaft joint boot from the front wheel driveshaft.

[FIGURE: E8900B.gif]

[FIGURE: E6857C.gif]

 Assembly 

 CAUTION: The front wheel driveshaft joint components must be lubricated with 
Ford Constant Velocity Joint Grease — High Temperature 
E43Z-19590-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESP-M1C207-A prior to 
assembly. 

If necessary, cover the front wheel driveshaft splines with tape and 
install the front wheel driveshaft joint boot. 

Align the marks on the tripod bearing and the front wheel driveshaft. 

Use a soft faced hammer to gently tap the tripod bearing on the front 
wheel driveshaft.

[FIGURE: E6871A.gif]

Use snap ring pliers to install the snap ring. 

Fill the outer race with 100 g (3.5 ounces) of Ford Constant Velocity 
Joint Grease — High Temperature E43Z-19590-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESP-M1C207-A. 

Align the marks and install the outer race over the tripod bearing and 
install the wire ring bearing retainer. 

Position the front wheel driveshaft joint boot so that the front wheel 
driveshaft joint boot is fully seated in the grooves in the front wheel 
driveshaft and outer race. 

Extend or compress the front wheel driveshaft joint as necessary until 
the distance between the front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamp grooves 
measures 104.3mm (4.11 inches).

[FIGURE: E6865B.gif]

Insert a dulled screwdriver blade between the front wheel driveshaft 
joint boot and the outer race to allow trapped air to escape from the front 
wheel driveshaft joint boot.

[FIGURE: E8901B.gif]

 NOTE: Always use new front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamps. 

Install new front wheel driveshaft joint boot clamps. Wrap the front 
wheel driveshaft joint boot clamps around the front wheel driveshaft joint 
boots in a clockwise direction, pull tight with pliers, and bend the locking 
tabs to secure in position.

[FIGURE: E6862C.gif]

Work the front wheel driveshaft joint through its full range of travel 
at various angles. The front wheel driveshaft joint should flex, extend, and 
compress smoothly.

[FIGURE: E6872A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

CV Joint Boot Indentation

 Inspection 

Indentations or "dimples" in the inboard and/or outboard front wheel 
driveshaft joint boots (3A331) may occur due to improper handling during 
storage or service of the front wheel driveshaft and joints (3B437). If, 
during inspection, a front wheel driveshaft joint boot is observed to be 
"dimpled," proceed as follows: 

Inspect the front wheel driveshaft joint boot(s) for any sign of grease 
leakage in the dimple which would indicate a cut. Replace the front wheel 
driveshaft joint boot if a cut exists or if there is evidence of other damage. 

[FIGURE: E8880B.gif]

If the front wheel driveshaft joint boot is in good condition, the 
dimple can be removed as follows: 

Grasp the dimpled convolution on either side of the dimple using the 
forefinger and thumb of each hand. 

[FIGURE: E8881B.gif]

While grasping the front wheel driveshaft joint boot, pull the 
convolution by moving hands in opposite directions. The dimple should "pop 
out." If the dimple does not invert or if it dimples again, one front wheel 
driveshaft joint boot clamp (3B478) should be removed and the internal and 
external air pressure equalized. Refer to the appropriate front wheel 
driveshaft joint boot installation steps within assembly of the halfshaft 
assembly — inboard, in this section, for the necessary 
procedure. 

[FIGURE: E8882B.gif]

Extreme care should be taken not to allow the front wheel driveshaft 
joint boots to come in forceful contact with foreign objects that may cause 
the external front wheel driveshaft joint boot convolutions to become 
indented.

Section 06-00: Brake System — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Master Cylinder, Dual

The brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) is a clear plastic 
container. A brake fluid level switch is part of the reservoir body. The brake 
fluid level switch senses the level of brake fluid in the brake master 
cylinder reservoir. When the brake fluid level gets low the brake master 
cylinder float closes the contacts in the brake fluid level switch which 
causes the brake system warning indicator to illuminate. The brake master 
cylinder reservoir and brake master cylinder filler cap (2162) are serviced 
separately.

Testing reveals that in vehicles equipped with the anti-lock brake 
system (ABS), brake fluid pressure can cause undue wear to the primary cup of 
the secondary piston on conventional master cylinders during ABS operation. To 
prevent this condition, the relief port has been eliminated in ABS-equipped 
master cylinders and a center valve port has been provided in the secondary 
position.

================================================================================
PAGE 2549
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-00: Brake System — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Pressure Control Valve

A brake pressure control valve (2B091) is installed in the system to 
balance front to rear brake application. The brake pressure control valve 
reduces hydraulic pressure to the rear wheel cylinders (2261) to prevent rear 
wheel lockup. Internally, the brake pressure control valve contains plungers 
that are shifted by hydraulic pressure to limit the output pressure to the 
rear wheels.

================================================================================
PAGE 2550
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-00: Brake System — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Hydraulic

The hydraulic brake system is a diagonally split system with a dual 
piston master cylinder. The left front and right rear are on one brake circuit 
while the right front and left rear are on another brake circuit.

The hydraulic system is split in this manner as a safety precaution. If 
hydraulic pressure is lost in one circuit, the remaining circuit can provide 
less efficient, yet balanced braking.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Front Disc

The front disc brake system consists of a full-floating front disc 
brake caliper and a front disc brake rotor (1125). The front disc brake 
caliper (2B120) is attached to the front wheel knuckle (3K185) with two bolts 
that also serve as the caliper slide pins. In addition to providing a braking 
surface, the front disc brake rotor forms part of the front wheel hub (1104).

The front disc brake caliper applies brake shoes and linings (2001) 
that are held in position by a disc brake pad anti-rattle clip (2B164) and two 
disc brake caliper locating pins (2B296). The brake shoes and linings are 
prevented from rattling against the front disc brake caliper and disc brake 
caliper locating pins by an M-shaped anti-rattle spring that maintains a 
constant pressure on the brake shoes and linings.

A flexible front brake hose (2078) is used to connect the front disc 
brake caliper to the hydraulic system. Leakage at the hose connection is 
prevented by copper washers installed on either side of the hydraulic fitting.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Rear Drum

The rear brake drums (1126) are a standard, non-servo design. The 
brakes are applied by a double-acting rear wheel cylinder mounted at the top 
of each brake backing plate (2211).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Anti-Lock

Four-wheel anti-lock brake system (ABS) is optional on the Aspire. The 
system prevents wheel lockup by automatically modulating the brake pressure 
during an emergency stop. By not locking the wheels, the driver can maintain 
steering control, and stop the vehicle in the shortest possible distance, 
under most conditions. Refer to Section 06-09 for a detailed description and 
service procedures.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES, 
FLUSH EYES WITH RUNNING WATER FOR 15 MINUTES. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION IF 
IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET 
MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY. 

 CAUTION: Do not spill brake fluid onto painted surfaces. If spilled, wipe it up 
immediately. 

 NOTE: Always check the fluid level in the brake master cylinder (2140) before 
performing the test procedures. If the fluid level is not at the correct level 
indicated on the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478), add Ford High 
Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AA or DOT 3 equivalent fluid meeting 
Ford specification ESA-M6C25-A.

 NOTE: Prior to performing any diagnosis, make certain that the brake system 
warning indicator is functional. Refer to Section 13-01 .

Usually, the first and strongest indicator of anything wrong in the 
brake system is a change in the feeling through the brake pedal (2455) during 
application. The brake system warning indicator in the instrument cluster and 
the brake fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir are also 
indicators of a malfunction in the brake system.

 Road Test 

Perform a road test to compare actual vehicle braking performance with 
the performance standards expected by the driver. The ability of the test 
driver to make valid comparisons and detect performance deficiencies will 
depend on experience. 

The driver should have a thorough knowledge of brake system operation 
and accepted general performance guidelines, in order to make good comparisons 
and detect performance problems.

An experienced brake technician will always establish a route that will 
be used for all brake diagnosis road tests. The road selected will be 
reasonably smooth and level. Gravel or bumpy roads are not suitable because 
the surface does not allow the tires to grip the road equally. Crowned roads 
should be avoided because of the large amount of weight shifted to the low set 
of wheels on this type of road. Once the route is established and consistently 
used, the road surface variable can be eliminated from the test results. 

Before a road test, get a complete description of the customer concerns 
or suspected condition. From the description, your experience will allow you 
to match possible causes with symptoms. Certain components will be tagged as 
possible suspects while others will be eliminated by the evidence. More 
importantly, the customer's description can reveal unsafe conditions which 
should be checked or corrected before the road test. The description will also 
help form the basic approach to the road test by narrowing the problem to 
specific components, vehicle speed or conditions. 

Begin the road test with a general brake performance check. Keeping the 
description in mind, test the brakes at different vehicle speeds using both 
light and heavy pedal pressure. To determine if the problem is in the front or 
rear braking system, first use the brake pedal, then use the parking brake 
control (2780). If the condition (i.e., pull, vibration, pulsation) occurs 
only with the parking brake control, the problem is in the rear system. If the 
condition only occurs when the brake pedal is depressed, the problem is in the 
front system. 

Avoid locking the brakes and sliding the tires. Locked brakes and 
sliding tires do not indicate brake efficiency. A heavily braked, but turning 
wheel (1007), will stop the vehicle in less distance than locked brakes. If 
the problem becomes evident during this check, make sure it fits the 
description given before the road test. If the problem is not evident, attempt 
to duplicate the condition using the information from the description. 

If a problem exists, use the Symptom Chart in order to isolate it to a 
specific subsystem and condition description. From this description, a list of 
possible causes can be used to further narrow the cause to a specific 
component or condition.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Component Tests

 Brake Booster Functional Test 

 Brake Booster Operation Check 

Inspect all vacuum hoses and connections. All unused vacuum connectors 
should be capped. Hoses and their connections should be properly secured and 
in good condition with no holes or collapsed areas. Inspect the hose 
containing the check valve for damage. Check the power brake booster system 
operation as follows: 

Check the hydraulic brake system for leaks or insufficient fluid. 

With the transaxle in PARK (P) or NEUTRAL (N), stop the engine (6007), 
and apply the parking brake. Depress the brake pedal (2455) several times to 
exhaust all vacuum in the system. 

With the engine turned off and all vacuum in the system exhausted, 
depress the brake pedal and hold it in the applied position. Start the engine. 
If the vacuum system is operating, the brake pedal will tend to move downward 
under constant foot pressure. If no motion is felt, the power brake booster 
system is not functioning. 

Remove the vacuum booster hose (2A047) from the power brake booster 
(2005). Manifold vacuum should be available at the power brake booster end of 
the hose with the engine at idle speed and the transaxle in PARK (P) or 
NEUTRAL (N). Be sure that all unused vacuum outlets are properly secured, and 
that vacuum hoses are in good condition. 

When it is established that manifold vacuum is available, connect the 
vacuum booster hose to the power brake booster and repeat step 3. If no 
downward movement of the brake pedal is felt, replace the power brake booster. 

Operate the engine a minimum of 10 seconds at fast idle. Stop the 
engine, and let the vehicle stand for 10 minutes, then depress the brake pedal 
with approximately 89 N (20 pounds) of force. 

The brake pedal feel (brake application) should be the same as that 
noted with the engine operating. If the brake pedal feels hard replace the 
power brake booster.

If the brake pedal movement feels spongy, bleed the hydraulic system to 
remove air from the system. 

Run the engine at fast idle for 10 seconds or longer. Depress brake 
pedal and listen for noise. Compare results with a known good system. If the 
brake pedal is noisy, replace it.

 Check Valve 

 NOTE: The vacuum booster hose check valve is located in the center of the 
vacuum booster hose that attaches to the intake manifold (9424). The vacuum 
booster hose check valve is not serviced separately. 

To check the vacuum hose check valve, disconnect the vacuum booster 
hose at the intake manifold.

Apply suction and pressure to the vacuum booster hose from the engine 
side. Make sure air only flows toward the engine.

 Vacuum System Test 

To test the brake vacuum system, start and run the engine for 10 
seconds at fast idle. Stop the engine, and let stand for 10 minutes, then 
depress the brake pedal with approximately 89 N (20 pounds) of force.

The brake pedal feel (brake application) should be the same as that 
noted with the engine operating. If the brake pedal feels hard (no power 
assist), repeat test and listen for air leaks. Air leaks can occur at the 
vacuum booster hose connections, vacuum hose check valve, the hose itself, and 
in the power brake booster. Replace or repair the defective component.

 Brake Master Cylinder 

 Normal Conditions 

The following conditions are considered normal and are not indications 
that the brake master cylinder (2140) is in need of service. 

Condition 1: During normal operation of the brake master cylinder, the 
fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) will rise during 
brake application and fall during release. The net fluid level, i.e., after 
brake application and release, will remain unchanged. 

Condition 2: A trace of brake fluid will exist on the power brake 
booster shell below the brake master cylinder mounting flange. This results 
from the normal lubricating action of the master cylinder bore and seal. 

Condition 3: Fluid level will decrease with brake shoes and linings 
(2001) wear. 

 Abnormal Conditions 

Changes in brake pedal feel or travel are indicators that something 
could be wrong in the brake system. Refer to brake system Symptom Chart for 
abnormal condition diagnosis. 

 Bypass Condition Test 

Check the brake master cylinder fluid level. 

With the brake master cylinder filler cap (2162) removed, observe the 
fluid level when the brake pedal is slowly depressed for one stroke and then 
quickly released. 

If the fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir rises while 
the brake pedal goes down and drops when the brake pedal is released, but the 
net (overall) fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir remains 
unchanged, the brake master cylinder is bypassing. Service the brake master 
cylinder. Refer to Section 06-06 for the service procedure. 

 Non-Pressure Leaks 

An empty brake master cylinder reservoir condition may be caused by two 
types of non-pressure external leaks. 

Type 1: An external leak may occur at the brake master cylinder 
reservoir because of improper positioning of the brake master cylinder filler 
cap. 

Type 2: An external leak may occur at the mounting end of the brake 
master cylinder because of a bore end seal leak. Service the brake master 
cylinder. Refer to Section 06-06 for the service procedure.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Compensator Port Check

If it is believed that the brake master cylinder (2140) is failing to 
return to the fully released position, proceed as follows: 

Raise the front of the vehicle and support it on safety stands. 

With the brakes off, attempt to rotate both front wheels by hand. To 
minimize brake shoe and lining drag, rock the wheel on the front wheel 
knuckles (3K185) as it is rotated. 

If an excessive amount of brake drag is apparent at both wheels, the 
brake master cylinder may not be returning to the released position. Proceed 
to the next step. 

If an excessive amount of brake drag is apparent at only one wheel, it 
indicates a possible seized front disc brake caliper piston. 

Check the brake on/off (BOO) switch adjustment to make sure the BOO 
switch is not holding the brake pedal (2455) in the partially applied 
position. If necessary, adjust the BOO switch. Refer to Section 17-01 for the 
procedure. If the BOO switch is properly adjusted, proceed to the next step. 

Loosen the nuts attaching the brake master cylinder to the power brake 
booster (2005) and pull the brake master cylinder away from the power brake 
booster. If the brake drag disappears, the power brake booster is binding and 
should be replaced. If the brake drag continues, the brake master cylinder is 
not operating properly and should be replaced. 

 Brake Pressure Control Valve 

 NOTE: The brake line coming out of the outlet port of the brake master 
cylinder leads to the inlet port of the brake pressure control valve (2B091). 
For easier access, the pressure gauge is inserted at the brake master cylinder. 

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

T92C-20215-AH

Using Proportioning Valve Test Gauge Set T92C-20215-AH, connect one 
pressure gauge to the outlet port of the brake pressure control valve and the 
other pressure gauge to the outlet port of the brake master cylinder. 

[FIGURE: H9202A.gif]

Bleed the brake system as outlined in this section.

Depress the brake pedal until the inlet fluid pressure (on the brake 
master cylinder side of the brake pressure control valve) and the outlet fluid 
pressure (on the rear brake side of the brake pressure control valve) meet the 
specifications listed in the chart below.

If the outlet fluid pressures are out of specification, replace the 
brake pressure control valve.

Bleed the brake system as outlined in Section 06-06 .

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Brake System Test Procedure

Internal and external leaks are two problems that can affect a brake 
hydraulic system. The hydraulic brake system will not cause the vehicle to do 
any of the following:

Vibrate

Pull

Grab

Squeal

Allow the brake pedal (2455) to pulse

An inspection of the brake hydraulic system begins with: 

If the fluid level is below the line in the brake master cylinder 
reservoir (2K478), add the required amount of fluid. Make sure the brake fluid 
meets the required specifications.

When in the brake master cylinder area, check the brake tubes and brake 
master cylinder mounting. The brake tube flare nuts must be tight. The brake 
tubes must not show any signs of leakage. 

The following conditions are considered normal and are not indications 
that the brake master cylinder (2140) is in need of service:

Low fluid level detected without signs of leakage. This condition is 
caused by displacement of fluid from the brake master cylinder reservoir into 
the front disc brake calipers (2B120) to compensate for normal brake shoes and 
linings (2001) wear. Add fluid as needed.

A momentary or slight squirt of brake fluid from the brake master 
cylinder reservoir upon application of the brake pedal. This condition is 
caused by fluid displacement through the brake master cylinder reservoir 
compensating port as the master cylinder pistons move forward in the bore when 
the brakes are applied.

Slight turbulence in the reservoir fluid when the brake pedal is 
released. Turbulence occurs as brake fluid returns to the brake master 
cylinder after releasing the brakes.

A trace of brake fluid found on the power brake booster (2005) shell 
below the brake master cylinder mounting flange. This condition results from 
the lubricating action of the master cylinder wiping seal.

Inspect the brake lines under the vehicle for damage and proper 
routing. Check the front brake hoses (2078) connecting the brake lines to the 
front disc brake calipers for any signs of damage, cracking or softening. The 
hose fittings must be tight without signs of leakage.

If signs of leakage are not present but the brake master cylinder is 
definitely low, it is possible that evidence of fluid leakage may have been 
washed off by rain or snow because brake fluid is water soluble. To determine 
if a leak exists, proceed as follows:

Refill the system

Bleed the system

Apply the brakes several times

Examine the system to verify that the brake master cylinder reservoir 
level is actually dropping

Locate and correct the external leak 

 Air Trapped in Brake System 

 NOTE: Pumping the brake pedal compresses trapped air. When the brake pedal is 
released, the compressed air expands, forcing brake fluid back into the brake 
master cylinder with sufficient force to form a geyser. 

Check the brake master cylinder fluid level. 

Place the brake master cylinder filler cap (2162) loosely on the brake 
master cylinder. 

With one technician acting as an observer at the brake master cylinder, 
and another technician applying the brakes, pump the brakes rapidly 20 times. 

On the final application, hold the brake pedal in the depressed 
position. 

Remove the brake master cylinder filler cap, and observe the fluid in 
the brake master cylinder reservoir. Quickly release the brake pedal. A geyser 
will spout in the brake master cylinder reservoir if the system has air in it.

If necessary, bleed the system. Refer to the procedure in Section 06-06 . 

 Brake Pedal Reserve Check 

With the engine (6007) off, pump the brake pedal several times to 
deplete the vacuum reserve in the power brake booster. 

Install Rotunda Brake Pedal Effort Gauge 014-R1051 or equivalent. 

Press on the brake pedal with a force of about 589 N (132 lbs.) and 
measure the brake pedal travel. If necessary, refer to the brake pedal travel 
measurement procedure in this section.

If brake pedal to floor clearance is less than 74mm (about 2.92 
inches), bleed the brakes and recheck brake pedal to floor clearance. 

If the brake pedal is still believed to be bottoming out, brake pedal 
reserve can be confirmed as follows: 

Press the brake pedal with moderate to severe pressure and note the 
amount of brake pedal travel. 

 NOTE: The brake system is diagonally split. Therefore, open the bleeder screw 
at either the right front disc brake caliper an d left rear wheel cylinder 
(2261) or at the left front disc brake caliper (2B121) and right rear wheel 
cylinder. 

Open a bleeder screw at one front disc brake caliper and one rear wheel 
cylinder. 

Press the brake pedal and note the amount of brake pedal travel. The 
brake pedal should go to the floor. 

Close the bleeder screws and refer to the Symptom Chart for causes of 
excessive brake pedal travel.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Service Precautions 

Grease or any other foreign material must be kept off lining surfaces 
and braking surfaces of the front disc brake rotor (1125), and external 
surfaces of the wheel hub (1104) during service operation. In handling the 
front disc brake rotor and front disc brake caliper (2B120) assemblies, avoid 
deformation of the front disc brake rotor and nicking or scratching of the 
brake linings. 

 CAUTION: Do not pry on piston with a screwdriver or other tools, as this will 
cause chipping, nicks and gouges. 

If a caliper piston is removed for any reason, the piston seal must be 
replaced. Exercise care not to damage the piston by protecting it from contact 
with any metal or sharp objects. 

During removal and installation of a wheel and tire assembly, exercise 
care not to interfere with and damage the front disc brake rotor shield 
(2K004) or caliper bleeder screw. 

Before servicing any front end components, ensure the vehicle is 
centered on a hoist to avoid bending or damaging the front disc brake rotor 
shield on full RH or LH wheel turns. 

Do not attempt to clean or restore oil or grease-soaked brake shoes and 
linings (2001). When contaminated brake shoes and linings are found, the brake 
shoe and lining must be replaced in complete axle sets and the front disc 
brake rotor braking surfaces wiped clean. 

The front disc brake caliper must be installed with the bleeder screws 
in an upward position for proper bleeding of air from the brake system. 

Always replace the brake shoe and lining shims when replacing the brake 
shoes and linings.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Brakes, Disc 

 Front 

Inspect the front disc brake caliper (2B120) and front disc brake 
caliper mounting for loose or damaged parts. Verify that the brake caliper 
bolts (2W303) are tightened to the specified torque. Check the front brake 
hose (2078) and front disc brake caliper fitting for leaks or damage. 
Thoroughly check the front disc brake caliper for damp areas that might 
indicate a leaking front disc brake caliper seal. Check for brake fluid 
contamination, which might also indicate a leaking front disc brake caliper 
seal. If a leaking seal is indicated, disassemble and inspect the front disc 
brake caliper. Refer to Section 06-03 for the disassembly and assembly 
procedure. 

Check the front disc brake rotor (1125) for obvious damage. Unless 
damage is obvious, the need to resurface, recondition, or replace the front 
disc brake rotor cannot be determined by a visual inspection. Tolerances on 
front disc brake rotor thickness, parallelism, and runout are very critical 
and must be measured with precision tools. Refer to the adjustment procedures 
in this section for visual inspection and measurement techniques.

Compare the brake shoes and linings (2001) on both front brakes for 
different degrees of wear. If the set of brake shoes and linings on one brake 
is excessively worn, the caliper piston may be seized in its bore. If such a 
condition exists, disassemble the front disc brake caliper and inspect the 
suspected seized piston. Refer to Section 06-03 for the procedure.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Brakes, Drum

To inspect the brake drum (1126), first remove the brake drum. Refer to 
 Section 06-02 for the removal procedure. 

Inspect the brake shoes and linings (2001) for wear beyond service 
limits, uneven wear, cracks, scoring, gouges, and brake fluid or grease 
contamination. 

Inspect the rear wheel cylinders (2261) for leaking. 

Inspect the shoe pads on the brake backing plate (2211) for scoring. 
The shoe pads should be smooth and have a light coating of white lithium 
grease. 

Inspect the brake drum for scratches, scoring, bell mouth, and 
out-of-round condition. 

Inspect the brake shoe hold-down spring (2068) and brake shoe 
retracting spring (2035) for bends, coil damage, loss of tension, and heat 
damage. A heat-damaged spring will ring when dropped onto a concrete floor. A 
good spring will make a dull thud sound.

Refer to Section 06-02 for additional service and repair procedures.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Hydraulic System 

Internal and external leaks affect the efficiency of the hydraulic 
brake system. Leaks generally do not cause vibration, pulling, grabbing, 
squealing, and brake pedal pulsation. The hydraulic system usually does not 
cause brake drag. Such conditions are usually due to other causes in the brake 
system. It is advisable to inspect the entire hydraulic system for leaks first 
when diagnosing any brake problem.

 Brake Master Cylinder 

Check the level of the brake fluid in the brake master cylinder (2140). 
If necessary, add brake fluid of approved specification to bring the level 
between the MAX and MIN lines in the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478). 
Check the brake line fittings at the brake master cylinder for tightness and 
leaking.

 The following conditions are normal. They do not indicate that the 
brake master cylinder requires service. 

Condition 1 — Low fluid level without leaking. This 
condition is caused by displacement of the fluid from the brake master 
cylinder reservoir into the disc brake calipers (2B120) to compensate for 
normal lining wear. Fill the brake master cylinder reservoir to a level 
between the MAX and MIN lines. 

Condition 2 — A momentary or slight squirt of brake 
fluid from the brake master cylinder reservoir upon application of the brake 
pedal (2455). This condition is caused by fluid displacement through the brake 
master cylinder reservoir compensating port as the brake master cylinder 
pistons move forward in the bore. 

Condition 3 — A slight turbulence in the brake master 
cylinder reservoir fluid when the brake pedal is released. Turbulence normally 
occurs when the brake fluid returns to the brake master cylinder after the 
brakes are released. 

Condition 4 — A trace of brake fluid on the power brake 
booster (2005) below the brake master cylinder mounting flange. This condition 
is the normal result of the lubricating action of the brake master cylinder 
wiping seal.

 Brake Tubing 

Double wall steel tubing is used throughout the brake system with the 
exception of the flexible brake hoses at the front and rear wheels. 

Always bleed the applicable primary or secondary brake system after 
primary or secondary brake system hose or brake tube replacement.

When connecting a tube to a hose, tube connector or the brake master 
cylinder, tighten the brake tube flare nut to specification. 

Inspect the brake lines under the vehicle for damage and proper 
routing. Inspect the front brake hoses (2078) connecting the brake lines to 
the front disc brake calipers and to the rear mountings for damage, cracking, 
and softening. Verify that all fittings are tight and do not leak. 

If no signs of leakage are evident, yet the fluid level in the brake 
master cylinder is low, all indications of leakage may have been washed away 
by rain or snow. To verify this condition, fill the brake master cylinder to 
the proper level, bleed the brake system, apply the brakes several times, and 
inspect the brake master cylinder reservoir to verify that the fluid level has 
dropped. Locate and repair any external leaks.

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Pedal Free Height Measurements

Peel back the floor carpet (13000) and sound deadener to expose the 
front floor pan (11135) immediately below the brake pedal (2455). 

Measure the distance from the top center of the brake pedal pad (2454) 
to the front floor pan. 

If the distance measures 204-209 mm (8.03-8.23 inches), the brake pedal 
height is within specification. 

If the brake pedal height is not within specification, continue with 
the procedure. 

[FIGURE: H5751B.gif]

Inspect the brake pedal mounting for missing, worn or damaged brake 
pedal bushings and loose hardware. Service as required. If the pedal bushings 
and hardware are in good condition, continue with the procedure. 

Disconnect the brake on/off (BOO) switch electrical connector. 

Loosen BOO switch jam nuts and move the BOO switch rearward until it no 
longer contacts the brake pedal. 

Loosen the power brake booster to brake master cylinder push rod jam 
nut on the power brake booster to brake master cylinder push rod. 

Turn the power brake booster to brake master cylinder push rod in or 
out to obtain the specified brake pedal height. 

While holding the power brake booster to brake master cylinder push rod 
in position, tighten the power brake booster to brake master cylinder push rod 
jam nut.

[FIGURE: H5752F.gif]

Adjust the BOO switch. Refer to the adjustment procedure in Section 17-01 .

ADJUSTMENTS

Hydraulic Brake Fluid Color

Hydraulic brake fluid color must conform with the requirements of 
Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 116. Under this standard, brake fluids 
are visually different from other automotive fluids (such as transmission, 
power steering, and engine fluids).

The color of the fluid in a normal brake system in service can vary 
from its original color for many reasons. Color may appear to vary between 
cast steel and die cast aluminum brake master cylinder reservoirs. Some of the 
reasons for the apparent difference in color in a system are listed below:

Fluid discoloration can occur due to heat and/or aging.

Fluid discoloration can exist when different brands/shades of brake 
fluid are used in topping off during normal service.

Fluid discoloration can occur through dissolution of the color dye used 
on the brake master cylinder internal springs in the manufacturer's assembly 
procedure.

Brake fluid contaminated with a hydrocarbon/mineral based fluid (power 
steering or transmission fluid) can be detected by an obvious swelling of the 
brake master cylinder cap seal. If the swollen brake master cylinder seal 
condition is present, all brake system rubber parts must be replaced. All 
brake tubes and hoses must be thoroughly flushed with Ford High Performance 
DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3 equivalent fluid meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M6C25-A before the vehicle goes back into service.

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Fluid Level Check

 Brake System Service 

Brake fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) should 
be between 4mm (0.16 inch) below the MAX line on the side of the reservoir and 
the MAX line. If brake fluid is low, the brake system warning indicator will 
illuminate. To add brake fluid, clean and remove the brake master cylinder 
filler cap (2162) and pour clean brake fluid into the top of the brake master 
cylinder reservoir. Fill to specification mentioned above. Use Ford High 
Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3 equivalent fluid meeting 
Ford specification ESA-M6C25-A. If brake fluid has to be added often, check 
all hydraulic connections for leaks.

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Rotor, Disc

 Runout 

Use Dial Indicator/Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent to measure 
the runout at the outer edge of the contact surface of the front disc brake 
rotor (1125). The maximum runout is 0.1mm (0.004 inch). Replace the front disc 
brake rotor if runout exceeds this limit.

 Parallelism 

Parallelism is the variation in the thickness of the disc brake rotor. 
If the two rubbing surfaces of the disc brake rotor are not parallel, the disc 
brake rotor may cause excessive brake pedal (2455) travel, a pulsating brake 
pedal, or noise.

Two methods can be used to check if the two faces of a disc brake rotor 
are parallel. A micrometer can be used to measure the disc brake rotor 
thickness at 12 points approximately 30 degrees apart and 25.4mm (1 inch) from 
the outer edge of the disc brake rotor.

The other method is to measure the disc brake rotor on a precision 
lathe designed for machining disc brake rotors. Attach two dial indicators, 
one on each side of the disc brake rotor, so that the stylus of each indicator 
contacts the rubbing surface directly opposite each other, approximately 
25.4mm (1 inch) from the outer edge of the disc brake rotor.

Zero both indicators and rotate the disc brake rotor while watching 
both dials. If the total readings of both indicators exceed the specified 
limit for parallelism, the disc brake rotor must be refinished or replaced.

 Refinishing 

 NOTE: Machining thinner than the limit permits the front disc brake rotor to 
wear past the discard limit while in service. Afront disc brake rotor at or 
below the discard limit may result in severe overheating and fade because the 
thin front disc brake rotor may be unable to dissipate the heat generated 
during braking.

Front disc brake rotor refinishing should only be performed using 
equipment that produces a simultaneous straddle cut. Machining one side of the 
front disc brake rotor at a time can produce a tapered front disc brake rotor. 
Rotunda On-The-Car Lathe Package 104-00129 with Drive Plate Attaching Bolts 
104-00163 or equivalents are acceptable. To ensure a correct surface finish, 
make sure the cutting bit is sharp and follow the lathe manufacturer's 
recommendations for feed and speed. 

 Service Limits 

 CAUTION: If refinishing will cause the front disc brake rotor to fall below the 
minimum thickness, the front disc brake rotor must be discarded. Refer to the 
Brake System Component Specifications chart in this section. 

Front disc brake rotor minimum thickness is the thickness at which the 
front disc brake rotor becomes unsafe to use. It is also referred to as the 
discard thickness. The minimum thickness of the front disc brake rotor is 
labeled on the face of the front disc brake rotor.

The front disc brake rotor minimum thickness dimensions are as follows:

Automatic transaxle (A/T) vehicles: 20mm (0.78 inch)

Manual transaxle (M/T) vehicles: 16mm (0.63 inch)

The minimum thickness that a front disc brake rotor can be machined is 
0.762mm (0.030 inch) plus the minimum thickness dimension labeled on the front 
disc brake rotor. This allows for front disc brake rotor wear after the front 
disc brake rotor has been resurfaced and returned to service.

================================================================================
PAGE 2578
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-00: Brake System — Service

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Drum

 Refinishing 

Minor scores on a brake drum (1126) can be removed with sandpaper. Do 
not refinish brake drums to remove score marks. A brake drum surface which is 
highly polished can cause the brake to lock up. This polished condition should 
be removed either with sandpaper or by refinishing the brake drum. A brake 
drum that is out of round sufficiently enough to cause vehicle vibration or 
noise when braking should be refinished. Remove only enough stock to true-up 
the brake drum. Brake drum maximum inside diameter is shown on each brake 
drum. If the maximum inside diameter shown on the brake drum is exceeded 
either through wear or refinishing, the brake drum must be replaced. 

Check the inside diameter of the brake drum with Brake Adjustment Gauge 
D81L-1103-A, or Rotunda Brake Drum Micrometer 104-00046 or equivalent. 

After a brake drum is refinished, wipe the refinished surface with a 
cloth soaked in clean denatured alcohol. If one brake drum is refinished, the 
brake drum on the opposite side of the vehicle should also be refinished to 
the same diameter.

Brake, Service

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake, Parking

The parking brake is a mechanical, rather than hydraulic, method of 
applying the rear brakes. Normally, the parking brake is used whenever the 
vehicle is parked to prevent unexpected vehicle movement.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Shoe Automatic Adjustment

The self adjuster is part of the rear brake operating lever (2N511). 
When the clearance between the brake shoe and lining (2001) and brake drum 
(1126) becomes excessive, the brake shoe and lining pulls the adjuster cam, 
disengaging the teeth on the self adjuster cam and the rear brake operating 
lever. A spring rotates the self adjuster cam to a new position that holds the 
brake shoes and linings closer to the brake drum.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Lug Bolt Torque Requirement

 WARNING: REPLACE WHEELS IF THEY ARE BENT, CRACKED, LEAKING AIR OR HEAVILY RUSTED 
OR IF THE WHEEL HUB BOLTS OFTEN BECOME LOOSE. DO NOT USE BENT WHEELS THAT HAVE

Connect the brake tube and tighten securely.

Install the brake shoe and lining. Refer to the procedure in this 
section.

Bleed the brakes. Refer to the procedure in Section 06-06 .

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cleaning

 WARNING: BRAKES MAY CONTAIN ASBESTOS FIBERS. AVOID BREATHING DUST. BREATHING 
ASBESTOS DUST MAY CAUSE ASBESTOSIS AND CANCER. 

 BREATHING ASBESTOS DUST IS HAZARDOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. 

 DUST AND DIRT PRESENT ON WHEEL BRAKE AND CLUTCH 
ASSEMBLIES MAY CONTAIN ASBESTOS FIBERS THAT ARE HAZARDOUS TO HEALTH WHEN MADE 
AIRBORNE BY CLEANING WITH COMPRESSED AIR OR BY DRY BRUSHING. 

 WHEEL BRAKE ASSEMBLIES AND CLUTCH FACINGS SHOULD BE 
CLEANED USING A VACUUM CLEANER RECOMMENDED FOR USE WITH ASBESTOS FIBERS SUCH 
AS ROTUNDA BRAKE/CLUTCH/SERVICE VACUUM 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT. DUST AND DIRT 
FROM VACUUM SHOULD BE DISPOSED OF IN A MANNER THAT PREVENTS DUST EXPOSURE, 
SUCH AS SEALED BAGS. THE BAG MUST BE LABELED AS PER OSHA INSTRUCTIONS AND THE 
TRASH HAULER NOTIFIED AS TO THE BAG'S CONTENTS. 

 IF A VACUUM SUITABLE FOR ASBESTOS IS NOT AVAILABLE, 
CLEANING SHOULD BE DONE WET. IF DUST GENERATION IS STILL POSSIBLE, TECHNICIANS 
SHOULD WEAR GOVERNMENT-APPROVED TOXIC DUST PURIFYING RESPIRATORS. 

 GRINDING OR SANDING ON BRAKE LININGS, PADS, ROTORS, 
DRUMS, OR CLUTCH FACINGS SHOULD BE DONE ONLY WHILE USING PROPERLY 
EXHAUST-VENTILATED EQUIPMENT. 

 OSHA REQUIRES AREAS WHERE ASBESTOS DUST GENERATION IS 
POSSIBLE TO BE ISOLATED AND POSTED WITH WARNING SIGNS. ONLY TECHNICIANS 
CONCERNED WITH PERFORMING BRAKE OR CLUTCH SERVICE SHOULD BE PRESENT IN THE AREA.

================================================================================
PAGE 2594
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-02: Brakes, Rear Drum

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Inspection 

 Rear Wheel Cylinders 

The rear wheel cylinders (2261) should not be disassembled unless they 
are leaking. Pull back each dust boot as shown and inspect for leakage.

[FIGURE: H8608C.gif]

Excessive fluid at this point indicates leakage past the piston seals 
and a need for rear wheel cylinder overhaul. A slight amount of fluid is 
almost always present and acts as a lubricant for the pistons. If evidence of 
leakage is noted, the rear wheel cylinder should be disassembled, inspected 
and overhauled. 

Inspect the rear wheel cylinder bore for scratches and pitting. If the 
rear wheel cylinder is pitted or has deep scratches, the rear wheel cylinder 
must be replaced.

 Brake Drums 

Inspect the inside of the brake drum (1126) for scratches and uneven or 
abnormal wear. 

Resurface if damage is minor or replace if damage is excessive. 

Measure the inside diameter of the brake drum using Rotunda Brake Drum 
Micrometer 104-00046, or equivalent.

[FIGURE: H5324D.gif]

 CAUTION: Be sure to check the drum-to-shoe contact after repairing or replacing 
the brake drum. 

The standard inner brake drum diameter is 200mm (7.87 inches). Replace 
the brake drum if the diameter is larger than 201.5mm (7.93 inches).

[FIGURE: H5715C.gif]

 Brake Lining 

Check the brake linings for peeling, cracks, or extremely uneven wear. 

 CAUTION: Always replace the brake linings as a set, with linings of equal 
quality. 

If brake lining thickness is less than 1.0mm (0.04 inch), replace the 
brake shoes and linings (2001).

[FIGURE: H8611A.gif]

 Springs 

Check springs for: 

Spread or collapsed coils 

Twisted, bent or damaged shanks 

Discoloration — This is a sign of brake overheating. 
Overheated springs lose some of their tension and should be replaced.

[FIGURE: H8612A.gif]

 Brake Backing Plate 

Inspect the rivets. 

The rivets must be tight and securely peened.

Inspect the shoe pads (where the brake shoes and linings rest). 

[FIGURE: H6022B.gif]

Deep grooves in the shoe pads could restrict brake shoe and lining 
movement. 

If grooves exist, hand sand the shoe pads. 

If the grooves are still present after hand sanding, the brake backing 
plate (2211) must be replaced. Any attempt to remove the grooves by grinding 
may result in improper brake shoe and lining to brake drum contact.

PAGE 2595
================================================================================
