Section 06-02: Brakes, Rear Drum

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Shoe and Lining 

 Drums Removed 

The rear brakes are automatically adjusted while driving the vehicle. 
Manual brake adjustment is required only after the brake shoes and linings 
(2001) have been replaced, or if the adjuster has malfunctioned and has been 
repaired or replaced. Perform the manual adjustment with the brake drum (1126) 
removed, using Brake Adjustment Gauge D81L-1103-A or equivalent and the 
procedure described below. 

When adjusting the brake shoes and linings, check the front parking 
brake cable and conduit (2853) for proper adjustment. Make sure the equalizer 
operates freely. Refer to the procedure in Section 06-05 for parking brake 
service.

Raise and support the vehicle. 

Remove the wheel and tire assembly. 

Remove the brake drum. Refer to the procedure in this section. 

Use Rotunda Brake/Clutch/Service Vacuum 164-R3600 or equivalent to 
remove any dust present on the brake assembly. 

Carefully remove the brake shoe hold-down springs (2068). Using 
sandpaper, clean the shoe pads on the brake backing plate (2211) while holding 
the brake shoe and lining away from the brake backing plate.

Check brake backing plate for damage. If any damage is found, it must 
be replaced. Refer to the procedure in this section. If no damage is found, 
apply a small amount of Silicone Brake Caliper Grease and Dielectric Compound 
D7AZ-19A331-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M1C171-A to the 
shoe pads. Be careful not to get the lubricant on the linings. 

[FIGURE: H6022B.gif]

Install the brake shoe hold-down springs.

Use Brake Adjustment Gauge D81L-1103-A or equivalent to measure the 
inside diameter of the brake drum braking surface.

[FIGURE: H8609A.gif]

Use Brake Adjustment Gauge D81L-1103-A or equivalent to measure the 
distance between the brake shoes and linings.

[FIGURE: H8610A.gif]

Insert a screwdriver into the self adjuster on the rear brake operating 
lever (2N511) as shown. Adjust the brake shoes and linings to the same 
measurement of the brake drum.

[FIGURE: H8613C.gif]

Install the brake drum. Refer to the procedure in this section.

Install the wheel and tire assembly on the brake drum. Tighten the lug 
bolts (1107) to 88-118 Nm (65-87 lb-ft). Remove the safety 
stands and lower the vehicle. 

Complete the adjustment by sharply applying the brakes several times 
while driving the vehicle alternately forward and reverse. 

After adjusting the brake shoes and linings, check brake operation by 
making several stops while driving forward.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Disc

The front disc brake system consists of a full-floating front disc 
brake caliper (2B120) and a front disc brake rotor (1125). The front disc 
brake caliper is attached to the front wheel knuckle (3K186) with two brake 
caliper bolts (2W303) that also serve as the front disc brake caliper slide 
pins. In addition to providing a braking surface, the front disc brake rotor 
forms part of the front wheel hub (1104).

The single piston front disc brake caliper applies the brake shoes and 
linings (2001) that are held in position by a disc brake pad anti-rattle clip 
(2B164) and two disc brake caliper locating pins (2B296). The brake shoes and 
linings are prevented from rattling against the front disc brake caliper and 
disc brake caliper locating pins by an M-shaped anti-rattle spring that 
maintains a constant pressure on the brake shoes and linings.

A flexible front brake hose (2078) is used to connect the front disc 
brake caliper to the hydraulic system. Leakage at the hose connection is 
prevented by copper washers installed on either side of the hydraulic fitting.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Caliper 

The front disc brake caliper (2B120) consists of a pin slider-type 
front disc brake caliper housing, inner and outer brake shoes and linings, 
caliper piston, dust boot, and piston seal. The front disc brake caliper is 
attached to the front wheel knuckle (3K185) with two brake caliper bolts 
(2W303) that also serve as the front disc caliper slide pins.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Shoe and Linings 

The brake shoes and linings (2001) are held in position by a disc brake 
pad anti-rattle clip (2B164) and two disc brake caliper locating pins (2B296). 
The inboard brake shoe and lining is equipped with a wear indicator. The wear 
indicator contacts the front disc brake rotor (1125) and makes a squealing 
noise when the brake shoes and linings are worn. This assures that the brake 
shoes and linings will be replaced before any front disc brake rotor damage 
occurs.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Service Precautions

Grease or any other foreign material must be kept off the brake shoe 
and lining surfaces and braking surfaces of the front disc brake rotor (1125), 
and the external surfaces of the wheel hub (1104) during service operation. In 
handling the front disc brake rotor and front disc brake caliper (2B120), 
avoid deformation of front disc brake rotor, and nicking or scratching of the 
brake shoes and linings (2001).

 CAUTION: Do not pry on the caliper piston with a screwdriver or other tools, as 
this will cause chipping, nicks and gouges. 

If a caliper piston is removed for any reason, the piston seal must be 
replaced. Exercise care not to damage the caliper piston by protecting it from 
contact with any metal or sharp objects.

During removal and installation of a wheel assembly, exercise care not 
to interfere with and damage the front disc brake rotor shield (2K005) or 
bleeder screw.

Before servicing any front end components, ensure the vehicle is 
centered on a hoist to avoid bending or damaging the front disc brake rotor 
shield on full RH or LH wheel turns.

Do not attempt to clean or restore oil or grease-soaked brake shoes and 
linings. When contaminated brake shoes and linings are found, brake shoes and 
linings must be replaced in complete sets and the front disc brake rotor 
braking surfaces wiped clean.

The front disc brake calipers must be installed with the bleeder screw 
in an upward position for proper bleeding of air from the brake system.

Boot (Part of 2221)

Remove the bleeder screw and drain the brake fluid out of the front 
disc brake caliper (2B120).

Remove the retaining ring.

[FIGURE: H5768D.gif]

Position a block of wood or a roll of shop towels between the caliper 
piston and the front disc brake caliper.

 WARNING: DO NOT USE AN EXCESSIVE AMOUNT OF AIR PRESSURE TO REMOVE THE PISTON. 
EXCESSIVE PRESSURE CAN FORCE THE PISTON OUT OF THE CALIPER BORE WITH ENOUGH 
FORCE TO CAUSE PERSONAL INJURY. NEVER ATTEMPT TO CATCH THE PISTON BY HAND AS 
IT COMES OUT OF THE CALIPER BORE. 

Apply the air pressure through the inlet port. Apply only enough 
pressure to ease the caliper piston out of the bore.

[FIGURE: H5769C.gif]

Remove the dust boot from the caliper piston and discard.

[FIGURE: H5770C.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not use a screwdriver or other metal tool. A metal tool can scratch 
or nick the seal groove resulting in a possible leak. 

Remove the piston seal from the caliper bore. Use a plastic or wooden 
pick to remove the seal. 

[FIGURE: H5771D.gif]

Remove the bleeder screw. 

Remove the front caliper sleeves (2B393) and the boots.

[FIGURE: H5772C.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not use petroleum-based solvent, kerosene, or gasoline for cleaning 
caliper parts. Their use as a cleaning agent can leave residues which can 
damage the rubber seals. 

Wash the parts in clean denatured alcohol and dry with compressed air.

 Assembly 

Lubricate the piston seal with the pink grease contained in the 
overhaul kit and install it in the front disc brake caliper.

[FIGURE: H5773C.gif]

Lubricate the caliper piston with brake fluid and partially install the 
caliper piston. The dust boot seal must remain above the caliper bore.

[FIGURE: H5774B.gif]

Lubricate the dust boot with the pink grease contained in the overhaul 
kit then install it on the caliper piston. 

[FIGURE: H5775C.gif]

Press the caliper piston into the front disc brake caliper until the 
caliper piston bottoms in the bore. 

Install a new retaining ring. 

Install the bleeder screw. 

Install the front caliper sleeves and new boots. 

Lubricate the inside surface of the boots and the outer surface of the 
front caliper sleeves with the pink grease contained in the overhaul kit. Do 
not allow the grease to enter the bushing bore.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cleaning

 WARNING: BREATHING ASBESTOS DUST IS HAZARDOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. 

DUST AND DIRT PRESENT ON THE DISC BRAKE ASSEMBLY MAY CONTAIN ASBESTOS 
FIBERS THAT ARE HAZARDOUS TO YOUR HEALTH WHEN MADE AIRBORNE BY CLEANING WITH 
COMPRESSED AIR OR BY DRY BRUSHING. 

THE DISC BRAKE ASSEMBLY SHOULD BE CLEANED USING A VACUUM CLEANER 
RECOMMENDED FOR USE WITH ASBESTOS FIBERS, SUCH AS THE ROTUNDA 
BRAKE/CLUTCH/SERVICE VACUUM 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT. DUST AND DIRT FROM THE 
VACUUM SHOULD BE DISPOSED OF IN A MANNER THAT PREVENTS DUST EXPOSURE, SUCH AS 
SEALED BAGS. THE BAG MUST BE LABELED PER OSHA INSTRUCTIONS AND THE TRASH 
HAULER NOTIFIED AS TO ITS CONTENTS. 

IF A VACUUM SUITABLE FOR ASBESTOS IS NOT AVAILABLE, CLEANING SHOULD BE 
DONE WET. IF DUST GENERATION IS STILL POSSIBLE, TECHNICIANS SHOULD WEAR 
GOVERNMENT APPROVED TOXIC DUST PURIFYING RESPIRATORS. 

GRINDING OR SANDING ON BRAKE PADS OR FRONT DISC BRAKE ROTORS SHOULD BE 
DONE USING PROPER EXHAUST VENTILATED EQUIPMENT. 

OSHA REQUIRES AREAS WHERE ASBESTOS DUST GENERATION IS POSSIBLE TO BE 
ISOLATED AND POSTED WITH WARNING SIGNS. ONLY TECHNICIANS CONCERNED WITH 
PERFORMING BRAKE SERVICE SHOULD BE PRESENT IN THE AREA. 

DENATURED ALCOHOL IS ACCEPTABLE FOR CLEANING COMPONENT PARTS PROVIDED 
THE PARTS ARE COMPLETELY AIR DRIED BEFORE INSTALLATION. 

 CAUTION: Do not use denatured alcohol for flushing the hydraulic system or 
cleaning assemblies where alcohol could be trapped and subsequently 
contaminate the brake fluid. Contaminated brake fluid may cause eventual 
failure of rubber components in the system. 

To remove brake fluid contamination, clean all parts except the brake 
shoes and linings (2001) with denatured alcohol. Do not attempt to clean 
contaminated brake shoes and linings. 

Contaminated brake shoes and linings must be replaced.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Caliper

Whenever the front disc brake caliper (2B120) is rebuilt, inspect the 
front disc brake caliper bore, piston seal groove, and caliper piston for: 

Cuts.

Deep scratches.

Pitting.

The caliper piston and front disc brake caliper bore may be lightly 
polished with crocus cloth, but if deep scratches remain, the front disc brake 
caliper must be replaced. The piston seal groove in the front disc brake 
caliper must be free of deep scratches that would prevent the piston seal from 
working properly.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Rotor 

Whenever the brakes are serviced, the front disc brake rotor (1125) 
must be visually inspected to check for any abnormal wear, and checked with a 
micrometer to make sure the thickness is within the specifications. Minimum 
thickness for the front disc brake rotor is 20mm (0.78 inch) for ATX vehicles 
and 16mm (0.63 inch) for MTX vehicles. 

There must be no front wheel bearing free play when checking for front 
disc brake rotor runout. Measure the front disc brake rotor runout at the 
outermost diameter on the contact surface of the brake shoes and linings 
(2001). Refer to the procedure in this section.

Parallelism is checked by measuring the front disc brake rotor 
thickness in several places with a micrometer. The front disc brake rotor 
thickness variation must not be more than 0.025mm (0.001 inch). The front disc 
brake rotors may be resurfaced if they do not fall below the minimum thickness 
specification after machining. If the front disc brake rotor thickness 
variation is below specification after resurfacing, the front disc brake rotor 
must be replaced.

Rotor and Brake Shoe and Lining Hand Sanding

If there are only surface irregularities, the front disc brake rotor 
(1125) may be resurfaced by lightly sanding the face with a fine emery cloth.

the front disc brake rotor can be sanded where the front disc brake caliper

disc brake rotor must be resurfaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Control Assemblies

 Cable Actuated Rear Wheel Parking Brake 

The parking brake is a system of levers with an interconnecting metal 
cable used to mechanically apply the rear brakes. The parking brake control 
(2780) used for application of the parking brake is mounted on the front floor 
pan (11135) between the two front seats. From the parking brake control, the 
front parking brake cable and conduit (2853) extends to an equalizer attached 
to the rear axle torsion beam. The equalizer serves as a dividing point where 
the cable splits and connects to a rear brake operating lever (2N511) at each 
rear brake. 

When the parking brake control is pulled upward, its motion is 
transferred through the front parking brake cable and conduit to the 
equalizer. The action of the equalizer divides the force transferred through 
the cables to each rear brake. The rear brake operating lever at the rear 
brake transfers its motion through a strut which pushes the rear brake shoes 
and linings (2200) outward against the brake drum (1126). 

Pressing the release button on the end of the parking brake control 
releases the lock pawl holding the parking brake in the applied position. As 
the parking brake control is lowered to the vehicle floor, springs in the rear 
brake assembly will pull the rear brake shoes and linings away from the brake 
drums.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification

Check the operation of the parking brake with the vehicle on a hoist 
and the parking brake fully released. If there is any slack in the cables or 
if the rear brakes drag when the wheels are turned, adjust as required. Check 
for any cable damage and replace if necessary.

brake control. The parking brake must fully set within 11-16 notches. If not 
as specified, adjust the front parking brake cable and conduit (2853).

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Fluid Level Check

Brake fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) should 
be between 4mm (0.16 inch) below the MAX line on the side of the reservoir and 
the MAX line. If brake fluid is low, the brake system warning indicator will 
illuminate. To add brake fluid, clean and remove the brake master cylinder 
filler cap (2162) and pour clean brake fluid into the top of the brake master 
cylinder reservoir. Fill to the specification mentioned above. Use Ford High 
Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3 equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M6C25-A. If brake fluid has to be added often, check all 
hydraulic connections for leaks.

Section 06-06: Brake System, Hydraulic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System

The brake system uses the principles of hydraulics to apply the front 
and rear brakes.

The brake pedal (2455) is connected to a hydraulic servo called the 
brake master cylinder (2140). 

When the brake pedal is pushed, a solid column of fluid is pushed from 
the brake master cylinder through metal tubing and flexible hoses to the rear 
wheel cylinders (2261) and front disc brake calipers (2B120). 

The rear wheel cylinders and front disc brake calipers are hydraulic 
actuators where the hydraulic pressure produced in the brake master cylinder 
is converted into motion. 

The pistons in the rear wheel cylinders are forced outward against the 
brake shoes and linings (2001) which contact a metal braking surface on the 
brake drum (1126). 

The front brake caliper pistons move inward against the brake shoes and 
linings and contact the metal braking surface of the front disc brake rotor 
(1125). 

When the brake pedal is released, the pressure in the system is 
relieved and the brake shoes and linings return to their neutral or unapplied 
position.

Brake Master Cylinder

brake lines. This pressure forces the front disc brake caliper pistons and the 
rear wheel cylinder pistons to move the brake shoes and linings (2001) into 
contact with the metal braking surfaces.

 Dual Hydraulic Brake System 

The brake lines are arranged to form a split diagonal hydraulic system. 
Although the physical layout of the brake lines do not indicate it, they are 
arranged to form an "X." One side of the "X" supplies hydraulic pressure to 
the left front and right rear. The remaining circuit supplies pressure to the 
right front and left rear. The hydraulic system is split in this manner as a 
safety precaution. If hydraulic pressure is lost in one circuit, the remaining 
circuit can provide less efficient but balanced braking between the front and 
rear brakes. 

If brake fluid is lost from one or both circuits, a brake fluid level 
switch in the brake master cylinder will illuminate a brake system warning 
indicator in the instrument cluster. The brake system warning indicator comes 
on when the brake master cylinder float in the brake master cylinder drops too 
low and completes the circuit. Once the circuit is closed, the brake system 
warning indicator will come on and remain on whenever the ignition switch 
(11572) is in the ON or START position. The same brake system warning 
indicator also indicates when the parking brake is applied. If the brake 
system warning indicator is on, make sure the parking brake is fully released.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Master Cylinder Fluid Level Sensor

The brake master cylinder fluid level sensor (2B372) is contained 
inside the body of the plastic brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) and 
activates the brake system warning indicator whenever the brake fluid level is 
low. The brake master cylinder fluid level sensor is activated by a brake 
master cylinder float inside the brake master cylinder reservoir.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Pressure Control Valve

A brake pressure control valve (2B091) is installed in the system to 
balance front-to-rear brake application. The brake pressure control valve 
reduces hydraulic pressure to the rear wheel cylinders (2261) to prevent rear 
wheel lockup. Internally, the brake pressure control valve contains plungers 
that are shifted by hydraulic pressure to limit the output pressure to the 
rear brakes. 

Do not attempt to service the brake pressure control valve. It is 
serviced only as an assembly.

The brake pressure control valve is located in the engine compartment. 
It is mounted on the bulkhead, below and to the right of the power brake 
booster (2005).

Brake Master Cylinder Reservoir

into the brake master cylinder.

Lubricate the inside of the seals with clean brake fluid, and press the 
brake master cylinder reservoir into the brake master cylinder.

connector.

Fill the brake master cylinder reservoir with Ford High Performance DOT 
3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3 equivalent fluid meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M6C25-A to the MAX line or 4.0mm (0.156 inch) below. 

Install the brake master cylinder filler cap.

Check the new brake master cylinder reservoir for leaks.

 Disassembly 

Clamp the brake master cylinder in a vise equipped with protective jaw 
caps. 

Remove the brake master cylinder reservoir screw.

[FIGURE: H8520D.gif]

Carefully pry the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) out of the 
brake master cylinder.

[FIGURE: H8709C.gif]

Remove the brake master cylinder reservoir seals from the brake master 
cylinder.

Push the primary piston into the brake master cylinder bore to ease 
snap ring removal. Remove the primary piston snap ring and the primary piston.

[FIGURE: H5786C.gif]

Push the secondary piston into the bore before removing the secondary 
piston stop screw. Remove the secondary piston stop screw.

[FIGURE: H5788B.gif]

 NOTE: Air pressure can be used to remove the secondary piston from the bore. 
If this method is used, safety precautions must be taken. Cover the end of the 
brake master cylinder with shop towels and use only enough air pressure to 
ease the secondary piston out of the bore. The secondary piston can also be 
removed by tapping the brake master cylinder on a wooden surface. 

Remove the secondary piston.

Remove the seals from the secondary and primary pistons. 

 CAUTION: Do not use petroleum based solvent, kerosene, or gasoline for cleaning 
brake master cylinder parts. Their use as a cleaning agent can leave residues 
which can damage the rubber seals. 

Wash the parts in clean denatured alcohol and dry with compressed air.

 Assembly 

 NOTE: As the brake master cylinder parts are assembled, they must be 
lubricated with clean brake fluid. 

Install new seals on the primary and secondary pistons. 

 NOTE: To prevent damage to the seal lip, ease the piston into the brake 
master cylinder bore while slowly rotating and pushing. 

Lubricate the secondary piston with brake fluid and install. 

 NOTE: While installing the secondary piston stop screw, bottom the secondary 
piston in the bore. 

Install the secondary piston stop screw. 

 NOTE: To prevent damage to the seal lip, lubricate with brake fluid and ease 
the piston into the bore while slowly rotating and pushing. 

Install the primary piston.

Install the primary piston snap ring. Push the primary piston into the 
bore to ease primary piston snap ring installation. 

Lubricate the new brake master cylinder reservoir seals with clean 
brake fluid and press them into the brake master cylinder. 

Install the brake master cylinder reservoir by placing the brake master 
cylinder reservoir upside down and pressing the brake master cylinder downward 
onto it using hand pressure.

[FIGURE: H8710C.gif]

Install the brake master cylinder reservoir screw and the brake master 
cylinder filler cap (2162).

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Hydraulic System Bleeding 

When any part of the hydraulic system has been disconnected for 
service, air may enter the system and cause spongy pedal action. Bleeding is a 
simple procedure used to remove air from the hydraulic circuits. 

The brake hydraulic circuits form a split diagonal hydraulic system. 
The left front and right rear form one circuit while the right front and left 
rear form the other circuit. When bleeding one of these circuits, bleed the 
rear wheel first and then the front wheel at the opposite corner.

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES, 
FLUSH EYES WITH RUNNING WATER FOR 15 MINUTES. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION IF 
IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET 
MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY. 

 CAUTION: Brake fluid will damage a vehicle's finish. Do not allow brake fluid to 
come into contact with painted surfaces. 

Ford High Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 
3-equivalent fluid meeting Ford specification ESA-M6C25-A must be used in the 
brake system. 

Never reuse brake fluid that has been drained from the hydraulic system 
or that has been allowed to stand in an open container for an extended period 
of time.

When a new brake master cylinder (2140) has been installed, or the 
brake system emptied or partially emptied, brake fluid may not flow to the 
bleeder screws during normal bleeding. It may be necessary to prime the system 
using the following procedure: 

Using a tubing wrench, remove the brake tubes from the brake master 
cylinder. 

Install short brake tubes in the brake master cylinder and position 
them so that they point back into the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) 
and the ends of the tubes are submerged in brake fluid. 

Fill the brake master cylinder with new Ford High Performance DOT 3 
Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3-equivalent fluid meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M6C25-A.

Cover the brake master cylinder reservoir with a shop towel. 

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash it with water. 

Pump the brakes until clear, bubble-free brake fluid comes out of both 
temporary brake tubes. 

Remove the temporary brake tubes and reinstall the brake tubes. Tighten 
the brake tube flare nuts to 13-21 Nm (10-15 lb-ft).

Bleed each brake tube at the brake master cylinder using the following 
procedure: 

Have an assistant pump the brake pedal (2455) 10 times and then hold 
firm pressure on the brake pedal. 

Loosen the rear brake tube flare nut with a tubing wrench until a 
stream of brake fluid comes out. Have an assistant maintain pressure on the 
brake pedal until the brake tube flare nut is tightened again. 

Repeat this operation until clear, bubble-free brake fluid comes out 
from around the brake tube flare nut. 

Repeat this bleeding operation at the front brake tube flare nut. 

If any of the brake tubes have been removed, it may be helpful to prime 
the system by gravity bleeding it. This should be done after the brake master 
cylinder is primed and bled. 

To gravity bleed the brake system: 

Fill the brake master cylinder reservoir with new Ford High Performance 
DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3-equivalent fluid meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M6C25-A.

One at a time, loosen the two rear bleeder screws and leave them open 
until clear brake fluid flows out. Be sure to check the brake fluid level 
often and do not let the brake master cylinder reservoir run dry. 

Tighten the two rear bleeder screws. 

One at a time, loosen the two front bleeder screws. Leave the bleeder 
screws open until clear brake fluid flows out. Be sure to check the brake 
fluid level often and do not let the brake master cylinder reservoir run dry. 

Tighten the two front bleeder screws.

After the brake master cylinder has been primed, the brake tubes bled 
at the brake master cylinder, and the brake system primed, normal brake system 
bleeding can resume at each wheel. 

 Manual Bleeding 

Clean all the dirt from the brake master cylinder filler cap (2162). 

 NOTE: During the bleeding operation do not allow the brake master cylinder to 
run dry. 

Fill the brake master cylinder with the specified brake fluid.

If the brake master cylinder is known or suspected to contain air it 
must be bled before the individual wheels. 

Remove the bleeder screw cover from the appropriate bleeder screw. 

 NOTE: The bleeder hose has to fit snugly around the bleeder screw. 

Attach a bleeder hose to the bleeder screw.

Submerge the free end of the bleeder hose in a container partially 
filled with brake fluid. 

Loosen the bleeder screw approximately 3/4 of a turn. 

Have an assistant push the brake pedal slowly through its full travel 
and hold it there.

Close the bleeder screw. 

Have an assistant release the brake pedal.

Repeat the bleeding process until air bubbles cease to appear at the 
submerged end of the bleeder hose. 

When the brake fluid entering the bottle is completely free of bubbles, 
tighten the bleeder screw, remove the bleeder hose, and install the bleeder 
screw cover. 

Repeat the bleed procedure at the appropriate diagonal brake. 

Check the fluid level. If necessary, fill to the correct level with the 
specified brake fluid. 

Check the brake pedal feel. If the brake pedal remains spongy, repeat 
the bleeding process or, if necessary, refer to the diagnostic charts in 
 Section 06-00 .

 Pressure Bleeding 

When using pressure bleeding equipment, use a bladder type bleeder tank 
such as Rotunda Brake Bleeder 104-00064 or equivalent. In this type of 
bleeder, the brake fluid is separated from the air by a rubber diaphragm. 

The bleeder tank must contain enough brake fluid to complete the 
bleeding operation and should be charged with 10-30 pounds of air pressure. 
Never exceed 50 pounds of pressure. 

Clean all dirt from the brake master cylinder filler cap. 

If necessary fill the brake master cylinder to the correct level with 
the specified brake fluid.

 NOTE: Follow the manufacturer's instructions when installing and connecting 
the master cylinder adapter. 

Install the bleeder adapter tool on the brake master cylinder and 
attach the hose from the bleeder tank to the fitting on the adapter.

Open the valve on the bleeder tank. 

 NOTE: If the brake master cylinder is known or suspected to contain air it 
must be bled before the individual wheels are bled. 

Remove the bleeder screw cover from the appropriate bleeder screw. 

 NOTE: The bleeder hose has to fit snugly around the bleeder screw. 

Attach a bleeder hose to the bleeder screw.

Submerge the free end of the bleeder hose in a container partially 
filled with brake fluid. 

Loosen the bleeder screw approximately 3/4 of a turn. 

When the brake fluid entering the bottle is completely free of bubbles, 
tighten the bleeder screw, remove the bleeder hose, and install the bleeder 
screw cover. 

Repeat the pressure bleeding procedure at the appropriate diagonal 
brake. 

Close the valve at the bleeder tank, disconnect the bleeder hose from 
the master cylinder adapter, and remove the master cylinder adapter. 

Check the fluid level. If necessary, fill to the correct level with the 
specified brake fluid. 

Check brake pedal feel. If the brake pedal remains spongy, repeat the 
bleeding process or, if necessary, refer to the diagnostic charts in this 
 Section 06-00 .

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Brake Master Cylinder 

Inspect the brake master cylinder parts for the following: 

Pistons for scratches, scoring or other visible damage. 

Bore for score marks or corrosion. Staining should not be confused with 
corrosion. Corrosion can be identified as pits or excessive roughness. Light 
scratches or slightly corroded spots may be polished out using crocus cloth. 
Never use emery paper or sandpaper. 

Make sure the brake line ports are open and that the brake line seats 
are in a serviceable condition. 

Check the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) for cracks or other 
signs of damage. If the brake master cylinder reservoir is damaged, the brake 
master cylinder reservoir must be replaced.

================================================================================
PAGE 2660

Brake Booster to Master Cylinder Push Rod

The brake booster to master cylinder push rod does not usually need

Section 06-07: Brake System, Power

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Booster, Power

The power brake booster (2005) reduces the effort required to push the 
brake pedal (2455) and apply the brakes. Power assist is affected by a 
pressure differential within the power brake booster . When the engine (6007) 
is running with the brakes released, engine vacuum is present on both sides of 
a diaphragm within the power brake booster. As the brake pedal is pressed, a 
valve rod and plunger assembly moves forward within a power piston until a 
vacuum port is closed. At this point, vacuum is still applied to both sides of 
the diaphragm. As the valve rod and plunger assembly continues to move 
forward, an atmospheric port is opened. Atmospheric pressure then enters the 
rear half of the power brake booster. Engine vacuum on the front half of the 
diaphragm and atmospheric pressure on the rear side of the diaphragm assist 
the valve rod and plunger assembly in pushing the diaphragm plate forward. 
This movement forces the master cylinder push rod against the brake master 
cylinder piston. 

If the brake pedal is held depressed, the diaphragm will momentarily 
continue to move forward to compress the outer edges of a reaction disc. This 
movement causes the center of the reaction disc to press the valve rod and 
plunger assembly back and close the vacuum port or the atmospheric port, 
depending on whether the brake pedal is released or depressed further.

A rubber vacuum hose between the engine and power brake booster 
contains an internal check valve. This valve closes when the engine is shut 
off or under a low manifold vacuum situation, trapping vacuum in the power 
brake booster. This reserve vacuum allows several power assisted applications 
of the brakes, even without the engine running.

Remove the brake master cylinder (2140). Refer to Section 06-06 for the 
removal procedure. 

Disconnect the vacuum booster hose (2A047) from the power brake booster.

[FIGURE: H5742C.gif]

From inside the vehicle, remove the cotter pin securing the clevis pin. 
Discard the cotter pin.

Remove the clevis pin from the clevis. 

Have a second technician support the power brake booster in the engine 
compartment. 

Remove the four power brake booster nuts securing the power brake 
booster to the bulkhead. 

Remove the power brake booster. 

Remove the brake booster mounting bracket gasket (2B022).

 Installation 

To install, reverse the removal procedure.

Lubricate the clevis pin with white lithium grease and install a new 
cotter pin. 

Tighten the four power brake booster nuts to 19-26 Nm 
(14-19 lb-ft). 

Tighten the two brake master cylinder nuts to 10-16 Nm 
(7-12 lb-ft).

Adjustment of the brake booster to master cylinder push rod is usually 
only made during replacement of the brake master cylinder (2140). Proper 
adjustment of the brake booster to master cylinder push rod is critical. If 
the brake booster to master cylinder push rod adjustment is too long, the

be low. Master Cylinder Gauge T87C-2500-A is required for accurate measurement

[FIGURE: H5799D.gif]

removal procedure. 

Position Master Cylinder Gauge T87C-2500-A on the end of the brake 
master cylinder. Loosen the set screw, and push the gauge plunger against the 
bottom of the brake master cylinder primary piston.

[FIGURE: H9232A.gif]

While holding the gauge in position, tighten the set screw. 

Invert Master Cylinder Gauge T87C-2500-A and place it over the brake 
booster to master cylinder push rod. 

Check the clearance between the end of the gauge and the brake booster 
to master cylinder push rod. 

If the clearance is not zero, loosen the brake booster to master 
cylinder push rod locknut and adjust the brake booster to master cylinder push 
rod. 

Install the brake master cylinder. Refer to Section 06-06 for the 
installation procedure.

After the brake master cylinder is installed, the brake booster to 
master cylinder push rod clearance should be as follows:

No vacuum — 0mm (0 inch)

500 mm-Hg vacuum — 0.1-0.4mm (0.004- 0.016 inch)

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Booster, Power

The power brake booster (2005) reduces the effort required to push the 
brake pedal (2455) and apply the brakes. Power assist is affected by a 
pressure differential within the power brake booster. When the engine (6007) 
is running with the brakes released, engine vacuum is present on both sides of 
a diaphragm within the power brake booster. As the brake pedal is pressed, a 
valve rod and plunger assembly moves forward within a power piston until a 
vacuum port is closed. At this point, vacuum is still applied to both sides of 
the diaphragm. As the valve rod and plunger assembly continues to move 
forward, an atmospheric port is opened. Atmospheric pressure then enters the 
rear half of the power brake booster. Engine vacuum on the front half of the 
diaphragm and atmospheric pressure on the rear side of the diaphragm assist 
the valve rod and plunger assembly in pushing the diaphragm plate forward. 
This movement forces the power brake booster-to-master cylinder push rod 
against the master cylinder piston. 

If the brake pedal is held depressed, the diaphragm will momentarily 
continue to move forward to compress the outer edges of a reaction disc. This 
movement causes the center of the reaction disc to press the valve rod and 
plunger assembly back and close the vacuum port or the atmospheric port, 
depending on whether the brake pedal is released or depressed further.

A vacuum booster hose (2A047) between the engine and power brake 
booster contains an internal brake booster check valve. This valve closes when 
the engine is shut off or under a low manifold vacuum situation, trapping 
vacuum in the power brake booster. This reserve vacuum allows several power 
assisted applications of the brakes, even without the engine running.

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Master Cylinder

The brake master cylinder (2140) is a tandem hydraulic servo. When the 
brake pedal (2455) is pressed, the brake master cylinder distributes 
pressurized brake fluid through steel brake tubes to the hydraulic anti-lock 
actuator assembly ports. The primary circuit of the brake master cylinder 
supplies brake fluid to the left front and right rear wheels. The secondary 
circuit supplies the right front and left rear wheels. The top portion of the 
brake master cylinder is a brake fluid reservoir.

================================================================================
PAGE 2677
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Control Valve, Brake Pressure

A brake pressure control valve (2B091) is installed in the system to 
balance front-to-rear brake application. The brake pressure control valve 
reduces hydraulic pressure to the rear wheel cylinders (2261) to prevent rear 
wheel lockup. Internally, the brake pressure control valve contains plungers 
that are shifted by hydraulic pressure to limit the output pressure to the 
rear wheels.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Master Cylinder and Brake Fluid Level Switch

If brake fluid is lost from any circuit, a brake fluid level switch in 
the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) will illuminate a brake system 
warning indicator in the instrument cluster. The brake system warning 
indicator comes on when a float in the brake master cylinder reservoir drops 
below a specified level and completes the circuit. Once the circuit is closed, 
the brake system warning indicator will come on and remain on whenever the 
ignition switch (11572) is in the ON or START position.

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hydraulic Anti-Lock Actuator Assembly

The hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly contains:

Motor

Two buffer chambers

Two damper chambers

Two pumps

Two inlet ports

Four outlet ports

Four flow control valves

Four solenoid valves

During normal braking, fluid from the brake master cylinder (2140) 
enters the two inlet ports located on the top of the hydraulic anti-lock 
actuator assembly. The fluid then passes through the normally open solenoid 
valves to each respective wheel location. If the anti-lock brake control 
module (2B373) senses that a wheel (1007) is about to lock, the anti-lock 
brake control module sends an electronic signal to close the flow control 
valve of the affected circuit. This action regulates the brake fluid entering 
the affected brake circuit, preventing wheel lockup. If the anti-lock brake 
control module senses the affected wheel is continuing to decelerate, the 
anti-lock brake control module sends a signal to open the flow control valve 
in the affected circuit. This action reduces any pressure that is trapped 
between the flow control valve and the affected brake actuator. The brake 
fluid is returned back to the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478).

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Control Module, Anti-Lock Brake

The anti-lock braking system is controlled by the anti-lock brake 
control module (2B373). Located behind the LH side of the instrument panel 
(04320), the anti-lock brake control module receives wheel speed readings from 
each rear brake anti-lock sensor (2C190) and front brake anti-lock sensor 
(2C204), and uses this information to compare wheel speeds.

By continuously monitoring and comparing the rotational speed of each 
wheel, the anti-lock brake control module activates the anti-lock braking 
system only when it senses wheel lockup under severe braking conditions. The 
anti-lock brake control module decides which wheels' brakes need to be 
controlled, and sends the appropriate signals to the hydraulic anti-lock 
actuator assembly.

The anti-lock brake control module also has self-diagnostic 
capabilities and stores diagnostic trouble codes in its memory. If a 
diagnostic trouble code is present in the anti-lock brake module memory, the 
instrument panel anti-lock brake warning indicator will illuminate when the 
engine (6007) is running. Refer to Diagnosis 
and Testing in this section for diagnositc trouble code procedures.

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Sensor, Anti-Lock 

The anti-lock brake system uses two variable-reluctance front brake 
anti-lock sensors (2C204) and two variable reluctance rear brake anti-lock 
sensors (2C190) and front brake anti-lock sensor indicators (2C182) and rear 
brake anti-lock sensor indicators (2C189) to determine the rotational speed of 
each wheel (1007) . The anti-lock sensors operate on the magnetic induction 
principle. As the teeth on the brake anti-lock sensor indicator rotate past 
the stationary brake anti-lock sensor, a signal proportional to the speed of 
the rotation is generated and sent to the anti-lock brake control module 
(2B373) through a coaxial cable and shielded wiring. 

 Front 

The front brake anti-lock sensors are attached to the front wheel 
knuckles (3K186). The front brake anti-lock sensor indicators are pressed onto 
the outer ends of the front wheel driveshaft and joints (3B436). 

[FIGURE: H9222B.gif]

 Rear 

The rear brake anti-lock sensors are attached to the brake backing 
plates (2211). The rear brake anti-lock sensor indicators are pressed onto the 
inner hub of the brake drums (1126).

The rear brake anti-lock sensor produces electrical pulses by 
monitoring the rotation of the rear brake anti-lock sensor indicator.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Anti-Lock

The Anti-Lock Brake System (ABS) functions by releasing and applying 
fluid pressure to the front disc brake calipers (2B120) and rear wheel 
cylinders (2261) during special braking conditions. The ABS does not function 
under normal braking conditions, nor does it affect front-to-rear brake 
proportioning. When one or more wheels approach a slip condition, the ABS 
automatically senses the slip and activates the fluid pressure control 
function. 

Through its preprogramming, the anti-lock brake control module (2B373) 
decides which actuators need brake pressure modulation. Once the decision is 
made, the anti-lock brake control module sends appropriate signals to the 
solenoid valves located in the hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly. These 
solenoid valves allow adjoining flow control valves to modulate fluid 
pressure, resulting in a pressure reduction at the front disc brake calipers 
and rear wheel cylinders to prevent further lockup.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Electrical System 

The anti-lock brake system (ABS) consists of an anti-lock brake control 
module (2B373), hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly and anti-lock relay 
(2C013). These components work together with the rear brake anti-lock sensor 
(2C190), front brake anti-lock sensor (2C204), front brake anti-lock sensor 
indicator (2C182), rear brake anti-lock sensor indicator (2C189) and other 
brake system components to control braking. 

The hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly consists of four solenoids 
which control hydraulic fluid flow to the disc brake calipers (2B120) and rear 
wheel cylinders (2261). The system has independent front wheel control and 
select low resistance rear wheel control. 

Front wheel control has two solenoids acting as individual channels. 
Each front wheel receives independent braking signals, depending on wheel 
speed. 

Rear wheel control has two solenoids acting as a single channel. The 
rear wheels receive the same braking signal, depending on the wheel with the 
lowest braking resistance. 

This is a four-solenoid, three-channel system. 

The anti-lock brake control module continuously calculates wheel speed 
and vehicle speed. The anti-lock brake control module activates the anti-lock 
brake system only when it senses wheel lockup under severe braking conditions. 
If the anti-lock brake control module senses wheel lockup, it sends a pressure 
reduction signal through the anti-lock relay to the hydraulic anti-lock 
actuator assembly. The solenoid controls the flow of hydraulic fluid into a 
buffer chamber located in the hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly. 

When the wheel is no longer in danger of lockup, the anti-lock brake 
control module sends pressure increase signals through the anti-lock relay to 
the hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly. One signal tells the solenoid to 
allow hydraulic fluid pressure to increase while the other signal activates 
the pump motor to further increase pressure by returning fluid from the buffer 
chamber. This operation continues for all wheels until the wheels are no 
longer in danger of lockup. 

A fail-safe function is programmed into the anti-lock brake control 
module that reverts the system to normal braking if a malfunction is detected. 
A self-diagnosis function checks for problems within the ABS.The anti-lock 
brake control module stores diagnostic trouble codes in its memory to aid the 
technician in diagnosing problems. The anti-lock brake warning indicator is 
illuminated while the engine (6007) is on to notify the driver of a present 
failure. 

The anti-lock brake control module system performs the following 
functions: 

Calculates wheel speeds 

Estimates vehicle speed 

Senses wheel lockup 

Activates ABS

Utilizes self-diagnosis and fail-safe functions 

Stores diagnostic trouble codes in memory

================================================================================
PAGE 2684
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

System Relays

The anti-lock brake control module (2B373) controls the operation of the 
anti-lock relay (2C013). 

The anti-lock relay is grounded by the anti-lock brake control module 
to power up the system. The anti-lock brake control module consists of the 
fail-safe relay and the motor relay. The fail-safe relay inhibits solenoid 
operation and turns the anti-lock brake warning indicator on and off. The 
motor relay controls pump motor operation.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Inspection and Verification — Anti-Lock Brake System

 NOTE: Look for problems in other areas that may affect the ABS (suspension 
and steering components, tire integrity and air pressure, wheel bearings, and 
brake components that are common to all brake systems). 

Verify concern by driving the vehicle.

If all systems and components are satisfactory, proceed with the visual 
inspection and then proceed to the Symptom Chart . 

 NOTE: The hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly is not serviceable nor can it 
be pressure checked. If any of its components fail, it must be replaced as a 
complete unit. 

Visually inspect the following components of the anti-lock brake system 
(ABS):

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

 Warning Lamp Indicators 

The anti-lock brake warning indicator will come on to warn the driver 
of an ABS failure. Normal brake system operation will still be available. 
However, the wheels will lock up under hard stop.

 On-Board Diagnostics 

This diagnostic procedure is used only on Aspire vehicles equipped with 
an anti-lock brake system (ABS). The Quick Test procedure should be used only 
when diagnosing ABS symptoms. 

On-board diagnostics are divided into two specialized tests: the Key 
ON-Engine Running Test and the Continuous Test. Prior to performing either 
test, an inspection of the anti-lock brake warning indicator is required to 
determine if a fault has been detected by the anti-lock brake control module 
or if the system is operating normally. When the ABS is operating normally, 
the anti-lock brake warning indicator will illuminate during the Key ON-Engine 
Off and go off after the engine has started. If the anti-lock brake warning 
indicator stays on after the engine starts, this indicates a present failure. 
The logic circuit could keep the warning indicator on for up to 60 seconds 
after the engine starts. Failure codes are stored in the anti-lock brake 
control module until they are erased. 

 Diagnostic Codes, Retrieving 

When directed to a Pinpoint Test, look carefully at the schematic. Any 
time a repair is made, erase the anti-lock brake control module memory and 
repeat the Quick Test to ensure that the repair was effective. If all phases 
of the Quick Test result in a pass, it is likely that the problem is 
non-electronic related. Refer to Section 06-00 to diagnose non-electronic 
related problems. 

ABS diagnostic trouble codes may be retrieved using the following 
methods: 

Identifying voltage fluctuations on an analog voltmeter. 

The Rotunda New Generation Star (NGS) Tester 007-00500 or equivalent 
can be used to retrieve codes.

Reading a digital or audible code from a Rotunda Super STAR II Tester 
007-0041B using Rotunda Super MECS Adapter 007-00052 or equivalent. 

Identifying flashes of the anti-lock brake warning indicator. 

The test connector available for obtaining diagnostic trouble codes is 
the data link connector (DLC) located near the battery.

The diagnostic trouble codes may indicate different failures, and 
departing from the Quick Test procedure may result in code identification 
error. Therefore, it is recommended that the Quick Test procedure be followed 
in its entirety. Anti-lock brake warning indicator mode inspection and ABS 
diagnostic trouble code retrieval are covered in the Quick Test.

There are two tests used to retrieve codes. They are the Key ON-Engine 
Running (KOER) Test and the Continuous Test. These tests are described in the 
following steps:

The Key ON-Engine Running Test checks the anti-lock brake control 
module and system circuitry by testing its integrity and processing 
capability, and verifies that the various sensors and actuators are connected 
and operating properly. Code patterns will be retrieved through the DLC, and 
the anti-lock brake warning indicator will indicate the type of failure.

 NOTE: Remember to watch the analog VOM, Super STAR II, NGS Tester, and 
anti-lock brake warning indicator for any change which will indicate where the 
intermittent is located. 

The Continuous Test is intended as an aid in diagnosing intermittent 
failures in the ABS. It is identical to the Key ON-Engine Running Test, but 
also allows the technician to attempt to recreate an intermittent failure by 
tapping, moving, and wiggling the harness and/or suspected sensor. Faults will 
be indicated by diagnostic trouble codes using an analog VOM, Super STAR II 
Tester or NGS Tester. With the knowledge of the affected circuits, a close 
check of the harness and associated connectors can be made.

 Diagnostic Trouble Codes, Erasing 

 NOTE: 

The anti-lock brake warning indicator should illuminate while 
performing the memory cancel. 

When the memory cancel operation is completed, the anti-lock brake 
warning indicator should illuminate for 2-3 seconds, then go off. 

After the memory cancel, the anti-lock brake control module performs 
self-diagnosis. 

Memory is not canceled by disconnecting the battery (10655). 

Memory codes cannot be canceled if the following occur: 

Intervals for depressing the brake pedal exceed one (1) second. 

Brake on/off (BOO) switch has malfunctioned. 

If using an analog VOM, be sure to remove the jumper wire from the data 
link connector after all checks and repairs are made.

Two methods can be used to erase diagnostic trouble codes. One uses an 
analog VOM, the other uses the Super STAR II Tester or NGS Tester. These 
methods are described below.

 Method A 

Using an analog VOM, perform the following:

Connect pins "TBS" and "GND" at the data link connector with jumper 
wire. 

[FIGURE: H9217B.gif]

Key ON. 

Output diagnostic trouble codes using the analog VOM. 

After the first code is repeated, depress the brake pedal 10 times at 
intervals of less than one (1) second. 

Key OFF. 

Disconnect the jumper wire at the data link connector.

 Method B 

Using the Super STAR II Tester or NGS Tester, perform the following:

Connect the Super STAR II Tester to the data link connector with Super 
MECS Adapter 007-00052 or the NGS Tester. 

Key ON. 

Output diagnostic trouble codes using the Super STAR II Tester or NGS 
Tester. 

After the first code is repeated, depress the brake pedal 10 times at 
intervals of less than one (1) second. 

Key OFF. 

Disconnect the Super STAR II Tester or NGS Tester from the data link 
connector.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Pinpoint Tests 

Do not perform any of the following Pinpoint Tests unless you are 
instructed to by a Quick Test. Each Pinpoint Test assumes that a fault has 
been detected in the system with direction to enter a specific repair routine. 
Doing any Pinpoint Test without direction from the Quick Test may produce 
incorrect results and replacement of non-defective components. Correct test 
results for the Quick Test are dependent on the proper operation of related 
components/systems. Refer to Section 06-00 . It may be necessary to correct any 
defects in these areas before passing the Quick Test. 

Do not replace any parts unless the test results indicate they should 
be replaced. 

When more than one diagnostic trouble code is received, always start 
service with the first code received. 

Do not measure voltage or resistance at the anti-lock brake control 
module (2B373) or connect any test lamps to it, unless otherwise specified. 

Isolate both ends of a circuit, and turn key OFF whenever checking for 
shorts or continuity unless otherwise specified. 

Disconnect solenoids and switches from the harness before measuring for 
continuity, resistance, or energizing by way of 12 volt source. 

In using the Pinpoint Tests, follow each step in order, starting from 
the first step in the appropriate test. Follow each step until the fault is 
found. 

After completing any repairs to the ABS, verify that all components are 
properly reconnected and repeat the functional Quick Test (Retest).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Hydraulic Anti-Lock Actuator Assembly

 Removal 

Remove the battery (10655). Refer to Section 14-01 for the removal 
procedure.

Remove the two hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly electrical 
connectors from the bracket.

Disconnect the hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly electrical 
connectors.

[FIGURE: H8702A.gif]

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash the surface 
with water. 

 NOTE: Note the routing of the brake tubes to ensure proper installation.

Remove the brake tube flare nuts from the hydraulic anti-lock actuator 
assembly.

Loosen the three hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly nuts.

[FIGURE: H8703A.gif]

Remove the hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly.

[FIGURE: H8704A.gif]

 Installation 

To install, reverse the removal procedure.

Tighten the three hydraulic anti-lock actuator assembly nuts to 19-22 Nm
 (14-16 lb-ft).

Tighten the brake tube flare nuts to 13-21 Nm (10-15

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Master Cylinder Reservoir Checking and Filling

Brake fluid level in the brake master cylinder reservoir (2K478) should 
be between 4mm (0.16 inch) below the MAX line on the side of the reservoir and 
the MAX line. If brake fluid is low, the brake system warning indicator will 
illuminate. To add brake fluid, clean and remove the cap and pour clean brake 
fluid into the top of the brake master cylinder reservoir. Fill to the 
specification mentioned above. Use Ford High Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid 
C6AZ-19542-AB or DOT 3 equivalent fluid meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M6C25-A. If brake fluid has to be added often, check all hydraulic 
connections for leaks.

Automatic Transaxle

The automatic transaxle combines an automatic transmission and 
differential into a single component designed for front wheel drive 
applications. The automatic transaxle is a hydraulically controlled unit and 
uses a torque converter (7902) equipped with a centrifugal type torque

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Transaxle Identification

The U.S. Motor Vehicle Theft Law Enforcement Act of 1984 requires 
identification of certain high theft vehicles to reduce the National Auto 
Theft Rate. This federal law requires Ford Motor Company to affix the Vehicle 
Identification Number (VIN) on specific parts. These body parts are the 
bumpers, front fenders (16006), hood (16612), front doors (20124), rear doors 
(24630), quarter panels and liftgate. The other affected components are engine 
(6007) and transaxles. In addition, the service replacement parts must be 
identified as service parts.

The production vehicle parts are identified by an adhesive backed white 
label approximately 2 3/16 inches long by 5/8 inch wide. Printed on this label 
is the VIN number and Ford logo. The service parts are identified by a similar 
label approximately 2 3/4 inches long and 5/8 inch wide. Printed on this label 
is the letter R and the Ford logo. Other information on this label is printed 
in gray lettering.

In the event of collision damage not requiring part replacement or 
drivetrain service, the persons making the repair should take care not to 
damage or remove the labels, unless such action is reasonably necessary in 
performing the repair.

The areas selected for the location of the production and service 
labels are unlikely to be affected during normal servicing and non-collision 
repairs.

PAGE 2705

1997 Aspire

Section 07-01: Transaxle, Automatic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Gear Shift Lever and Shift Patterns

The gearshift lever (7210) allows the driver to select any of six gear 
positions. These are:

 Park 

The PARK (P) position allows no powerflow through the transaxle and 
engages a parking pawl (7A441) into a parking gear which locks the output 
shaft (7060) into a fixed position, allowing no rotation of the wheels.

 Reverse 

The REVERSE (R) position allows the vehicle to be operated in a 
rearward direction at a reduced gear ratio. The internal operation is as 
follows:

The direct clutch locks the turbine shaft (7F351) to the sun gear 
driving it clockwise.

The low/reverse clutch holds the rear carrier causing the rear planet 
pinion gears to rotate counterclockwise.

This rotates the rear internal ring gear counterclockwise driving the 
output gear counterclockwise.

These actions provide a gear ratio of 2.4:1 at the output gear.

 Neutral 

The NEUTRAL (N) position allows no powerflow through the transaxle and 
allows the wheels to rotate freely.

 Drive 

 NOTE: In D position first gear, the one-way clutch holds the rear planet 
carrier stationary only on acceleration and allows the carrier to freewheel 
during deceleration. This prevents engine braking from occurring in D position 
first gear.

In the DRIVE (D) position the automatic transaxle upshifts and 
downshifts as determined by road speed and engine load signals sent to the 
main control valve body. Internal transaxle operation is as follows:

D position first gear:

The forward clutch locks the front internal ring gear which drives the 
front planet carrier clockwise.

This drives the sun gear counterclockwise.

The low one-way clutch holds the rear planet carrier stationary 
causing the rear planet pinion gears to rotate clockwise.

This drives the rear ring gear and output gear clockwise.

These actions provide a gear ratio of 2.841:1 at the output gear.

D position second gear:

The forward clutch locks the turbine shaft to the front ring gear, 
driving it clockwise.

The intermediate band holds the sun gear stationary. This forces the 
front planet carrier to rotate around the fixed sun gear clockwise, driving 
the output gear clockwise.

These actions provide a gear ratio of 1.541:1 at the output shaft.

D position third gear:

The forward clutch locks the turbine shaft to the front ring gear, 
driving it clockwise.

The direct clutch locks the sun gear to the forward clutch housing, 
driving the sun gear clockwise at turbine shaft speed.

With two planetary members being driven in the same direction at the 
same speed the entire gearset rotates clockwise at turbine shaft speed.

This provides a gear ratio of 1:1 at the output gear.

 Second 

In the SECOND (2) position the transaxle will start out from a stop in 
second gear. No upshifts or downshifts will occur without manually moving the 
gearshift lever. This allows the transaxle to provide better traction, with 
minimum wheel spin, when the vehicle is operated on slippery surfaces such as 
mud or snow. Operation of the internal transaxle components in 2 position 
second gear is the same as in D position second gear.

 Manual Low 

 NOTE: Because the low/reverse clutch holds the rear planet carrier stationary 
during both acceleration and deceleration, engine braking will occur in 
,MANUAL LOW (1) position first gear.

In the MANUAL LOW (1) position first gear, no upshifts can occur. 
Internal operation is as follows:

The forward clutch locks the front internal ring gear which drives the 
front planet carrier clockwise.

This drives the sun gear counterclockwise.

The low/reverse clutch holds the rear planet carrier causing the rear 
planet pinion gears to rotate clockwise.

These drive the rear internal ring gear and output gear clockwise.

These actions provide a gear ratio of 2.841:1 at the output gear.

Section 07-01: Transaxle, Automatic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Torque Converter

The torque converter (7902) automatically couples the transaxle to the 
engine (6007) at engine speeds above idle. At high loads and low road speeds 
the torque converter also multiplies engine torque. The following components 
make up the torque converter.

 Converter Cover 

The converter cover bolts to the engine's flywheel (6375) and encloses 
the other torque converter components.

 Turbine 

The turbine splines to the turbine shaft (7F351). Fluid motion from the 
impeller causes the turbine to rotate allowing the transfer of power from the 
engine to the transaxle. At engine idle fluid motion is not great enough to 
overcome vehicle weight, so the engine can idle without having to place the 
transaxle in NEUTRAL (N).

 Impeller 

The impeller connects to the converter cover and throws transmission 
fluid against the turbine, causing turbine rotation.

 Reactor 

The reactor redirects fluid returning from the turbine to the impeller. 
This not only improves fluid flow, but also multiplies the torque the turbine 
is driven with.

================================================================================
PAGE 2707
================================================================================
1997 Aspire

Section 07-01: Transaxle, Automatic

1997 Aspire Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Geartrain

The control of the planetary geartrain provides the transaxle with 
three forward gears and reverse. The geartrain is a Simpson Compound planetary 
gearset which consists of two planet carriers (front and rear), two ring gears 
(7A153) (front and rear) and a common sun gear.

The gearset is controlled using three multi-disc clutches (direct, 
forward, and low/reverse), a band (intermediate band), and a one-way roller 
clutch (low one-way clutch).

Rear Planet Carrier

 Direct Clutch 

The direct clutch is a multi-disc clutch that couples the turbine shaft 
(7F351) to the front sun gear during operation of third gear and reverse.

 Forward Clutch 

The forward clutch is a multi-disc clutch that couples the turbine 
shaft to the front ring gear in first, second, and third gear.

 Sun Gear and Sun Shell 

The sun gear and sun shell connect the front planetary gearset to the 
rear planetary gearset. It is either driven by the direct clutch or held by 
the intermediate band.

 Low One-Way Clutch 

The low one-way clutch holds the rear planet carrier to the transaxle 
case in DRIVE (D) position first gear during acceleration. During deceleration 
it overruns allowing the vehicle to coast without engine braking.

 Intermediate Band 

The intermediate band wraps around the direct clutch drum and holds it 
and the sun gear stationary to the transaxle case in second gear.

 Planet Carrier 

The two planet carriers are located on either side of the common sun 
gear which connects them. They carry the pinion gears which are surrounded by 
ring gears. The front planet (7A398) splines to the output shaft (7060) and is 
the output from the front planetary gearset. The rear planet carrier can be 
held by either the one-way clutch (7A089) or the low/reverse clutch.

 Low/Reverse Clutch 

The low/reverse clutch holds the rear planet carrier stationary to the 
transaxle case. It is the holding device for reverse and provides for engine 
braking in MANUAL LOW (1) position first gear.

 Park Gear and Parking Pawl 

The park gear (7A233) attaches to the output gear and locks the output 
gear to the transaxle case. This is accomplished by a parking lever actuating 
rod (7A232) which presses the parking pawl (7A441) into the teeth of the park 
gear when the gearshift lever (7210) is placed in the PARK (P) position.

 Output Gear 

The output gear attaches to the output shaft and transfers power from 
the planetary gearset to the idler gear (7F475).

 Idler Gear 

The idler gear rides between the output gear and the differential ring 
gear. It is required because two external gears in mesh rotate in opposite 
directions. If the output gear connected directly to the differential ring 
gear, the ring gear would rotate backwards. The idler gear acts as the 
"middleman" and maintains the correct rotation.

 Differential Assembly 

The differential (4026) transfers power from the planetary gearset to 
the front wheel driveshaft and joints (3B436) and wheels. It allows for 
differences in wheel rotation speeds during cornering through the use of 
differential pinion gears (4215) and differential side gears (4236). The 
differential also provides the final gear reduction from the transaxle. The 
ratio it provides is 3.63:1.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hydraulic System

The hydraulic system controls the application of the multi-disc 
clutches and intermediate band, and also provides lubrication and cooling for 
the transaxle and torque converter (7902).

 Main Control Valve Body 

Fluid is directed to the various components at the correct pressures 
through the main control valve body (7A100). The main control valve body 
receives information on vehicle operating requirements from the governor 
(7C053), vacuum throttle valve diaphragm (7A377) (modulator), and kickdown 
solenoid. It interprets this information and selects the optimum operating 
configuration for the transaxle.

 Oil Pump 

The transaxle uses a positive displacement gear and crescent type oil 
pump. It is located at the rear of the transaxle, and is driven by a oil pump 
shaft (7B328) connected to the torque converter cover. Fluid output from the 
oil pump is controlled through the use of a pressure regulator valve.

 Governor 

The governor is a centrifugal type, and is driven by the governor drive 
gear located on the drum hub assembly. The governor sends road speed 
information to the main control valve body for use in determining shift 
strategy.

 Intermediate Servo 

The servo piston is a hydraulic piston connected to a rod. When the 
servo piston is actuated it forces the rod against the end of the intermediate 
band causing the intermediate band to hold the direct clutch and front sun 
gear stationary to the transaxle case.

 Vacuum Throttle Valve Diaphragm 

The vacuum throttle valve diaphragm regulates the position of the 
vacuum throttle valve. As engine vacuum changes the diaphragm within the 
vacuum throttle valve diaphragm moves the vacuum throttle valve diaphragm. As 
the vacuum throttle valve diaphragm moves, the vacuum throttle valve within the 
main control valve body moves modifying the throttle valve pressure.

 Shift Strategies 

Automatic upshifts and downshifts will occur according to road speed 
and engine load. The governor valve, which is driven by the drive hub, senses 
road speed. The throttle valve, which is controlled by a vacuum throttle valve 
diaphragm, senses engine load.

When engine load is high and road speed low the transaxle will 
automatically delay upshifts. When road speed is higher and engine load lower, 
the transaxle will upshift early.

If a forced downshift is desired for passing, an electric kickdown 
solenoid which is connected from the accelerator pedal and shaft (9725) to the 
main control valve body will cause the transaxle to downshift to a lower gear.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Automatic Transaxle

The automatic transaxle diagnosis and testing procedures are in order 
of difficulty and probability. The diagnostic steps are used to determine the 
causes of the transaxle malfunctions and to provide corrective actions. 

Engine (6007) or driveline problems can affect transaxle performance; 
therefore, these systems should be serviced first to avoid incorrect or 
unnecessary repairs. Always make sure that proper safety precautions are used 
when performing any test or repair. 

The diagnosis and testing should be performed in the following sequence: 

 Inspection and Verification: provide easy 
inspection to detect obvious problems with the transaxle. 

 Transmission Fluid Level Check: is important in 
detecting problems with the transaxle. Refer to the Transmission 
Fluid Level Check in this section.

 Symptom Charts: provide a breakdown to relate 
customer concerns to possible faults. The Symptom Charts refer the technician 
to the following: Pinpoint Tests, Stall Test, Road Test, or removal and 
installation. However, for an unlisted symptom, follow the diagnosis and 
testing sequence to completion. 

 Pinpoint Tests: provide further evaluation of the 
downshift circuit, and the vacuum throttle valve diaphragm (7A377).

 Component Tests: provide the technician with the 
necessary tests to diagnose the transaxle. The Symptom Charts refer to the 
technician to the appropriate Component Test based on the vehicle's symptoms.
